# Z-index

> While not a part of the CoreUI for React.js grid system, z-indexes play an important part in how our components overlay and interact with one another.

Several CoreUI for React components utilize `z-index`, the CSS property that helps control layout by providing a third axis to arrange content. We utilize a default z-index scale in CoreUI for React that's been designed to properly layer navigation, tooltips and popovers, modals, and more.

These higher values start at an arbitrary number, high and specific enough to ideally avoid conflicts. We need a standard set of these across our layered components—tooltips, popovers, navbars, dropdowns, modals—so we can be reasonably consistent in the behaviors. There's no reason we couldn't have used `100`+ or `500`+.

We don't encourage customization of these individual values; should you change one, you likely need to change them all.

```scss
$zindex-levels: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$zindex-levels: defaults(
  (
    n1: -1,
    0: 0,
    1: 1,
    2: 2,
    3: 3,
    dropdown: 1000,
    menu: 1000,
    sticky: 1020,
    fixed: 1030,
    sidebar-backdrop: 1034,
    sidebar: 1035,
    offcanvas: 1045,
    drawer: 1045,
    modal: 1055,
    dialog: 1055,
    popover: 1070,
    tooltip: 1080,
    toast: 1090
  ),
  $zindex-levels
);
```

Every layer above is also a [`z-index` utility](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/z-index/#overlays) — `.z-modal`, `.z-tooltip` and so on — so an element of your own can join a layer by name rather than by repeating its number.

To handle overlapping borders within components — buttons and inputs in input groups, pages in pagination — we use low single-digit values that raise the element you are interacting with above its siblings, so its border and focus ring are drawn whole instead of being clipped by the neighbor. The default state sets no `z-index` at all; from there the scale is `1` for `:hover`, `2` for `.active`, and `3` for `:focus-visible`. Focus sits highest because a focused element is the one in the user's attention, and its ring has to be fully visible.


---

# CSS Grid

> Learn how to enable, use, and customize our alternate layout system built on CSS Grid with examples and code snippets.

The CoreUI for React.js default grid system represents the culmination of over a decade of CSS layout techniques, tried and tested by millions of people. But, it was also created without many of the modern CSS features and techniques we're seeing in browsers like the new CSS Grid.

> **The CSS Grid system ships enabled as of v6.** Its responsive classes are powered by
> [container queries](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/container-queries/), so a `.grid` responds to its own
> width rather than to the viewport. Set `$enable-cssgrid: false` to leave it out of
> your build.

## How it works

With CoreUI, we've added the option to enable a separate grid system that's built on CSS Grid, but with a CoreUI twist. You still get classes you can apply on a whim to build responsive layouts, but with a different approach under the hood.

- **Both grid systems ship.** They are independent: set `$enable-grid-classes: false` to drop the default flexbox grid, or `$enable-cssgrid: false` to drop this one, then recompile your Sass.

- **Replace instances of `.row` with `.grid`.** The `.grid` class sets `display: grid` and creates a `grid-template` that you build on with your HTML.

- **Replace `.col-*` classes with `.g-col-*` classes.** This is because our CSS Grid columns use the `grid-column` property instead of `width`.

- **Columns and gutter sizes are set via CSS variables.** Set these on the parent `.grid` and customize however you want, inline or in a stylesheet, with `--cui-columns` and `--cui-gap`.

- **Responsive classes use container queries.** Each `.grid` is a query container (`container-type: inline-size`), so responsive `.g-col-*` and `.g-start-*` classes respond to the width of the `.grid` itself rather than the viewport.

In the future, CoreUI will likely shift to a hybrid solution as the `gap` property has achieved nearly full browser support for flexbox.

## Key differences

Compared to the default grid system:

- Flex utilities don't affect the CSS Grid columns in the same way.

- Gaps replaces gutters. The `gap` property replaces the horizontal `padding` from our default grid system and functions more like `margin`.

- As such, unlike `.row`s, `.grid`s have no negative margins and margin utilities cannot be used to change the grid gutters. Grid gaps are applied horizontally and vertically by default. See the [customizing section](#customizing) for more details.

- Inline and custom styles should be viewed as replacements for modifier classes (e.g., `style="--cui-columns: 3;"` vs `class="row-cols-3"`).

- Nesting works similarly, except every `.grid` starts from the defaults rather than picking up the grid around it. See the [nesting section](#nesting) for details.

## Examples

### Three columns

Three equal-width columns across all container sizes and devices can be created by using the `.g-col-4` classes. Add [responsive classes](#responsive) to change the layout by the `.grid` container's width.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-4">.g-col-4</div>
  <div className="g-col-4">.g-col-4</div>
  <div className="g-col-4">.g-col-4</div>
</div>
```

### Responsive

Use responsive classes to adjust your layout across breakpoints. Here we start with two columns on the narrowest containers, and then grow to three columns on medium containers and above.

Responsive `.g-col-*` and `.g-start-*` classes are powered by [container queries](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries) rather than media queries. The `.grid` is a query container, so its items respond to the width of the `.grid` itself instead of the viewport — a `.grid` placed inside a narrow column switches layout based on that column's width, not on the size of the browser window.

> **`container-type` implies layout containment**, which makes every `.grid` the containing block for absolutely and fixed-positioned descendants. A `position: fixed` element inside a `.grid` is therefore positioned against the grid, not the viewport. Our own floating panels are unaffected — they render through a portal, outside the grid — but your own fixed markup needs to live outside it.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-6 g-col-md-4">.g-col-6 .g-col-md-4</div>
  <div className="g-col-6 g-col-md-4">.g-col-6 .g-col-md-4</div>
  <div className="g-col-6 g-col-md-4">.g-col-6 .g-col-md-4</div>
</div>
```

Compare that to this two column layout at all container sizes.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
</div>
```

## Wrapping

Grid items automatically wrap to the next line when there's no more room horizontally. Note that the `gap` applies to horizontal and vertical gaps between grid items.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>

  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
</div>
```

## Starts

Start classes aim to replace our default grid's offset classes, but they're not entirely the same. CSS Grid creates a grid template through styles that tell browsers to "start at this column" and "end at this column." Those properties are `grid-column-start` and `grid-column-end`. Start classes are shorthand for the former. Pair them with the column classes to size and align your columns however you need. Start classes begin at `1` as `0` is an invalid value for these properties.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-3 g-start-2">.g-col-3 .g-start-2</div>
  <div className="g-col-4 g-start-6">.g-col-4 .g-start-6</div>
</div>
```

## Auto columns

When there are no classes on the grid items (the immediate children of a `.grid`), each grid item will automatically be sized to one column.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
</div>
```

This behavior can be mixed with grid column classes.

```html
<div className="grid text-center">
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
  <div>1</div>
</div>
```

## Nesting

Similar to our default grid system, our CSS Grid allows for easy nesting of `.grid`s. Every `.grid` declares its own rows, columns and gap, so a nested one starts from the defaults no matter what the grid around it is set to. Consider the example below:

- We set three columns on the outer grid with `--cui-columns: 3`.
- The nested grid in the first auto-column takes the default twelve columns — the outer value does not reach it.
- The nested grid in the second auto-column is set to three columns of its own, matching its parent.
- The third auto-column has no nested content.

That independence is the point: a component built on `.grid` keeps its own layout wherever you drop it, instead of silently taking the column count of whatever contains it.

```html
<div className="grid text-center overflow-x-auto" style={{ '--cui-columns': '3' }}>
  <div>
    First auto-column
    <div className="grid">
      <div className="g-col-6">6 of 12</div>
      <div className="g-col-4">4 of 12</div>
      <div className="g-col-2">2 of 12</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div>
    Second auto-column
    <div className="grid" style={{ '--cui-columns': '3' }}>
      <div>Auto-column</div>
      <div>Auto-column</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <div>Third auto-column</div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

Customize the number of columns, the number of rows, and the width of the gaps with local CSS variables.

| Variable | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--cui-rows` | `1` | The number of rows in your grid template |
| `--cui-columns` | `12` | The number of columns in your grid template |
| `--cui-gap` | `1.5rem` | The size of the gap between columns (vertical and horizontal) |

Every `.grid` declares all three, so they show up in your browser's dev tools and each grid is self-contained. Set them on the `.grid` you want to change — inline, or in a stylesheet — and only that grid changes.

### No grid classes

Immediate children elements of `.grid` are grid items, so they'll be sized without explicitly adding a `.g-col` class.

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-columns': '3' }}>
  <div>Auto-column</div>
  <div>Auto-column</div>
  <div>Auto-column</div>
</div>
```

### Columns and gaps

Adjust the number of columns and the gap.

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-columns': '4', '--cui-gap': '5rem' }}>
  <div className="g-col-2">.g-col-2</div>
  <div className="g-col-2">.g-col-2</div>
</div>
```

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-columns': '10', '--cui-gap': '1rem' }}>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-4">.g-col-4</div>
</div>
```

### Adding rows

Adding more rows and changing the placement of columns:

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-rows': '3', '--cui-columns': '3' }}>
  <div>Auto-column</div>
  <div className="g-start-2" style={{ gridRow: '2' }}>Auto-column</div>
  <div className="g-start-3" style={{ gridRow: '3' }}>Auto-column</div>
</div>
```

### Gaps

Change the vertical gaps only by modifying the `row-gap`. Note that we use `gap` on `.grid`s, but `row-gap` and `column-gap` can be modified as needed.

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ rowGap: '0' }}>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>

  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
</div>
```

Because of that, you can have different vertical and horizontal `gap`s, which can take a single value (all sides) or a pair of values (vertical and horizontal). This can be applied with an inline style for `gap`, or with our `--cui-gap` CSS variable.

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-gap': '.25rem 1rem' }}>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>

  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
  <div className="g-col-6">.g-col-6</div>
</div>
```

### Sass

One limitation of the CSS Grid is that our default classes are still generated by two Sass variables, `$grid-columns` and `$grid-gutter-x`. This effectively predetermines the number of classes generated in our compiled CSS. You have two options here:

- Modify those default Sass variables and recompile your CSS.
- Use inline or custom styles to augment the provided classes.

For example, you can increase the column count and change the gap size, and then size your "columns" with a mix of inline styles and predefined CSS Grid column classes (e.g., `.g-col-4`).

```html
<div className="grid text-center" style={{ '--cui-columns': '18', '--cui-gap': '.5rem' }}>
  <div style={{ gridColumn: 'span 14' }}>14 columns</div>
  <div className="g-col-4">.g-col-4</div>
</div>
```

# Reboot

> Reboot, a collection of element-specific CSS changes in a single file, kickstart CoreUI for React to provide an elegant, consistent, and simple baseline to build upon.

## Approach

Reboot builds upon Normalize, providing many HTML elements with somewhat opinionated styles using only element selectors. Additional styling is done only with classes. For example, we reboot some `<table>` styles for a simpler baseline and later provide `.table`, `.table-bordered`, and more.

Here are our guidelines and reasons for choosing what to override in Reboot:

- Update some browser default values to use `rem`s instead of `em`s for scalable component spacing.
- Avoid `margin-top`. Vertical margins can collapse, yielding unexpected results. More importantly though, a single direction of `margin` is a simpler mental model.
- For easier scaling across device sizes, block elements should use `rem`s for `margin`s.
- Keep declarations of `font`-related properties to a minimum, using `inherit` whenever possible.

## CSS variables

_Added in 4.1.0._

With v4.1.0, we standardized our required `@import`s across all our CSS bundles (including `coreui.css`, `coreui-reboot.css`, and `coreui-grid.css` to include `_root.scss` . This adds `:root` level CSS variables to all bundles, regardless of how many of them are used in that bundle. Ultimately CoreUI will continue to see more CSS variables added over time.

Reboot styles bare HTML, so its variables live on `:root` rather than on a class — set any of them there, or on a subtree, to restyle the elements underneath:

```scss
$reboot-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-paragraph-margin-bottom: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-heading-margin-bottom: var(--cui-spacer-3),
    --cui-heading-font-family: inherit,
    --cui-heading-font-style: inherit,
    --cui-heading-font-weight: var(--cui-font-weight-medium),
    --cui-heading-line-height: 1.2,
    --cui-sub-sup-font-size: .75em,
    --cui-hr-margin-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-hr-color: inherit,
    --cui-hr-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-hr-opacity: .25,
    --cui-legend-margin-bottom: var(--cui-spacer-3),
    --cui-legend-font-size: clamp(1.275rem, 1.275rem + .3vw, 1.5rem),
    --cui-legend-font-weight: inherit,
    --cui-list-padding-x: 2rem,
    --cui-dt-font-weight: var(--cui-font-weight-bold),
    --cui-initialism-font-size: var(--cui-small-font-size),
    --cui-code-font-size: var(--cui-small-font-size),
    --cui-pre-color: inherit,
  ),
  $reboot-tokens
);
```

`<kbd>` carries its own, on the element:

```scss
$reboot-kbd-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-kbd-padding-y: .1875rem,
    --cui-kbd-padding-x: .375rem,
    --cui-kbd-font-size: var(--cui-small-font-size),
    --cui-kbd-color: var(--cui-bg-body),
    --cui-kbd-bg: var(--cui-fg-2),
    --cui-kbd-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-3),
  ),
  $reboot-kbd-tokens
);
```

The `<body>` rules show how a variable is consumed:

```scss
body {
  margin: 0; // 1
  font-family: var(--cui-body-font-family);
  font-size: var(--cui-body-font-size);
  font-weight: var(--cui-body-font-weight);
  line-height: var(--cui-body-line-height);
  color: var(--cui-fg-body);
  background-color: var(--cui-bg-body); // 2
  -webkit-text-size-adjust: 100%; // 3
  -webkit-tap-highlight-color: transparent; // 4
}
```

Which means the page can be restyled from the markup, with no recompile:

```html
<body style="--cui-body-color: #333; --cui-paragraph-margin-bottom: 1.5rem;">
  <!-- ... -->
</body>
```

## Page defaults

The `<html>` and `<body>` elements are updated to provide better page-wide defaults. More specifically:

- The `box-sizing` is globally set on every element—including `*::before` and `*::after`, to `border-box`. This ensures that the declared width of element is never exceeded due to padding or border.
  - No base `font-size` is declared on the `<html>`, but `16px` is assumed (the browser default). `font-size: 1rem` is applied on the `<body>` for easy responsive type-scaling via media queries while respecting user preferences and ensuring a more accessible approach. This browser default can be overridden by modifying the `$font-size-root` variable.
- The `<body>` also sets a global `font-family`, `font-weight`, `line-height`, and `color`. This is inherited later by some form elements to prevent font inconsistencies.
- For safety, the `<body>` has a declared `background-color`, defaulting to `#fff`.
- `accent-color` is set to `--cui-primary` on the root, so native controls that we do not restyle — a bare checkbox, radio, range or `<progress>` — are drawn in your brand color instead of the browser's blue.

## Links

Links take `--cui-link-color` and switch to `--cui-link-hover-color` on hover. Inside anything that sets a theme, both follow it: the link reads `--cui-theme-fg` and hovers to `--cui-theme-fg-emphasis`, so a link on a colored surface stays part of that surface. The underline sits `.2em` below the text through `--cui-link-underline-offset`, clearing descenders; the [`.underline-offset-*` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/link/#underline-offset) adjust it per link, and setting the token to `auto` restores the browser default.

Placeholder links — an `<a>` with neither `href` nor a class — keep the surrounding text color and get no underline, so an anchor waiting for its URL doesn't read as a working link.

```html
<p><a href="#">This is a link</a></p>
<p><a>This is a placeholder link</a></p>
```

## Native font stack

CoreUI for React utilizes a "native font stack" or "system font stack" for optimum text rendering on every device and OS. These system fonts have been designed specifically with today's devices in mind, with improved rendering on screens, variable font support, and more. Read more about [native font stacks in this *Smashing Magazine* article](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2015/11/using-system-ui-fonts-practical-guide/).

```scss
$font-family-sans-serif:
  // Cross-platform generic font family (default user interface font)
  system-ui,
  // Safari for macOS and iOS (San Francisco)
  -apple-system,
  // Windows
  "Segoe UI",
  // Android
  Roboto,
  // older macOS and iOS
  "Helvetica Neue"
  // Linux
  "Noto Sans",
  "Liberation Sans",
  // Basic web fallback
  Arial,
  // Sans serif fallback
  sans-serif,
  // Emoji fonts
  "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji", "Segoe UI Symbol", "Noto Color Emoji" !default;
```

Note that because the font stack includes emoji fonts, many common symbol/dingbat unicode characters will be rendered as multi-colored pictographs. Their appearance will vary, depending on the style used in the browser/platform's native emoji font, and they won't be affected by any CSS `color` styles.

This `font-family` is applied to the `<body>` and automatically inherited globally throughout Bootstrap. To switch the global `font-family`, update `$font-family-base` and recompile Bootstrap.

## Headings and paragraphs

All heading elements—e.g., `<h1>`—and `<p>` are reset to have their `margin-top` removed. Headings have `margin-bottom: .5rem` added and paragraphs `margin-bottom: 1rem` for easy spacing.

| Heading | Example |
| --- | --- |
| `<h1></h1>` | <span class="h1">h1. Bootstrap heading</span> |
| `<h2></h2>` | <span class="h2">h2. Bootstrap heading</span> |
| `<h3></h3>` | <span class="h3">h3. Bootstrap heading</span> |
| `<h4></h4>` | <span class="h4">h4. Bootstrap heading</span> |
| `<h5></h5>` | <span class="h5">h5. Bootstrap heading</span> |
| `<h6></h6>` | <span class="h6">h6. Bootstrap heading</span> |

## Horizontal rules

The `<hr />` element has been simplified. Similar to browser defaults, `<hr />`s are styled via `border-top`, have a default `opacity: .25`, and automatically inherit their `border-color` via `color`, including when `color` is set via the parent. They can be modified with text, border, and opacity utilities.

```html
<hr />

<div className="fg-success">
  <hr />
</div>

<hr className="border border-danger border-2 opacity-50" />
<hr className="border border-primary border-3 opacity-75" />
```

## Lists

All lists—`<ul>`, `<ol>`, and `<dl>`—have their `margin-top` removed and a `margin-bottom: 1rem`. Nested lists have no `margin-bottom`. We've also reset the `padding-left` on `<ul>` and `<ol>` elements.

For simpler styling, clear hierarchy, and better spacing, description lists have updated `margin`s. `<dd>`s reset `margin-left` to `0` and add `margin-bottom: .5rem`. `<dt>`s are **bolded**.

## Inline code

Wrap inline snippets of code with `<code>`. Be sure to escape HTML angle brackets.

```html
For example, <code>&lt;section&gt;</code> should be wrapped as inline.
```

## Code blocks

Use `<pre>`s for multiple lines of code. Once again, be sure to escape any angle brackets in the code for proper rendering. The `<pre>` element is reset to remove its `margin-top` and use `rem` units for its `margin-bottom`.

```html
<pre><code>&lt;p&gt;Sample text here...&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;And another line of sample text here...&lt;/p&gt;
</code></pre>
```

## Variables

For indicating variables use the `<var>` tag.

```html
<var>y</var> = <var>m</var><var>x</var> + <var>b</var>
```

## User input

Use the `<kbd>` to indicate input that is typically entered via keyboard.

```html
To switch directories, type <kbd>cd</kbd> followed by the name of the directory.<br />
To edit settings, press <kbd><kbd>ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>,</kbd></kbd>
```

## Sample output

For indicating sample output from a program use the `<samp>` tag.

```html
<samp>This text is meant to be treated as sample output from a computer program.</samp>
```

## Tables

Tables are slightly adjusted to style `<caption>`s, collapse borders, and ensure consistent `text-align` throughout. Additional changes for borders, padding, and more come with [the `.table` class](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/table/).

```html
<table>
  <caption>
    This is an example table, and this is its caption to describe the contents.
  </caption>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Table heading</th>
      <th>Table heading</th>
      <th>Table heading</th>
      <th>Table heading</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
      <td>Table cell</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

## Forms

Various form elements have been rebooted for simpler base styles. Here are some of the most notable changes:

- `<fieldset>`s have no borders, padding, or margin so they can be easily used as wrappers for individual inputs or groups of inputs.
- `<legend>`s, like fieldsets, have also been restyled to be displayed as a heading of sorts.
- `<label>`s are set to `display: inline-block` to allow `margin` to be applied.
- `<input />`s, `<select>`s, `<textarea>`s, and `<button>`s are mostly addressed by Normalize, but Reboot removes their `margin` and sets `line-height: inherit`, too.
- `<textarea>`s are modified to only be resizable vertically as horizontal resizing often "breaks" page layout.
- `<button>`s and `<input />` button elements have `cursor: pointer` when `:not(:disabled)`.

These changes, and more, are demonstrated below.

> ##### Date & color input support
> 
> Keep in mind date inputs are [not fully supported](https://caniuse.com/input-datetime) by all browsers, namely Safari.

Two more form resets worth knowing about:

- Every segment of a date or time input — including seconds, milliseconds, the week number and the AM/PM field — has its browser padding removed, so a `<input type="time" step="1">` is the same height as a text input.
- `tel`, `url`, `email` and `number` inputs stay left-to-right whatever the document direction is, because their content is not language text.

### Pointers on buttons

Reboot includes an enhancement for `role="button"` to change the default cursor to `pointer`. Add this attribute to elements to help indicate elements are interactive. This role isn't necessary for `<button>` elements, which get their own `cursor` change.

```html
<span role="button" tabIndex="0">Non-button element button</span>
```

## Misc elements

### Address

The `<address>` element is updated to reset the browser default `font-style` from `italic` to `normal`. `line-height` is also now inherited, and `margin-bottom: 1rem` has been added. `<address>`s are for presenting contact information for the nearest ancestor (or an entire body of work). Preserve formatting by ending lines with `<br />`.

### Blockquote

The default `margin` on blockquotes is `1em 40px`, so we reset that to `0 0 1rem` for something more consistent with other elements.

### Inline elements

The `<abbr>` element receives basic styling to make it stand out amongst paragraph text.

### Summary

The default `cursor` on summary is `text`, so we reset that to `pointer` to convey that the element can be interacted with by clicking on it.

## HTML5 `[hidden]` attribute

HTML5 adds [a new global attribute named `[hidden]`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/hidden), which is styled as `display: none` by default. Borrowing an idea from [PureCSS](https://purecss.io/), we improve upon this default by making `[hidden] { display: none !important; }` to help prevent its `display` from getting accidentally overridden.

```html
<input type="text" hidden>
```

> ##### jQuery incompatibility
> 
> `[hidden]` is not compatible with jQuery's `$(...).hide()` and `$(...).show()` methods. Therefore, we don't currently especially endorse `[hidden]` over other techniques for managing the `display` of elements.

To merely toggle the visibility of an element, meaning its `display` is not modified and the element can still affect the flow of the document, use [the `.invisible` class](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/visibility/) instead.

## iframe color-scheme

`<iframe>` is set to `color-scheme: light dark`, and its border is removed.

The reason is a browser safeguard rather than a style preference. When an embedded document's color scheme differs from the iframe element's, the browser paints an opaque canvas behind the frame — on a dark page, a white box. An embedded document cannot see your `data-coreui-theme` attribute; it follows the system preference. Pinning the iframe to the system preference too keeps the embed transparent, including on a page where you force a theme.

```html
<div data-coreui-theme="dark" className="bg-body fg-body p-4">
  <iframe className="w-100 border-0" style={{ colorScheme: 'unset' }} title="Default iframe" src="data:text/html,%3C!DOCTYPE%20html%3E%3Chtml%3E%3Cmeta%20name='color-scheme'%20content='light%20dark'%3E%3Cbody%20style='background-color:transparent;color:gray;'%3E%3Ch4%3EDefault%20iframe%3C/h4%3E%3C/body%3E%3C/html%3E"></iframe>
  <iframe className="w-100 border-0" title="iframe with color-scheme" src="data:text/html,%3C!DOCTYPE%20html%3E%3Chtml%3E%3Cmeta%20name='color-scheme'%20content='light%20dark'%3E%3Cbody%20style='background-color:transparent;color:gray;'%3E%3Ch4%3Eiframe%20with%20color-scheme:%20light%20dark%3C/h4%3E%3C/body%3E%3C/html%3E"></iframe>
  <iframe className="w-100 border-0" title="Embed that declares no color scheme" src="data:text/html,%3C!DOCTYPE%20html%3E%3Chtml%3E%3Cbody%20style='background-color:transparent;color:gray;'%3E%3Ch4%3EEmbed%20that%20declares%20no%20color%20scheme%3C/h4%3E%3C/body%3E%3C/html%3E"></iframe>
</div>
```

The first two embeds declare `<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark">`, so they follow the system preference and stay transparent. The third declares nothing, which is what most third-party embeds do — set your system to dark mode and the browser paints a white box behind it.

### Third-party embeds with no dark mode

Payment buttons, comment widgets and review widgets often ship light-only. The white background the browser paints behind them in dark mode is deliberate: it keeps the embed's own light content readable, and no stylesheet of ours can remove it.

Pin that one frame to light instead, so the browser has no mismatch to guard against:

```html
<iframe style="color-scheme: light" src="..."></iframe>
```

> Use this only for an embed that has no dark mode. Safari and Firefox pass the value into the embedded document, so an embed that *does* have a dark mode will be forced into its light one.

# React Autocomplete Component

> Build powerful React Autocomplete components with dynamic search, dropdown suggestions, and external data integration. The ultimate React Autocomplete solution for modern web applications.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Overview

The React Autocomplete Component is a powerful, feature-rich autocomplete solution that enhances form usability by providing intelligent suggestions as user types. Whether you're building a React autocomplete with static array data, fetching data from APIs, or implementing complex search logic, this autocomplete component delivers a smooth, accessible user experience with extensive customization options.

Key features of this React Autocomplete include:
- Dynamic dropdown suggestions with real time filtering
- External data integration with API support
- Customizable templates and custom styles
- Advanced search capabilities
- Performance optimization with virtual scrolling
- Accessibility-first design

## Basic example

A straightforward demonstration of how to implement a basic autocomplete input field, highlighting essential attributes and configurations.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteBasicExample = () => {
  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      cleaner
      highlightOptionsOnSearch
      indicator
      defaultValue="Bootstrap"
      label="Framework"
      options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
      placeholder="Search technologies..."
      searchNoResultsLabel="No results found"
      showHints
      text="Start typing to search option or provide value"
    />
  )
}
```

You can also use objects with `option` property for more structured data:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteBasic2Example = () => {
  const options = [
    {
      label: 'Angular',
      value: 1,
    },
    {
      label: 'Bootstrap',
      value: 2,
    },
    {
      label: 'Next.js',
      value: 3,
    },
    {
      label: 'React.js',
      value: 4,
    },
    {
      label: 'Vue.js',
      value: 5,
    },
  ]

  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      cleaner
      highlightOptionsOnSearch
      indicator
      defaultValue={4}
      label="Framework"
      options={options}
      placeholder="Search technologies..."
      searchNoResultsLabel="No results found"
      showHints
      text="Start typing to search option or provide value"
    />
  )
}
```

For a minimal implementation without additional features:

```jsx
<CAutocomplete
  label="Framework"
  options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
  placeholder="Search technologies..."
  text="Start typing to search option or provide value"
/>
```

## With form field

Wrap the control in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) to lay it out with its label and description, and to get validation feedback in the right place.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CFormLabel, CFormText } from '@coreui/react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteFormFieldExample = () => {
  return (
    <CFormField>
      <CFormLabel htmlFor="autocompleteField">Framework</CFormLabel>
      <CAutocomplete
        id="autocompleteField"
        name="framework"
        options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
        placeholder="Search frameworks..."
      />
      <CFormText>Start typing to filter the list.</CFormText>
    </CFormField>
  )
}
```

Inside a `<form>`, <kbd>Enter</kbd> with the list closed submits the form. A form reset brings an uncontrolled autocomplete back to its `defaultValue` or the first option marked `selected`, or to the text of `defaultInputValue` (an empty field without it), and reports a changed selection through `onChange`. A controlled autocomplete asks for the `value` it started with through `onChange` and shows the label of its current `value` until you take it, or the text of `defaultInputValue` when `value` selects nothing. A reset that a listener cancels changes nothing.

## Search functionality

The field filters the options as the user types.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteSearchExample = () => {
  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
      placeholder="Search technologies..."
    />
  )
}
```

### Where typing goes

Typing reaches the field from anywhere in the component — the picker button, the options panel — so a keystroke never depends on where the focus happens to be. The space bar and keyboard shortcuts stay with whatever has the focus.

Set `globalSearch={false}` to keep typing local: a keystroke then counts only while the field has the focus.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteSearchLocalExample = () => {
  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      globalSearch={false}
      options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
      pickerIcon
      placeholder="Typing stays local..."
    />
  )
}
```

### External search

When external search is enabled (`search="external"`), the component delegates search operations to your custom logic or external API. This is perfect for server-side filtering, complex search algorithms, or third-party search services:

```jsx
<CAutocomplete 
  options={filteredOptions} 
  onInput={handleSearch} 
  search="external" 
/>
```

See the [External Data](#external-data) section for a complete working example.

## Restricted selection

Limit users to only select from the provided options by enabling `allowOnlyDefinedOptions`. This prevents custom value entry:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteRestrictedSelectionExample = () => {
  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      allowOnlyDefinedOptions
      options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
      placeholder="Only predefined options allowed..."
    />
  )
}
```

Text that names no option a user can select is cleared when the field loses focus, unless it is the label of the current selection, and <kbd>Enter</kbd> does not submit the form while the field holds it.

## Floating labels

Set `floatingLabel` and the component renders the label itself — no wrapper markup needed — and the text also becomes the field's accessible name; the component's own `placeholder` is hidden while the label rests inside the field, so the two never overlap.

```html

  <CAutocomplete
    floatingLabel="Framework"

    options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}

  />

```

Set `floatingLabelAlways` to keep the label [always floating](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/floating-labels/#always-floating) with the placeholder showing.

## Validation

The text input carries the value, so `required` blocks the submit of an empty field and the browser shows its message over the input. The state shows on the frame as the `.is-*` class, and while it is `'invalid'` the input carries `aria-invalid="true"` and is described by the message after the frame.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete, CButton, CForm } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteValidationExample = () => {
  const [countryState, setCountryState] = useState<string | undefined>('invalid')

  return (
    <CForm className="row g-4" noValidate validate>
      <div className="col-md-6">
        <CAutocomplete
          allowOnlyDefinedOptions
          feedbackInvalid="Pick a framework from the list."
          id="validationFramework"
          label="Framework"
          name="framework"
          options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
          placeholder="Search frameworks..."
          required
        />
      </div>
      <div className="col-md-6">
        <CAutocomplete
          defaultValue="Spain"
          feedback="We do not ship to Spain yet."
          id="validationCountry"
          label="Shipping country"
          name="country"
          onValidationStateChange={setCountryState}
          options={['Germany', 'Poland', 'Spain']}
          validationState={countryState}
        />
      </div>
      <div className="col-12">
        <CButton color="primary" type="submit">
          Submit
        </CButton>
      </div>
    </CForm>
  )
}
```

The state comes from three places, in this order:

- `validationState`: `'valid'`, `'invalid'` or a state you added to `$form-validation-states`. The `invalid` and `valid` props still work as deprecated aliases; `invalid` wins when both are set, and both are ignored once `validationState` is set. While it is set, the component draws it instead of what the browser reports. While it is `'invalid'`, the input blocks the submit with the text of the linked message, or `Invalid value.` when there is none, unless the component is `disabled` or `readOnly`.
- A validation that reports the input invalid: a submit, `checkValidity()` or `reportValidity()`, which [`CForm`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/validation/) and the stepper call as well. From then on the frame and the input show it invalid whenever the value is invalid, until the form is reset, and the message after the frame shows.
- In a form with `validate`, the `:user-invalid` state of the input, and with `validate="valid"` also its `:user-valid` state.

A state you give is a verdict on the value it was given for. When the user changes the text, or the form is reset, the component calls `onValidationStateChange(undefined)`; pass your state setter there to drop the state, as the second field above does. The text changes by typing, by a pick of an option whose label differs from the text, letter case included, by the cleaner, by <kbd>Backspace</kbd> or <kbd>Delete</kbd> that removes text from the selected option, and with `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` by leaving the field with text no option matches. One action asks once, before `onChange`, so a state you set from `onChange` while the action runs stays. A change your code makes through `value` or `options` keeps the state, and so does an action that leaves the text as it was, such as picking an option whose label is exactly the text or <kbd>Enter</kbd> on text that names no option. While the field is invalid, the input is also described by an `.invalid-feedback` you render after it yourself. A reset asks once it has run, so a state you set from a `reset` listener on the form gets the same call, and your handler decides whether to drop it. A native reset of the form puts back the selection given by `defaultValue` or the options' `selected`, and leaves a controlled `value` to you. An `aria-invalid` passed to the component is ignored: set `validationState` instead.

## Disabled

Disable the component to prevent user interaction. A group given with `disabled: true` disables every option in it; a plain string option inside it reaches your templates and callbacks as `{ label, value, disabled: true }`. A disabled option keeps the user out, not your code: `value`, `defaultValue` or an option marked `selected` still selects it, and a form reset brings it back.

```html

    <CAutocomplete
      disabled
      options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
      placeholder="Disabled autocomplete..."
    />
  )
}
```

## Cleaner functionality

Set `cleaner` for a button that empties the field, the selection and the text. It shows while an option is selected and, unless `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` is set, while the field holds text. It is not a Tab stop, so the field stays the only one, and a click leaves the focus in the field; from the keyboard, select the text and delete it. With a controlled `value`, the field empties once the page takes the cleared selection.

## Custom templates

The CoreUI React Autocomplete Component provides the flexibility to personalize options and group labels by utilizing custom templates. You can easily customize the options using the `optionsTemplate`, and for groups, you can use `optionsGroupsTemplate`, as demonstrated in the examples below:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { cifPl, cifDe, cifUs, cifEs, cifGb } from '@coreui/icons'
import CIcon from '@coreui/icons-react'
import { CCol, CRow } from '@coreui/react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

type FlagsMap = {
  [key: string]: string[]
}

export const AutocompleteCustomOptionsExample = () => {
  const flags: FlagsMap = {
    de: cifDe,
    es: cifEs,
    gb: cifGb,
    pl: cifPl,
    us: cifUs,
  }

  const countries = [
    {
      value: 'pl',
      label: 'Poland',
    },
    {
      value: 'de',
      label: 'Germany',
    },
    {
      value: 'us',
      label: 'United States',
    },
    {
      value: 'es',
      label: 'Spain',
    },
    {
      value: 'gb',
      label: 'United Kingdom',
    },
  ]

  const cities = [
    {
      label: 'United States',
      code: 'us',
      options: [
        {
          value: 'au',
          label: 'Austin',
        },
        {
          value: 'ch',
          label: 'Chicago',
        },
        {
          value: 'la',
          label: 'Los Angeles',
        },
        {
          value: 'ny',
          label: 'New York',
        },
        {
          value: 'sa',
          label: 'San Jose',
        },
      ],
    },
    {
      label: 'United Kingdom',
      code: 'gb',
      options: [
        {
          value: 'li',
          label: 'Liverpool',
        },
        {
          value: 'lo',
          label: 'London',
        },
        {
          value: 'ma',
          label: 'Manchester',
        },
      ],
    },
  ]

  return (
    <CRow>
      <CCol md={6}>
        <CAutocomplete
          highlightOptionsOnSearch
          label="Country"
          options={countries}
          optionsTemplate={(option) => (
            <div className="d-flex">
              <CIcon className="me-4" icon={flags[option.value]} size="xl" /> {option.label}
            </div>
          )}
          placeholder="Select country"
          showHints
        />
      </CCol>
      <CCol md={6}>
        <CAutocomplete
          highlightOptionsOnSearch
          label="City"
          options={cities}
          optionsGroupsTemplate={(option) => (
            <div className="d-flex align-items-center">
              <CIcon className="me-4" icon={flags[option.code]} size="xl" /> {option.label}
            </div>
          )}
          placeholder="Select city"
          showHints
        />
      </CCol>
    </CRow>
  )
}
```

## External Data

One of the most powerful features of the React Autocomplete component is its ability to work with external data sources, such as REST APIs, GraphQL endpoints, or server-side search services. This is essential when dealing with large datasets that shouldn't be loaded entirely into the client.

### Implementation example

Here's how to implement external data loading with proper debouncing to optimize API calls:

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CAutocomplete, useDebouncedCallback } from '@coreui/react-pro'
import type { Option } from '@coreui/react-pro/src/components/multi-select/types'

export const AutocompleteExternalDataExample = () => {
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
  const [users, setUsers] = useState([])

  const getUsers = async (name = '') => {
    setLoading(true)
    try {
      const response = await fetch(`https://apitest.coreui.io/demos/users?first_name=${name}`)
      const result = await response.json()

      setUsers(
        result.records.map((record: Option) => ({
          value: record.id,
          label: record.first_name,
        }))
      )
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Error fetching users:', error)
      setUsers([]) // Optionally handle an error state
    } finally {
      setLoading(false)
    }
  }

  // Use the debounced callback for API calls
  const debouncedGetUsers = useDebouncedCallback((value: string) => {
    getUsers(value)
  }, 300)

  return (
    <CAutocomplete
      cleaner
      highlightOptionsOnSearch
      indicator
      label="Users"
      loading={loading}
      onInput={debouncedGetUsers} // Debounce the actual API call
      // onInput={(value) => getUsers(value)} // API call without debounce
      onShow={getUsers} // Triggers the getUsers function when the dropdown is shown
      options={users}
      placeholder="Search users..."
      search="external"
      showHints
      text="Please select your user."
      virtualScroller
    />
  )
}
```

### Key features for external data

- **`useDebouncedCallback`**: Prevents excessive API calls during rapid typing
- **`search="external"`**: Disables internal filtering to rely on server-side search
- **`loading` prop**: Marks the list busy and shows a `loadingLabel` row below the options during API requests; the options stay usable
- **`virtualScroller`**: Efficiently renders large result sets
- **`searchNoResultsLabel`**: Provides user feedback when no results are found

### Required imports

```jsx
import { useDebouncedCallback } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

The `useDebouncedCallback` hook is a utility available in `@coreui/react-pro` that delays function execution until after a specified timeout has elapsed since the last invocation. This prevents excessive API calls during rapid input changes and improves overall performance.

## Performance optimization

For large datasets, the React Autocomplete component includes several performance optimizations:

- **Virtual scrolling**: Use `virtualScroller={true}` to render only visible options
- **Debounced search**: Implement search debouncing to reduce API calls
- **External filtering**: Delegate filtering to the server with `search="external"`
- **Lazy loading**: Load data only when needed

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The selection, the text of the field and the dropdown panel each work either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode, independently for each of them.

| | uncontrolled seed | controlled prop | change callback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Selection | `defaultValue` | `value` | `onChange` |
| Text | `defaultInputValue` | `inputValue` | `onInputChange` |
| Panel | `defaultShow` | `show` | `onShowChange` |

The callbacks fire in **both** modes — `onChange` with the selected option (or `null`), `onInputChange` with the new text, `onShowChange` whenever the panel requests an open-state change (a dismiss gesture like Escape or an outside click, or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle) — so you can watch either state without taking it over. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

### Selection

`defaultValue` seeds the uncontrolled selection with the option whose value, compared as text, equals it, so `1` and `'1'` pick the same option. It waits for options that arrive later, until the user picks, types or clears a value first. The autocomplete manages the selection from there. The per-option `selected` flags are the same seed in another spelling: each flag is applied **once**, when its option first appears, and ignored entirely when `defaultValue` or `value` is set.

```jsx
<CAutocomplete defaultValue="react" options={options} />
```

Pass `value` and the selection is fully controlled: it renders exactly what you pass, a pick only fires `onChange`, and nothing moves until you feed the change back. `value` is matched against the option values like `defaultValue`, so feed back the option's `value` rather than its label (the label for an option without a value, the string for a plain string option), and `null` for no selection. A selected option that later leaves `options`, for example after an external search, keeps its label in the field. `resetSelectionOnOptionsChange` follows the same contract — in controlled mode it only requests the cleared selection through `onChange(null)`. Every request waits for the page the same way: the cleaner and `resetSelectionOnOptionsChange` empty the field only once the page takes the `null`, and with `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` leaving the field with text no option matches puts back the label of the `value` the page kept. Check **Ignore picks** below and click an option: the selection and the field stay as they are.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CCheckbox, CFormField } from '@coreui/react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'
import type { Option } from '@coreui/react-pro/src/components/autocomplete/types'

export const AutocompleteControlledValueExample = () => {
  const [ignorePicks, setIgnorePicks] = useState(false)
  const [value, setValue] = useState<string | number | null>('react')

  return (
    <>
      <CFormField className="mb-4">
        <CCheckbox
          checked={ignorePicks}
          id="autocompleteControlledValueIgnore"
          label="Ignore picks (the selection stays)"
          onChange={(event) => setIgnorePicks(event.target.checked)}
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CAutocomplete
        label="Framework"
        onChange={(option: Option | null) => {
          if (ignorePicks) {
            return
          }

          setValue(
            option === null || typeof option === 'string' ? option : (option.value ?? option.label)
          )
        }}
        options={[
          { label: 'Angular', value: 'angular' },
          { label: 'Bootstrap', value: 'bootstrap' },
          { label: 'Next.js', value: 'next' },
          { label: 'React.js', value: 'react' },
          { label: 'Vue.js', value: 'vue' },
        ]}
        placeholder="Search technologies..."
        value={value}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

### Text

The text of the field is a state of its own, next to the selection. Typing changes the text and clears the selection, and a pick writes the option's label once the selection takes it. Text the user types without a pick stays in the field and is posted with the form under `name`, with two exceptions: <kbd>Enter</kbd> with text that is the label of an option, letter case aside, picks that option, and so does leaving the field when only one option has that label; with `allowOnlyDefinedOptions`, leaving the field with text no option matches empties it. A selection that goes to none, from the cleaner, from new options or from your code, empties only the text that showed it; text the user typed stays. `onInputChange` reports every change of the text, and `onInput` reports the search the options are filtered by: the typed text, until a pick or the cleaner empties it.

`defaultInputValue` starts the field with a text, for example one the user typed before, and a form reset brings it back. Pass `inputValue` to control the text: the field shows it and nothing else, and typing, a pick or the cleaner only ask for a new text through `onInputChange`. A text you set that is not the selected option's label filters the options like typed text, but gets no hint; with `search="external"` you filter by the text you set. Nothing is reported at mount, and a form reset asks a controlled text for the label of the start selection or an empty text. When you control both `value` and `inputValue`, a `value` you change leaves the text alone, so set both.

### Panel

Every example above leaves the panel uncontrolled — the autocomplete manages it itself. `defaultShow` seeds it open on mount.

```jsx
<CAutocomplete defaultShow options={options} />
```

Pass `show` and the panel renders what you pass — dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange`, so feed the change back, or nothing closes. That includes a pick: selecting an option, which would normally close the panel, only requests the close through `onShowChange`. Here a checkbox pins the panel open, and a dismiss gesture unchecks it.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CCheckbox, CFormField } from '@coreui/react'
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const AutocompleteControlledExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CFormField className="mb-4">
        <CCheckbox
          checked={show}
          id="autocompleteControlledShow"
          label="Keep the panel open"
          onChange={(event) => setShow(event.target.checked)}
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CAutocomplete
        label="Framework"
        onShowChange={setShow}
        options={['Angular', 'Bootstrap', 'Next.js', 'React.js', 'Vue.js']}
        placeholder="Search technologies..."
        show={show}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when the open state belongs to something else — a route, a tour step, or a control outside the autocomplete like the checkbox above.

## Accessibility

The Autocomplete component includes several accessibility features:

- **ARIA attributes**: Proper `role`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-haspopup`, and `aria-autocomplete` attributes
- **Screen reader support**: Descriptive labels and announcements for state changes
- **Keyboard navigation**: Full keyboard support with arrow keys, Enter, Escape, and Tab
- **Focus management**: Proper focus handling and visual focus indicators
- **Semantic markup**: Uses appropriate HTML elements and structure

The text field is the combobox, so it carries the accessible name: from `label` or `floatingLabel`, from a `<label>` pointing at its `id`, or from `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` passed to `CAutocomplete`, which land on the field rather than on the frame around it. So do `aria-description`, `aria-details`, `aria-errormessage`, `aria-placeholder`, `aria-readonly` and `aria-required`; attributes that apply to the whole control, such as `aria-hidden`, stay on the frame.

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Arrow Down</kbd> | Navigate to the next option or open dropdown |
| <kbd>Arrow Up</kbd> | Navigate to the previous option |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> | Move the caret to the start of the text |
| <kbd>End</kbd> | Move the caret to the end of the text |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Select the highlighted option, or the option whose label is the typed text; with the list closed, also submit the form |
| <kbd>Escape</kbd> | Close the dropdown; the input keeps focus and the highlighted option clears |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Accept hint completion (when hints are enabled) |
| <kbd>Backspace/Delete</kbd> | Delete one character and clear a held selection |
| Any character, <kbd>Backspace</kbd>, <kbd>Delete</kbd> on the picker button or in the panel | Move the focus to the field and type there, unless `globalSearch` is `false` |

# React Autocomplete Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Autocomplete component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## CAutocomplete

```jsx
import { CAutocomplete } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` | `boolean` | `false` | Only allow selection of predefined options. When `true`, users cannot enter custom values that are not in the options list. When `false`, users can enter and select custom values. |
| `ariaCleanerLabel` | `string` | `Clear selection` | Sets the accessible label (`aria-label`) for the cleaner button, describing its action for screen readers. |
| `ariaPickerLabel` | `string` | `Toggle options list` | Sets the accessible label (`aria-label`) for the indicator button that toggles the options list. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. These classes will be merged with the default React autocomplete classes. |
| `cleaner` | `boolean` | `false` | Enables the cleaner: a button that empties the field, the selection and the text. It shows when an option is selected and, unless `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` is set, when the field holds text, never while the component is disabled or read-only. With `value` set, the field empties once you take the `null` it reports. It stays out of the Tab order and gives the focus back to the field. |
| `clearSearchOnSelect` | `boolean` | `true` | Whether a pick, or <kbd>Enter</kbd> on text that names no option, empties the search the options are filtered by, so the list opens in full next time. The field shows the picked option's label either way. |
| `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment \| (() => Element \| DocumentFragment \| null) \| null` | - | The element the dropdown is rendered into instead of `document.body`. Implies `portal`. Inside a modal dialog it goes into the dialog instead, because the rest of the page is inert. |
| `defaultInputValue` | `string` | - | The text the field starts with and goes back to on a form reset, for example a value the user typed earlier without picking an option. It filters the options like typed text, without a hint. A selected option writes its label over it. Ignored when `inputValue` is set. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial open state of the uncontrolled dropdown panel — read once on mount. |
| `defaultValue` | `string \| number` | - | The initial selection for the uncontrolled mode: the value of the option to select, compared as text, so `1` and `'1'` select the same option. It is applied as soon as the options contain it, unless the user has picked, typed or cleared by then. Ignored when `value` is set. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. When `true`, the React.js autocomplete is non-interactive and appears visually disabled. Users cannot type, select options, or trigger the dropdown. |
| `feedback` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback for the current `validationState` — rendered only while the state is set, and styled after it. For the client-side mode, where the browser owns the state, use `feedbackValid` and `feedbackInvalid` instead. |
| `feedbackInvalid` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback the stylesheet reveals while the control is invalid — always rendered, so it works with client-side validation, where the browser decides the state. |
| `feedbackValid` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback the stylesheet reveals while the control is valid — always rendered, so it works with client-side validation, where the browser decides the state. |
| `floatingLabel` | `ReactNode` | - | Provide a floating label for the component — the text rests inside the field and floats once it has focus or a value. |
| `floatingLabelAlways` | `boolean` | - | Keeps the floating label floated and the placeholder visible while the field is empty. |
| `globalSearch` | `boolean` | `true` | Routes typing to the field from anywhere in the component, so a keystroke never depends on where the focus sits. Set to `false` to keep it local: a keystroke then counts only while the field has the focus. |
| `highlightOptionsOnSearch` | `boolean` | `false` | Highlight options that match the search criteria. When `true`, matching portions of option labels are visually highlighted based on the current search input value. |
| `id` | `string` | - | Set the id attribute for the native input element. This id is used for accessibility purposes and form associations. If not provided, a unique id may be generated automatically. |
| `inputValue` | `string` | - | The controlled text of the field. The field shows this text and nothing else: typing, a pick and the cleaner ask for a new text through `onInputChange`, so update `inputValue` there. A text that is not the selected option's label filters the options like typed text. When `value` is set as well, a `value` you change leaves the text alone: set both. |
| `invalid` | `boolean` | - | Mark the control invalid. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` | - | Add a caption for a component. |
| `loading` | `boolean` | - | When set, the options list is marked busy and shows a row with a spinner and `loadingLabel` below its options while you fetch them; the options it shows can still be picked. |
| `loadingLabel` | `string` | `Loading…` | Text of the loading row below the options, announced to screen readers when the shown list starts loading or the list shows up loading. |
| `name` | `string` | - | Name of the text input the form posts. That input holds what the user sees, the selected option's label or their own text when `allowOnlyDefinedOptions` is off, so `{ value: 'ng', label: 'Angular' }` posts `Angular`, not `ng`. Without a name the autocomplete is not submitted with the form. |
| `onChange` | `((option: Option \| null) => void)` | - | Execute a function when the selected option changes. Called with the option, or `null` when the selection is cleared. Text the user types without picking an option is not a selection: read it from `onInputChange`. |
| `onHide` | `(() => void)` | - | The callback is fired when the dropdown requests to be hidden. Called when the dropdown closes due to user interaction, clicks outside, escape key, or programmatic changes. |
| `onInput` | `((value: string) => void)` | - | Execute a function when the search changes, the text the options are filtered by: as the user types, and with an empty string when the autocomplete empties it, for example after a pick or with the cleaner. Use it for external search; the text of the field comes through `onInputChange`. |
| `onInputChange` | `((value: string) => void)` | - | Execute a function when the text of the field changes: as the user types, after a pick (the option's label), with the cleaner, on a form reset, and when the selection changes from outside. Pair it with `inputValue`. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | The callback is fired when the dropdown requests to be shown. Called when the dropdown opens due to user interaction, focus, or programmatic changes. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the dropdown panel requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, outside click, option pick) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the panel stays as it is. |
| `onValidationStateChange` | `((validationState: ValidationState \| undefined) => void)` | - | Callback fired with `undefined` when the user changes the text of the field, or the form is reset, while `validationState` (or `invalid`/`valid`) is set. A given state is a verdict on the value it was given for; clear it here to let the browser's own validation show again. |
| `options` | `(Option \| OptionsGroup)[]` | - | List of option elements. Can contain Option objects, OptionsGroup objects, or plain strings. Plain strings are converted to simple Option objects internally. This is a required prop - the React autocomplete needs options to function. |
| `optionsGroupsTemplate` | `((option: OptionsGroup) => ReactNode)` | - | Custom template for rendering option groups. Allows customization of how option group headers appear in the dropdown. The function receives an OptionsGroup object and should return a ReactNode. |
| `optionsMaxHeight` | `string \| number` | `auto` | Sets maxHeight of options list. Controls the maximum height of the dropdown options container. Can be a number (pixels) or a CSS length string (e.g., '200px', '10rem'). When content exceeds this height, a scrollbar will appear. |
| `optionsTemplate` | `((option: Option) => ReactNode)` | - | Custom template for rendering individual options. Allows complete customization of how each option appears in the dropdown. The function receives an Option object and should return a ReactNode. |
| `pickerIcon` | `ReactNode` | `false` | The button that opens the options menu: `true` for the built-in icon, a node for your own, `false` for no button. When `true`, displays a dropdown arrow button that can be clicked to manually show or hide the options dropdown. |
| `placeholder` | `string` | - | Specifies a short hint that is visible in the search input. Displayed when the input is empty to guide user interaction. Standard HTML input placeholder behavior. |
| `portal` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders the autocomplete dropdown in a React portal, allowing it to escape the parent container's styling constraints (like overflow, z-index, or positioning). When enabled, the dropdown is rendered into the open `<dialog>` the field sits in, otherwise into `document.body`, so it appears above other page elements and isn't clipped by parent containers. |
| `readOnly` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the readonly state for the component. When `true`, users can view and interact with the dropdown but cannot type in the search input or modify the selection through typing. Selection via clicking options may still be possible. |
| `required` | `boolean` | - | When it is present, it indicates that the user must choose a value before submitting the form. Adds HTML5 form validation requirement. The form will not submit until a valid selection is made. |
| `resetSelectionOnOptionsChange` | `boolean` | `false` | Determines whether the selected options should be cleared when the options list is updated. When `true`, any previously selected options will be reset whenever the options list undergoes a change. This ensures that outdated selections are not retained when new options are provided. |
| `search` | `"external"` | - | `'external'` hands the filtering to your code: the component shows the options you pass and reports what the user types through `onInput`. |
| `searchNoResultsLabel` | `ReactNode` | `false` | Sets the label for no results when filtering. - `false`: Don't show any message when no results found - `true`: Show default "No results found" message - `string`: Show custom text message - `ReactNode`: Show custom component/element |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the open state of the dropdown panel. When set, the panel renders what `show` says and dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `showHints` | `boolean` | `false` | Show hint options based on the current input value. When `true`, displays a preview/hint of the first matching option as semi-transparent text in the input field, similar to browser autocomplete. Only text the user types gets a hint. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "lg"` | - | Size the component small or large. - `'sm'`: Small size variant - `'lg'`: Large size variant - `undefined`: Default/medium size |
| `text` | `ReactNode` | - | Add helper text to the component. |
| `tooltipFeedback` | `boolean` | - | Display validation feedback in a styled tooltip. |
| `valid` | `boolean` | - | Mark the control valid. |
| `validationState` | `'valid' \| 'invalid' \| string` | - | The validation state, rendered as the `is-{state}` class on the frame; `'invalid'` also sets `aria-invalid` on the input and blocks the submit. Any custom state declared in the `$form-validation-states` Sass map is accepted. The user's next change of the text asks to drop it through `onValidationStateChange`. |
| `value` | `string \| number \| null` | - | The controlled selection: the value of the selected option, or `null` (an empty string too) for none. It is matched against the option values compared as text, so `1` and `'1'` select the same option, and the field keeps the label of a selected option that leaves `options`. Pair it with `onChange`; for the uncontrolled mode use `defaultValue` instead. |
| `virtualScroller` | `boolean` | `false` | Enable virtual scroller for the options list. When `true`, only visible options are rendered in the DOM for better performance with large option lists. Works in conjunction with `visibleItems` prop. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the visibility of autocomplete dropdown. Controls whether the dropdown is initially visible. The dropdown visibility can still be toggled through user interaction. |
| `visibleItems` | `number` | `10` | Amount of visible items when virtualScroller is enabled. Determines how many option items are rendered at once when virtual scrolling is active. Higher values show more items but use more memory. Lower values improve performance. |

# React Autocomplete Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Autocomplete component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

### CSS variables

Autocomplete has no variables of its own: the field is a [`.form-control-group`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/form-control-group/styling/#css-variables), so its frame, the cleaner and the toggle read the `--cui-control-*` and `--cui-control-group-*` tokens. `className` and `style` on `CAutocomplete` land on that frame, the `.autocomplete` element, so the tokens can be set on a single Autocomplete. The panel is rendered next to the field, or into `document.body` with `portal`, so `style` does not reach it; set its tokens with a rule on `.combobox-popup`. The panel is the shared combobox surface, which Multi Select renders too, so both read the same set.

```scss
$combobox-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-combobox-popup-min-width: 100%,
  ),
  $combobox-tokens
);
```

Everything inside the panel — the options, the group labels and the empty state — is a [List box](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/) and takes its `--cui-list-box-*` variables. `.list-box` declares them itself, so a value set on `.combobox-popup` or on `:root` does not reach it: set them with a rule on `.combobox-popup .list-box`, which covers the panels of Combobox, Autocomplete and Multi Select alike.

#### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-control-border-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
  '--cui-control-group-action-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
}

return <CAutocomplete options={options} style={customVars} />
```

# React Autocomplete Component Accessibility

> Detailed overview of the accessibility features implemented in CoreUI React Autocomplete, ensuring compliance with WAI-ARIA guidelines.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Accessibility

The React Autocomplete component includes several accessibility features:

- **ARIA attributes**: Proper `role`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-haspopup`, and `aria-autocomplete` attributes
- **Screen reader support**: Descriptive labels and announcements for state changes
- **Keyboard navigation**: Full keyboard support with arrow keys, Enter, Escape, and Tab
- **Focus management**: Proper focus handling and visual focus indicators
- **Semantic markup**: Uses appropriate HTML elements and structure

### Keyboard shortcuts

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Arrow Down</kbd> | Navigate to the next option or open dropdown |
| <kbd>Arrow Up</kbd> | Navigate to the previous option |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> | Move the caret to the start of the text |
| <kbd>End</kbd> | Move the caret to the end of the text |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> | Select the highlighted option, or the option whose label is the typed text; with the list closed, also submit the form |
| <kbd>Escape</kbd> | Close the dropdown; the input keeps focus and the highlighted option clears |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Accept hint completion (when hints are enabled) |
| <kbd>Backspace/Delete</kbd> | Delete one character and clear a held selection |
