# React Password Strength Component

> Show how strong a password is as it is typed — a segmented meter, a label, and a pluggable scorer that can be asynchronous so a real strength estimator or a breach check can drive it.

## Example

_Added in 6.0.0._

Pass the password to `<CPasswordStrength>` and it renders the meter, the label and the feedback itself — pair it with [Password Input](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/password-input/), which owns the field's frame and visibility toggle.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CFormLabel } from '@coreui/react'
import { CPasswordInput, CPasswordStrength } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const PasswordStrengthExample = () => {
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('')

  return (
    <>
      <CFormLabel htmlFor="strengthDemo">Password</CFormLabel>
      <CPasswordInput
        id="strengthDemo"
        className="mb-3"
        placeholder="Type a password…"
        value={password}
        onChange={(event) => setPassword(event.target.value)}
      />
      <CPasswordStrength value={password} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## How it works

- **The field stays yours.** The meter never wraps, moves or re-types the input — it just receives the password through the `value` property, so it works with any field you control.
- **The meter is built for you.** It renders the segments, the label, and the places a scorer's warning and suggestions go. Segments are one fewer than there are levels, so the top level fills the bar.
- **The score is a number from 0 to 4.** Level `0` is the worst. That is the same scale [zxcvbn](#zxcvbn) returns, so a real estimator drops in without a conversion step.
- **The meter is hidden from assistive technology** (`aria-hidden`) because it only restates the label. The label and its feedback sit in a polite live region, so a screen reader hears the verdict once, not twice.

## What the built-in scorer is worth

> **The built-in scorer is a UX hint, not a security control.** It counts length and character classes — lowercase, uppercase, digits, symbols. That measures *composition*, not how guessable a password actually is. `P@ssw0rd1` clears every rule it checks and is among the first passwords any attacker tries.
> 
> [NIST SP 800-63B](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-3/sp800-63b.html) recommends **against** composition rules of exactly this kind, and **for** checking the password against lists of known-breached secrets. Do that on the server, where it cannot be skipped. Treat this meter as encouragement while typing, and never as the thing that decides whether a password is allowed.

The default scorer stays small and rule-based on purpose: a real estimator ships a dictionary far larger than this entire library. Plug one in with `scorer`.

## Custom scorer

`scorer` replaces the built-in scoring completely. It receives the password and the [user inputs](#user-inputs), and returns either a bare number or an object:

```js
type StrengthResult = number | { score: number, warning?: string, suggestions?: string[] }
```

Return a number when that is all you have — the simple case stays simple:

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CPasswordInput, CPasswordStrength } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const PasswordStrengthScorerExample = () => {
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('')

  return (
    <>
      <CPasswordInput
        className="mb-3"
        placeholder="Length alone decides…"
        value={password}
        onChange={(event) => setPassword(event.target.value)}
      />
      <CPasswordStrength
        value={password}
        scorer={(value) => Math.min(4, Math.floor(value.length / 4))}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

Return an object to say *why*. The `warning` and `suggestions` are rendered below the label, and both are inserted as text — markup in them is never parsed. A score outside the range of `levels` is clamped, and a scorer that throws clears the meter rather than leaving a stale verdict on screen.

### Asynchronous scorers

`scorer` may return a promise. This is what makes a serious estimator possible: zxcvbn loads its language packs asynchronously, and a breach check is a network call. Three things the component handles so you do not have to:

- **Debounce.** Input is coalesced (`debounce`, 200 ms by default) so typing a password does not fire a request per keystroke.
- **Out-of-order results.** Every evaluation takes a sequence token. If a slow answer for an old password arrives after a newer one has already resolved, it is discarded. Without this, pausing mid-word and typing on can leave the meter showing the verdict for a prefix.
- **A pending state.** While a promise is outstanding the root gets `.password-strength-busy` and the label shows `busyLabel`. A synchronous scorer never gets this state, so it cannot flicker.

A rejected promise clears the meter, for the same reason a throw does.

> **A scorer that calls the network sends the password off the page.** Anything you `fetch` from inside `scorer` receives the secret the user is in the middle of typing — before they have submitted anything, and on every debounce tick.
> 
> If you check against a breach corpus, use a protocol built for it: the [Pwned Passwords range API](https://haveibeenpwned.com/API/v3#PwnedPasswords) takes the first five characters of the password's SHA-1 hash and returns every matching suffix, so the password itself never leaves the browser. Sending the raw password to a third party is a credential disclosure, whatever the endpoint promises.

### zxcvbn

[zxcvbn](https://github.com/dropbox/zxcvbn) and its maintained successor [zxcvbn-ts](https://github.com/zxcvbn-ts/zxcvbn) estimate how many guesses a password would survive, using dictionaries of common passwords, names, words and keyboard patterns. That is a different question from "does it have a capital letter", and a much more useful one.

We do not ship an adapter — the shapes already line up. zxcvbn returns `{ score, feedback: { warning, suggestions } }`, and `score` is 0–4 on the same scale this component uses. The language packs are large — load them on demand and let the promise support do the waiting:

```jsx
let zxcvbnReady = null

const loadZxcvbn = () => {
  zxcvbnReady ||= Promise.all([
    import('@zxcvbn-ts/core'),
    import('@zxcvbn-ts/language-common'),
    import('@zxcvbn-ts/language-en'),
  ]).then(([core, common, en]) => {
    core.zxcvbnOptions.setOptions({
      dictionary: { ...common.dictionary, ...en.dictionary },
      graphs: common.adjacencyGraphs,
      translations: en.translations,
    })

    return core.zxcvbn
  })

  return zxcvbnReady
}

const scorer = async (password, userInputs) => {
  const zxcvbn = await loadZxcvbn()
  const { score, feedback } = zxcvbn(password, userInputs)

  return { score, warning: feedback.warning, suggestions: feedback.suggestions }
}

return <CPasswordStrength value={password} scorer={scorer} />
```

Both run entirely in the browser, so neither sends the password anywhere.

## User inputs

A password containing the user's own email, username or site name is weak no matter how it is composed, and no amount of character-class counting notices that. `userInputs` is the list to penalize against.

Pass a function when the values live in fields the user is still filling in — it is called on every evaluation, so it always sees current values. Pass an array when they are fixed.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CFormInput } from '@coreui/react'
import { CPasswordInput, CPasswordStrength } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const PasswordStrengthUserInputsExample = () => {
  const [email, setEmail] = useState('ada@example.com')
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('')

  return (
    <>
      <CFormInput
        className="mb-3"
        aria-label="Email"
        value={email}
        onChange={(event) => setEmail(event.target.value)}
      />
      <CPasswordInput
        className="mb-3"
        placeholder="Try using the email above…"
        value={password}
        onChange={(event) => setPassword(event.target.value)}
      />
      <CPasswordStrength value={password} userInputs={() => [email]} />
    </>
  )
}
```

The built-in scorer returns `0` when the password contains any of these values (three characters or more, case-insensitive). A custom scorer receives the same list as its second argument and decides for itself — zxcvbn takes it directly.

## With form field

Wrap the control in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) to lay it out with its label and description, and to get validation feedback in the right place. The meter is a child of the field like any other, so it picks up the same gap.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CFormField, CFormLabel, CFormText } from '@coreui/react'
import { CPasswordInput, CPasswordStrength } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const PasswordStrengthFormFieldExample = () => {
  const [password, setPassword] = useState('')

  return (
    <CFormField>
      <CFormLabel htmlFor="strengthField">Password</CFormLabel>
      <CPasswordInput
        id="strengthField"
        placeholder="Type a password…"
        value={password}
        onChange={(event) => setPassword(event.target.value)}
      />
      <CPasswordStrength value={password} />
      <CFormText>At least 12 characters.</CFormText>
    </CFormField>
  )
}
```

## Accessibility

- The segmented bar is `aria-hidden`, because it carries no information the label does not.
- The label, warning and suggestions share one `role="status"` region with `aria-live="polite"`, so the verdict is announced without interrupting, and as a single message rather than three.
- Debouncing keeps that region from being updated on every keystroke, which is what makes a live region usable here at all.
- The strength label is never the only signal — it is text, not colour alone.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CPasswordStrength /&gt;](./api/#cpasswordstrength)

# React Password Strength Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Password Strength component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CPasswordStrength

```jsx
import { CPasswordStrength } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `busyLabel` | `string` | `Checking…` | Text announced while an asynchronous scorer is pending. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the component. |
| `debounce` | `number` | `200` | Milliseconds to wait after the last change before evaluating. |
| `levels` | `string[]` | `['Very weak', 'Weak', 'Fair', 'Good', 'Strong']` | Labels for the strength levels, weakest first. The meter renders one segment fewer than there are levels, and a score above the last label is clamped to it. |
| `minLength` | `number` | `8` | Minimum length the built-in scorer awards points for. |
| `onStrengthChange` | `((score: number \| null, level: string \| null) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the computed score changes. The password is masked. |
| `scorer` | `((password: string, userInputs: string[]) => StrengthResult \| Promise<StrengthResult>)` | - | Custom scorer - return a score (or `{ score, warning, suggestions }`), or a promise resolving to one. |
| `thresholds` | `number[]` | `[2, 4, 6]` | Point thresholds between the built-in scorer's levels. A threshold left out keeps its default. |
| `userInputs` | `string[] \| (() => string[])` | `[]` | Words the password must not contain - the user's name, e-mail, the site name. Pass a function to read them lazily. |
| `value` | `string` | - | The password to evaluate. |
| `weights` | `Record<string, number>` | `{ minLength: 1, extraLength: 1, longPassword: 1, lowercase: 1, uppercase: 1, numbers: 1, special: 1, multipleSpecial: 1, }` | Points the built-in scorer awards per fulfilled rule. A rule left out keeps its default, so the object is a set of overrides rather than a replacement. |

# React Password Strength Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Password Strength component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

### CSS variables

React Password Strength supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$password-strength-tokens: () !default;
$password-strength-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-password-strength-gap: .5rem,
    --cui-password-strength-meter-gap: .25rem,
    --cui-password-strength-segment-height: .25rem,
    --cui-password-strength-segment-bg: var(--cui-bg-2),
    --cui-password-strength-segment-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-pill),
    --cui-password-strength-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-password-strength-text-font-weight: 600,
    --cui-password-strength-warning-color: var(--cui-fg-2),
    --cui-password-strength-suggestions-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-password-strength-busy-opacity: .65,
    --cui-password-strength-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
  ),
  $password-strength-tokens
);
```

### Sass maps

Each level pairs a colour with the score it represents; add or override an entry to retint a level:

```scss
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$password-strength-levels: defaults(
  (
    "0": var(--cui-danger-base),
    "1": var(--cui-danger-base),
    "2": var(--cui-warning-base),
    "3": var(--cui-info-base),
    "4": var(--cui-success-base),
  ),
  $password-strength-levels
);
```

### Sass loops

```scss
@each $level, $color in $password-strength-levels {
  &[data-coreui-strength="#{$level}"] {
    --cui-password-strength-color: #{$color};
  }
}
```

# React Radio Components

> Create consistent cross-browser and cross-device radios with our React radio component.

## Approach

`<CRadio>` renders the `<input type="radio">`. That is the whole control — no wrapper, no extra element. Radios are for selecting one option out of many; to select several, reach for a [checkbox](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/checkbox/).

The `label` property renders a sibling `<label>` already wired to the input with `htmlFor`, so the label can be styled from the input's state. Wrap the pair in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) when you want the label, a description and validation feedback laid out for you. The dot is a CSS mask on the input's own `::before`, so its color is a token.

Radios in the same group share a `name` attribute; that is what makes them mutually exclusive.

## Basic radio

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="flexRadioDefault" id="flexRadioDefault1" label="Default radio" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="flexRadioDefault"
          id="flexRadioDefault2"
          label="Default checked radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Disabled

Add the `disabled` attribute; the associated `<label>` is styled to match, in a lighter color, to indicate the state.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioDisabledExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="flexRadioDisabled" id="flexRadioDisabled" label="Disabled radio" disabled />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="flexRadioDisabled"
          id="flexRadioCheckedDisabled"
          label="Disabled checked radio"
          defaultChecked
          disabled
        />
      </CFormField>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Stacked

Any number of radios that are immediate siblings stack vertically and are spaced by their `<CFormField>` wrappers.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioStackedExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="exampleRadios"
          id="exampleRadios1"
          value="option1"
          label="Default radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="exampleRadios"
          id="exampleRadios2"
          value="option2"
          label="Second default radio"
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="exampleRadios"
          id="exampleRadios3"
          value="option3"
          label="Disabled radio"
          disabled
        />
      </CFormField>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Inline

There is no inline property: the control is an inline element, so a row is a flex container with a gap.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioInlineExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex gap-4">
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="inlineRadioOptions" id="inlineRadio1" value="option1" label="1" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="inlineRadioOptions" id="inlineRadio2" value="option2" label="2" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="inlineRadioOptions"
          id="inlineRadio3"
          value="option3"
          label="3 (disabled)"
          disabled
        />
      </CFormField>
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Sizing

`size="sm"` and `size="lg"` size the whole row — the box, its label, and the space they sit in. Each sets one font size: the box is `1em`, so it follows, and so does the alignment margin, which is computed from the line. Nothing needs re-tuning per size, and a size of your own is one custom property.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioSizingExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex align-items-start gap-4">
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio size="sm" name="sizeRadio" id="radioSm" label="Small" defaultChecked />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="sizeRadio" id="radioMd" label="Default" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio size="lg" name="sizeRadio" id="radioLg" label="Large" />
      </CFormField>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Any other size is one custom property, and the alignment follows it:

```jsx
<CRadio style={{ '--cui-radio-size': '2em' }} aria-label="..." />
```

## Without a label

A radio with no label text is the input on its own. Give it an accessible name some other way — `aria-label`, for instance. The name says what the option is, like `aria-label="Red"` in a color picker, and replaces the `...` placeholder in the example below. See the [forms overview](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/overview/#accessibility) for details.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioWithoutLabelsExample = () => {
  return <CRadio name="radioNoLabel" id="radioNoLabel1" value="" aria-label="..." />
}
```

## With form field

Wrap the control in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) to lay it out with its label and description, and to get validation feedback in the right place. Nest one `<CFormField>` per radio inside an outer one to give the whole group a shared label.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CFormText, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioFormFieldExample = () => {
  return (
    <CFormField>
      <span className="form-label">Delivery</span>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="fieldRadio" id="fieldRadio1" label="Standard" defaultChecked />
        <CFormText>Three to five working days.</CFormText>
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="fieldRadio" id="fieldRadio2" label="Express" />
        <CFormText>Next working day, where available.</CFormText>
      </CFormField>
    </CFormField>
  )
}
```

## Radio toggle buttons

Create button-like radio buttons by using `button` boolean property on the `<CFormCheck type="radio">` component. These toggle buttons can further be grouped in a button group if needed. Toggle buttons use the deprecated `<CFormCheck>`'s button mode — it has no `<CRadio>` counterpart.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioToggleButtonsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option1"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Checked"
        defaultChecked
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option2"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option3"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
        disabled
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option4"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

### Outlined styles

Different variants of button, such at the various outlined styles, are supported.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioToggleButtonsOutlinedStylesExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'success', variant: 'outline' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options-outlined"
        id="success-outlined"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
        defaultChecked
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'danger', variant: 'outline' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options-outlined"
        id="danger-outlined"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Theme variants

Modify the appearance of checked radios with the [`theme`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) property — it sets the checked background and border color to the theme color.

```html
import React from 'react'

export const RadioThemeColorsExample = () => {

        />

      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          theme="secondary"
          name="radioThemeSecondary"
          id="radioThemeSecondary"
          label="Secondary radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          theme="success"
          name="radioThemeSuccess"
          id="radioThemeSuccess"
          label="Success radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          theme="danger"
          name="radioThemeDanger"
          id="radioThemeDanger"
          label="Danger radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          theme="warning"
          name="radioThemeWarning"
          id="radioThemeWarning"
          label="Warning radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          theme="info"
          name="radioThemeInfo"
          id="radioThemeInfo"
          label="Info radio"

```

# React Radio Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Radio component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CRadio

```jsx
import { CRadio } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the input. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` | - | The label rendered after the input, already wired to it with `htmlFor`. |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement, HTMLInputElement>` | - | Method called on the native `change` event, when the user checks or unchecks the input. A radio unchecked by another one in its group and a form reset do not call it. |
| `onValidationStateChange` | `((validationState: ValidationState \| undefined) => void)` | - | Callback fired with `undefined` when the user changes the checked state, or the form is reset, while `validationState` is set. A given state is a verdict on the choice it was given for; clear it here to let the browser's own validation show again. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "lg"` | - | Size the radio small or large. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the checked state to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `validationState` | `'valid' \| 'invalid' \| string` | - | The validation state, rendered as the `is-{state}` class; `'invalid'` also sets `aria-invalid` and blocks the submit. Any custom state declared in the `$form-validation-states` Sass map is accepted. The user's next change of the checked state asks to drop it through `onValidationStateChange`. |

## CFormCheck

```jsx
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `button` | `ButtonObject` | - | Create button-like checkboxes and radio buttons. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the component. |
| `feedback` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback for the current `validationState` — rendered only while the state is set, and styled after it. For the client-side mode, where the browser owns the state, use `feedbackValid` and `feedbackInvalid` instead. |
| `feedbackInvalid` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback the stylesheet reveals while the control is invalid — always rendered, so it works with client-side validation, where the browser decides the state. |
| `feedbackValid` | `ReactNode` | - | Feedback the stylesheet reveals while the control is valid — always rendered, so it works with client-side validation, where the browser decides the state. |
| `floatingLabel` | `ReactNode` | - | Provide a floating label for the component — the text rests inside the field and floats once it has focus or a value. |
| `id` | `string` | - | The id global attribute defines an identifier (ID) that must be unique in the whole document. |
| `indeterminate` | `boolean` | - | Input Checkbox indeterminate Property. |
| `inline` | `boolean` | - | Group checkboxes or radios on the same horizontal row. |
| `invalid` | `boolean` | - | Set component validation state to invalid. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` | - | The element represents a caption for a component. |
| `onChange` | `ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement, HTMLInputElement>` | - | Method called on the native `change` event, when the user checks or unchecks the input. A radio unchecked by another one in its group and a form reset do not call it. |
| `onValidationStateChange` | `((validationState: ValidationState \| undefined) => void)` | - | Callback fired with `undefined` when the user changes the checked state, or the form is reset, while `validationState` (or the deprecated `invalid`) is set. A given state is a verdict on the choice it was given for; clear it here to let the browser's own validation show again. |
| `reverse` | `boolean` | - | Put checkboxes or radios on the opposite side. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `tooltipFeedback` | `boolean` | - | Display validation feedback in a styled tooltip. |
| `type` | `"checkbox" \| "radio"` | `checkbox` | Specifies the type of component. |
| `valid` | `boolean` | - | Set component validation state to valid. |
| `validationState` | `'valid' \| 'invalid' \| string` | - | The validation state, rendered as the `is-{state}` class; `'invalid'` also sets `aria-invalid` and blocks the submit. Any custom state declared in the `$form-validation-states` Sass map is accepted. The user's next change of the checked state asks to drop it through `onValidationStateChange`. |

# React Radio Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Radio component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

### CSS variables

React Radio reads its own custom properties, so restyling it does not touch checkboxes or switches. Set them on the control itself — an ancestor cannot override a token the element declares for itself.

```scss
$radio-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-radio-size: var(--cui-control-size),
    --cui-radio-bg: var(--cui-btn-input-bg),
    --cui-radio-border: var(--cui-border-width) solid var(--cui-border-color),
    --cui-radio-border-radius: 50%,
    --cui-radio-checked-bg: var(--cui-control-checked-bg),
    --cui-radio-checked-border-color: var(--cui-control-checked-border-color),
    --cui-radio-mark-color: var(--cui-primary-contrast),
    --cui-radio-mark: #{escape-svg(url("data:image/svg+xml,<svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' viewBox='-4 -4 8 8'><circle r='2' fill='black'/></svg>"))},
    --cui-radio-disabled-opacity: var(--cui-control-disabled-opacity),
    --cui-radio-margin-top: calc((var(--cui-body-line-height) * 1em - var(--cui-radio-size)) * .5),
    --cui-radio-active-filter: var(--cui-control-active-filter),
    --cui-radio-label-disabled-opacity: var(--cui-control-label-disabled-opacity),
  ),
  $radio-tokens
);
```

#### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-radio-size': '1.25em',
  '--cui-radio-checked-bg': '#198754',
}

return <CRadio style={customVars} />
```

### Shared variables

The checkbox, the radio and the switch share their size and their focus, active and disabled states. Those live on `:root` as `--cui-control-*`, so one declaration retunes all three at runtime:

```scss
--cui-control-size: 1em,
--cui-control-checked-bg: var(--cui-primary-base),
--cui-control-checked-border-color: var(--cui-primary-base),
--cui-control-indeterminate-bg: var(--cui-primary-base),
--cui-control-indeterminate-border-color: var(--cui-primary-base),
--cui-control-active-filter: brightness(90%),
--cui-control-focus-border-color: var(--cui-btn-input-focus-border-color),
--cui-control-disabled-bg: var(--cui-bg-3),
--cui-control-disabled-opacity: .5,
--cui-control-label-disabled-opacity: .5,
--cui-control-transition-duration: .15s,
--cui-control-transition-timing: cubic-bezier(.34, 1.56, .64, 1),
```

# React Bootstrap Radio Component

> Learn how to build consistent, accessible, and customizable radio buttons using CoreUI’s React components styled with Bootstrap.

## How to use React Bootstrap Radio component

Use CoreUI’s `<CRadio>` component to create Bootstrap-styled radio buttons for selecting one option from many. These components are built to be accessible, customizable, and responsive.

### Default stacked radios

By default, multiple radio buttons rendered as siblings will be stacked vertically with proper spacing.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="flexRadioDefault" id="flexRadioDefault1" label="Default radio" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="flexRadioDefault"
          id="flexRadioDefault2"
          label="Default checked radio"
          defaultChecked
        />
      </CFormField>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Disabled state

Add the `disabled` prop to disable a radio button. The associated label will also receive a muted style to reflect its state.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioDisabledExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="flexRadioDisabled" id="flexRadioDisabled" label="Disabled radio" disabled />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="flexRadioDisabled"
          id="flexRadioCheckedDisabled"
          label="Disabled checked radio"
          defaultChecked
          disabled
        />
      </CFormField>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Inline radios

Display radio buttons in a horizontal row with a flex utility wrapper.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioInlineExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex gap-4">
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="inlineRadioOptions" id="inlineRadio1" value="option1" label="1" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio name="inlineRadioOptions" id="inlineRadio2" value="option2" label="2" />
      </CFormField>
      <CFormField>
        <CRadio
          name="inlineRadioOptions"
          id="inlineRadio3"
          value="option3"
          label="3 (disabled)"
          disabled
        />
      </CFormField>
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Reverse layout

The reverse layout exists only on the deprecated `<CFormCheck>` — its `reverse` property places the control after the label.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioReverseExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormCheck reverse type="radio" id="reverseOption1" value="option1" label="Reverse radio" />
      <CFormCheck
        reverse
        type="radio"
        id="reverseOption2"
        value="option2"
        label="Disabled reverse radio"
        disabled
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

### Radios without labels

You can omit visual labels, but make sure to provide accessible names using `aria-label` for screen readers.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRadio } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioWithoutLabelsExample = () => {
  return <CRadio name="radioNoLabel" id="radioNoLabel1" value="" aria-label="..." />
}
```

### Radio toggle buttons

Turn your radios into button-like toggles using the `button` prop. These can also be grouped using a button group component.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioToggleButtonsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option1"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Checked"
        defaultChecked
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option2"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option3"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
        disabled
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'secondary' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options"
        id="option4"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

#### Outlined toggle styles

You can apply outlined styles to toggle radios using Bootstrap's button variant system.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const RadioToggleButtonsOutlinedStylesExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'success', variant: 'outline' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options-outlined"
        id="success-outlined"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
        defaultChecked
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'danger', variant: 'outline' }}
        type="radio"
        name="options-outlined"
        id="danger-outlined"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio"
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

- [&lt;CFormCheck /&gt;](../api/#cformcheck)

# React Range Component

> React range component. Use our custom range inputs for consistent cross-browser styling and built-in customization.

## Overview

Create custom `<input type="range">` controls with `<CFormRange>`. The track (the background) and thumb (the value) are both styled to appear the same across browsers, and the track fills up to the thumb: the component renders the input inside a `.form-range` wrapper and writes the fill ratio to `--cui-range-fill`, which the CSS uses to draw the fill, the tooltip and the tick marks. The fill is a shade lighter than the thumb; `track={false}` leaves the track unfilled.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeExample = () => {
  return <CFormRange id="customRange1" label="Example range" />
}
```

For several thumbs on one track, a vertical orientation or ticks that move a thumb when pressed, use [`<CRangeSlider>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/range-slider/), which renders this markup.

## Tooltip

Set `tooltips` to show a tooltip with the value that follows the thumb. It appears while the pointer is over the input, while the thumb is held, and while the input has focus; `tooltips="always"` keeps it visible at all times. The tooltip is the markup and the look of the [tooltip](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/tooltip/) component, and `tooltipClassName` adds classes to it, for example a `theme-{color}`. `tooltipsFormat` formats the text, and a string it returns becomes the input's `aria-valuetext`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeTooltipExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CFormRange id="rangeTooltip" label="Brightness" defaultValue={60} tooltips />
      <CFormRange
        className="mt-5"
        id="rangeTooltipAlways"
        label="Brightness"
        defaultValue={60}
        tooltips="always"
        tooltipsFormat={(value) => `${value}%`}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Tick marks

Pass `ticks` and the component renders a tick mark for each entry. A number is a bare tick at that value, and an object sets `value`, `label`, `className` and `style`, so the ticks land on their values even when those are unevenly spaced. A labelled tick is drawn taller than an unlabelled one.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeTicksExample = () => {
  return (
    <CFormRange
      id="rangeTicks"
      label="Temperature"
      min={0}
      max={100}
      step={25}
      defaultValue={50}
      ticks={[
        { value: 0, label: 'Cold' },
        25,
        { value: 50, label: 'Mild' },
        75,
        { value: 100, label: 'Hot' },
      ]}
    />
  )
}
```

A string, or an object without `value`, is a label placed by its position in the array, the first at `min` and the last at `max`. While the thumb sits on a tick labelled with text, its `aria-valuetext` adds the label to the value, so a screen reader announces "50, Medium"; with `tooltipsFormat` the label follows the formatted text when the two differ.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeTickLabelsExample = () => {
  return <CFormRange id="rangePriority" label="Priority" ticks={['Low', 'Medium', 'High']} />
}
```

## With form field

Wrap the control in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) to lay it out with its label and description, and to get validation feedback in the right place.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CFormLabel, CFormRange, CFormText } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeFormFieldExample = () => {
  return (
    <CFormField>
      <CFormLabel htmlFor="rangeField">Volume</CFormLabel>
      <CFormRange id="rangeField" />
      <CFormText>Applies to notification sounds only.</CFormText>
    </CFormField>
  )
}
```

## Disabled

Add the `disabled` boolean attribute on an input to give it a grayed out appearance and remove pointer events.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeDisabledExample = () => {
  return <CFormRange id="disabledRange" label="Disabled range" disabled />
}
```

## Min and max

Range inputs have implicit values for `min` and `max`—`0` and `100`, respectively. You may specify new values for those using the `min` and `max` attributes.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeMinAndMaxExample = () => {
  return <CFormRange min={0} max={5} label="Example range" defaultValue="3" />
}
```

## Steps

By default, range inputs "snap" to integer values. To change this, you can specify a `step` value. In the example below, we double the number of steps by using `step={0.5}`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const FormRangeStepsExample = () => {
  return <CFormRange min={0} max={5} step={0.5} label="Example range" defaultValue="3" />
}
```

Inside a `<form>`, a native reset puts the thumb back on the value the range started with and calls `onChange` when that moves it; with `value` set, `onChange` only asks for the first `value`.

## Theme variants

Color the thumb and the fill with the [`theme`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) property.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react'

export const RangeThemeColorsExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex flex-column gap-3">
      <CFormRange theme="primary" id="rangeThemePrimary" label="Primary range" defaultValue="50" />
      <CFormRange
        theme="secondary"
        id="rangeThemeSecondary"
        label="Secondary range"
        defaultValue="50"
      />
      <CFormRange theme="success" id="rangeThemeSuccess" label="Success range" defaultValue="50" />
      <CFormRange theme="danger" id="rangeThemeDanger" label="Danger range" defaultValue="50" />
      <CFormRange theme="warning" id="rangeThemeWarning" label="Warning range" defaultValue="50" />
      <CFormRange theme="info" id="rangeThemeInfo" label="Info range" defaultValue="50" />
    </div>
  )
}
```

# React Form Range Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Form Range component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CFormRange

```jsx
import { CFormRange } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the component. |
| `defaultValue` | `string \| number` | - | The initial value of an uncontrolled range — read once on mount. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. |
| `hidden` | `boolean` | - | Hides the range. The attribute goes on the `.form-range` wrapper, so a `label` rendered before it stays visible. |
| `label` | `ReactNode` | - | Add a caption for a component. |
| `max` | `number` | `100` | Specifies the maximum value for the component. |
| `min` | `number` | `0` | Specifies the minimum value for the component. |
| `onChange` | `((event: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement, Element>, value: number) => void)` | - | Called when the value changes, with the change event of the input and the new value as a number. |
| `readOnly` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the readonly state for the component. |
| `step` | `number` | - | Specifies the interval between legal numbers in the component. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `ticks` | `(number \| string \| { value?: number, label?: ReactNode, className?: string \| string[], style?: CSSProperties })[]` | - | Tick marks under the track. A number is a bare tick at that value; a string is a label placed by its position in the array, the first at `min` and the last at `max`; an object sets `value`, `label`, `className` and `style`, and without a `value` is placed by its position. |
| `tooltipClassName` | `string` | - | Classes for the value tooltip, for example a `theme-{color}` class, since a tooltip does not inherit the `theme` of the range. |
| `tooltips` | `boolean \| "always"` | `false` | Shows a tooltip with the current value above the thumb: `true` while the input is hovered, dragged or focused, `'always'` at all times. |
| `tooltipsFormat` | `((value: number) => ReactNode)` | - | Formats the tooltip content. A string it returns is also the `aria-valuetext` of the input. |
| `track` | `boolean \| "fill"` | `fill` | Fills the track up to the thumb. Set `false` to leave the track unfilled. |
| `value` | `string \| number` | - | The value of a controlled range. |

# React Range Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Range component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

### CSS variables

`.form-range`, the wrapper `<CFormRange>` renders, carries the tokens; `className` and `style` land on it. The pseudo-elements that draw the thumb and the track cannot be reached from a stylesheet of your own in every engine, so a token on the wrapper is the way to restyle them:

```css
.form-range.brand {
  --cui-range-thumb-width: 1.5rem;
  --cui-range-track-height: .25rem;
  --cui-range-track-fill-bg: var(--cui-success-base);
}
```

`--cui-range-fill` is not a token: the component writes it from the value and the CSS reads it.

```scss
$form-range-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-range-track-width: 100%,
    --cui-range-track-height: .5rem,
    --cui-range-track-cursor: pointer,
    --cui-range-track-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg-2), var(--cui-bg-3)),
    --cui-range-track-border-radius: 1rem,
    --cui-range-track-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-inset),
    --cui-range-track-fill-bg: var(--cui-primary-base),
    --cui-range-track-disabled-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg-4), var(--cui-fg-3)),
    --cui-range-thumb-width: 1rem,
    --cui-range-thumb-height: var(--cui-range-thumb-width),
    --cui-range-thumb-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg),
    --cui-range-thumb-border: 0,
    --cui-range-thumb-border-radius: 1rem,
    --cui-range-thumb-box-shadow: 0 .1rem .25rem color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-black) 10%, transparent),
    --cui-range-thumb-active-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg-muted),
    --cui-range-thumb-disabled-bg: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-property: #{"background-color, border-color, box-shadow"},
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-duration: .15s,
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-timing: ease-in-out,
    --cui-range-thumb-focus-ring-width: var(--cui-focus-ring-width),
    --cui-range-tick-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-range-tick-height: .5rem,
    --cui-range-tick-minor-height: calc(var(--cui-range-tick-height) * .75),
    --cui-range-tick-bg: var(--cui-bg-4),
    --cui-range-tick-label-margin-top: .125rem,
    --cui-range-tick-label-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-range-tick-label-color: var(--cui-fg-2),
  ),
  $form-range-tokens
);
```

# React Range Slider Component

> Enhance your forms with our customizable React Range Slider component for advanced range selection.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Overview

The **React Range Slider** component allows users to select a value or range of values within a predefined range. It renders the markup of the [range](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/range/): a `<div class="form-range">` with one native `<input type="range">` per handle, so it looks like a range and reads its tokens, and adds what the range does not have: several handles on one track, `distance` between them, a press on the track that moves the nearest handle, clickable ticks and a vertical orientation. `className`, `style`, `theme`, `dir`, `hidden`, `role` and the `ref` land on the `.form-range`, which is a group named by `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby`; other input attributes, such as `id` (on the first handle) and `aria-describedby`, reach the handles.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      defaultValue={[25, 75]}
      ticks={['Low', 'Medium', 'High']}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum intensity', 'Maximum intensity']}
    />
  )
}
```

## Features

- **Multiple Handles:** Select single or multiple values within the range.
- **Ticks:** Draw ticks with labels at specific points on the slider.
- **Tooltips:** Show dynamic tooltips displaying current values.
- **Vertical Orientation:** Rotate the slider for vertical layouts.
- **Clickable Ticks:** Enable users to click on ticks to set slider values.
- **Disabled State:** Disable the slider to prevent user interaction.

## Basic React Range Slider

Create a simple range slider with default settings.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderBasicExample = () => {
  return <CRangeSlider defaultValue={50} ariaLabel={['Volume']} />
}
```

## With form field

Wrap the control in [`<CFormField>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/field/) to lay it out with its label and description, and to get validation feedback in the right place. Point `aria-labelledby` at the label and `aria-describedby` at the description: the slider is a group named by the label, "Budget" here, its handles carry their own names, "Minimum" and "Maximum", and the text below describes every handle (see [Accessibility](#accessibility)).

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CFormField, CFormText } from '@coreui/react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderFormFieldExample = () => {
  return (
    <CFormField>
      <span className="form-label" id="budgetLabel">
        Budget
      </span>
      <CRangeSlider
        aria-describedby="budgetHelp"
        aria-labelledby="budgetLabel"
        ariaLabel={['Minimum', 'Maximum']}
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        name={['budgetMin', 'budgetMax']}
      />
      <CFormText id="budgetHelp">Monthly spend, in thousands.</CFormText>
    </CFormField>
  )
}
```

## Multiple handles

Enable multiple handles to allow the selection of a range or/and multiple values. The handles share one track, the band runs from the lowest handle to the highest, and each handle is a native range input, so dragging, the keyboard, touch, form submission and form reset work as they do for one. The handles stay in order, a press on the track moves the nearest one and it follows the pointer until it is released, and when two of them meet the one that can still move stays on top.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderMultipleHandlesExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CRangeSlider
        className="mb-4"
        defaultValue={[20, 40]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        className="mb-4"
        defaultValue={[20, 40, 60]}
        ariaLabel={['Checkpoint 1', 'Checkpoint 2', 'Checkpoint 3']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        defaultValue={[20, 40, 60, 80]}
        ariaLabel={['Stage 1', 'Stage 2', 'Stage 3', 'Stage 4']}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Vertical Range Slider

Rotate the slider to a vertical orientation.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderVerticalExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex">
      <CRangeSlider className="me-4" defaultValue={20} vertical ariaLabel={['Volume']} />
      <CRangeSlider
        className="me-4"
        defaultValue={[20, 80]}
        vertical
        ariaLabel={['Minimum temperature', 'Maximum temperature']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        defaultValue={[20, 80, 100]}
        vertical
        ariaLabel={['Level 1', 'Level 2', 'Level 3']}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Disabled

Disable the slider to prevent user interaction.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderDisabledExample = () => {
  return (
    <>

        defaultValue={[50, 75]}

        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Min and max

React Range Slider component has implicit values for `min` and `max`—`0` and `100`, respectively. You may specify new values for those using the `min` and `max` attributes.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderMinAndMaxExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CRangeSlider
        className="mb-4"
        min={-50}
        max={150}
        defaultValue={50}
        ariaLabel={['Temperature']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        min={-50}
        max={150}
        defaultValue={[50, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum temperature', 'Maximum temperature']}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Steps

Range Slider inputs automatically "snap" to whole numbers. To modify this behavior, set a `step` value. In the example below, we increase the number of steps by specifying `step="0.25"`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderStepsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CRangeSlider className="mb-4" step={0.25} defaultValue={50} ariaLabel={['Weight']} />
      <CRangeSlider
        step={0.25}
        defaultValue={[50, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum weight', 'Maximum weight']}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Distance

Sets the minimum distance between multiple slider handles by setting `distance` and ensures that the handles do not overlap or get too close.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderDistanceExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      distance={10}
      defaultValue={[50, 75]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
    />
  )
}
```

## Ticks

Add ticks to specific points on the slider for better context. If you provide an array of strings, as in the example below, then ticks will be spaced at equal distances from the beginning to the end of the slider, each labelled with its string.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTicksExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      ticks={['Start', 'Middle', 'End']}
      defaultValue={[30, 70]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum progress', 'Maximum progress']}
    />
  )
}
```

### Ticks customization

Ticks can be configured as an array of strings, numbers or objects. A number is a bare tick at that value, with no text; with objects you can specify additional properties like `value`, `label`, `className`, and `style`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTicksCustomizationExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      min={-50}
      max={100}
      ticks={[
        {
          value: -50,
          label: '-50°C',
          className: 'fg-info',
        },
        {
          value: 0,
          label: '0°C',
          style: {
            fontWeight: 'bold',
          },
        },
        {
          value: 20,
          label: '20°C',
          className: ['fg-warning'],
        },
        {
          value: 100,
          label: '100°C',
          className: 'fg-danger',
        },
      ]}
      tooltipsFormat={(value) => `${value}°C`}
      defaultValue={[-10, 40]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum temperature', 'Maximum temperature']}
    />
  )
}
```

### Tick marks

Every tick is taller when it has text, so bare numbers and labelled points mix in one `ticks` array. All of them are laid out on one grid, so unevenly spaced values stay aligned.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTickMarksExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      defaultValue={[25, 75]}
      ticks={[
        { value: 0, label: 'Cold' },
        25,
        { value: 50, label: 'Mild' },
        75,
        { value: 100, label: 'Hot' },
      ]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum temperature', 'Maximum temperature']}
    />
  )
}
```

### Clickable ticks

By default, users can click on ticks to set the slider to specific values. You can disable this feature by setting `clickableTicks` to `false`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTicksClickableExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      clickableTicks={false}
      ticks={['Low', 'Medium', 'High']}
      defaultValue={[20, 80]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum level', 'Maximum level']}
    />
  )
}
```

## Tooltips

The value tooltip is the [Tooltip](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/tooltip/) component's markup: the component renders `<div class="form-range-tooltip tooltip bs-tooltip-top">` with the tooltip's arrow and body, so it takes the tooltip's look and its `--cui-tooltip-*` tokens. It does not inherit the slider's `theme`; give it its own through `tooltipClassName`.

By default, tooltips show the current value of a handle while the pointer is over it, while it is held, and while it has a visible focus. Set `tooltips` to `"always"` to keep them visible at all times, or to `false` to turn them off.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTooltipsExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex flex-column gap-5 pt-5">
      <CRangeSlider
        tooltips="always"
        defaultValue={[40, 60]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        tooltips={false}
        defaultValue={[40, 60]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Tooltips formatting

Customize the content of tooltips using the `tooltipsFormat` option. This can be a function that formats the tooltip text based on the current value.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTooltipsFormatingExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRangeSlider
      max={1000}
      ticks={[
        {
          value: 0,
          label: '$0',
        },
        {
          value: 250,
          label: '$250',
        },
        {
          value: 500,
          label: '$500',
        },
        {
          value: 1000,
          label: '$1000',
        },
      ]}
      tooltipsFormat={(value) => `$${value}`}
      defaultValue={[100, 350]}
      ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
    />
  )
}
```

## Track

The `track` property allows you to customize how the slider's track is displayed. By default, the `track` property is set to `'fill'` enabling dynamic filling of the track based on the slider's current value(s). This means the filled portion of the track will adjust automatically as the slider handle(s) move, offering a responsive visual representation of the selected range.

### Disable filling

If you set `track` to `false`, the slider's track will not display any fill. Only the default track background will be visible, which can be useful for minimalist designs or when you use more then two handles.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTrackExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CRangeSlider className="mb-4" track={false} defaultValue={50} ariaLabel={['Volume']} />
      <CRangeSlider
        className="mb-4"
        track={false}
        defaultValue={[50, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        track={false}
        defaultValue={[25, 50, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Checkpoint 1', 'Checkpoint 2', 'Checkpoint 3']}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Theme variants

Color the filled track and the handles with the [`theme`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) property.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderThemeColorsExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex flex-column gap-4">
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="primary"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Primary minimum', 'Primary maximum']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="secondary"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Secondary minimum', 'Secondary maximum']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="success"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Success minimum', 'Success maximum']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="danger"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Danger minimum', 'Danger maximum']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="warning"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Warning minimum', 'Warning maximum']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="info"
        defaultValue={[25, 75]}
        ariaLabel={['Info minimum', 'Info maximum']}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

The `theme` colors the track and the handles; the tooltip keeps its default look. To theme the tooltip, pass a class through `tooltipClassName` — it lands on the tooltip only. `theme-secondary` gives a grey tooltip on the default slider; `theme-danger` makes the tooltip match a danger slider.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderTooltipClassNameExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex flex-column gap-4">
      <CRangeSlider
        defaultValue={[40]}
        tooltipClassName="theme-secondary"
        ariaLabel={['Secondary tooltip']}
      />
      <CRangeSlider
        theme="danger"
        defaultValue={[60]}
        tooltipClassName="theme-danger"
        ariaLabel={['Danger slider, danger tooltip']}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Validation

_Added in 6.0.0._

A range never fails the browser's own validation: a handle always holds a value between `min` and `max` on a step, and `required` does not apply to it. A state comes from the page, when the value breaks a rule the browser does not know, such as a budget below the minimum of a plan.

- Give it with `validationState`. The state shows on the slider and on its handles: `'invalid'` colours the thumbs, sets `aria-invalid` on every handle and adds the invalid feedback that follows the slider to their `aria-describedby`.
- `'invalid'` blocks the submit through the first handle, with the text of the feedback as the message the browser shows, or `Invalid value.` without one, and the browser moves the focus to that handle. `'valid'` and a custom state do not block, and neither does a disabled slider.
- When the user moves a handle, or the form is reset, the slider calls `onValidationStateChange(undefined)` before it reports the change; pass your state setter there to drop the state. A change of `value` from your code keeps it.
- A validity you set on a handle with `setCustomValidity()` shows on the slider once a validation reports it, and a given `'valid'` shows over it.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CForm, CFormFeedback, CFormField } from '@coreui/react'
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderValidationExample = () => {
  const [budgetState, setBudgetState] = useState<string | undefined>('invalid')

  return (
    <CForm className="row g-4" noValidate validate>
      <CFormField className="col-12">
        <span className="form-label" id="planBudgetLabel">
          Budget
        </span>
        <CRangeSlider
          aria-labelledby="planBudgetLabel"
          ariaLabel={['Minimum', 'Maximum']}
          defaultValue={[5, 40]}
          name={['planBudgetMin', 'planBudgetMax']}
          onValidationStateChange={setBudgetState}
          validationState={budgetState}
        />
        <CFormFeedback validationState="invalid">
          The Team plan starts at 10 thousand a month.
        </CFormFeedback>
      </CFormField>
      <div className="col-12">
        <CButton color="primary" type="submit">
          Save
        </CButton>
      </div>
    </CForm>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The slider works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultValue` | the slider, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `value` | your component |

Both take a single number as well as an array of values, and `onChange` fires in **both** modes — so you can watch the state without taking it over. A native reset of the form puts back the values the slider started with and calls `onChange` when that moves a handle; a controlled slider only asks for its first `value` there.

### Uncontrolled

Give the slider a starting point and let it manage itself.

```jsx
<CRangeSlider defaultValue={[20, 80]} />
```

### Controlled

Pass `value` and the slider is fully controlled: it renders exactly what you pass, and dragging a handle only fires `onChange`. Feed the change back and the handle follows; ignore it and the handle stays on your value.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const RangeSliderControlledExample = () => {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<number[]>([25, 75])

  return (
    <>
      <CRangeSlider
        onChange={setValue}
        value={value}
        ariaLabel={['Minimum price', 'Maximum price']}
      />
      <div className="mt-4 d-flex align-items-center gap-4">
        <CButton theme="secondary" onClick={() => setValue([25, 75])}>
          Reset
        </CButton>
        <span>Current value: {value.join(' – ')}</span>
      </div>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Accessibility

Each handle is a native `<input type="range">`, so it is a slider with its value, minimum and maximum without any ARIA of its own, and the browser handles the keyboard: the arrow keys, <kbd>Page Up</kbd>, <kbd>Page Down</kbd>, <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd>. In a vertical slider the handles carry `aria-orientation="vertical"`, and <kbd>→</kbd> increases the value in every browser, as <kbd>↑</kbd> does.

The slider is a `group`. Give it the name of the field, with `aria-labelledby` pointing at a visible label or with `aria-label`: a screen reader announces the group, "Budget", when the focus enters it, and then each handle by its own name, so it can tell the handles of one slider from another's. A single handle repeats the name of the group, since it has none of its own. `aria-describedby` describes every handle. Name the handles themselves with `ariaLabel`: an array with one name per handle, or a function `(index, total) => string`. Without it, two handles are named "Minimum value" and "Maximum value" and more handles "Value 1", "Value 2" and so on. A single handle has no generated name: it takes the name of the group, followed by its `ariaLabel` when it has one, or a `<label>` for its `id`. A `role` you pass replaces `group` on the slider. While a handle sits on a tick labelled with text, its `aria-valuetext` adds the label to the value ("50, Medium", or the `tooltipsFormat` text followed by the label when they differ).

Tooltips and tick marks are hidden from assistive technology (`aria-hidden="true"`): a tooltip repeats the value the handle already announces, and a tick label reaches the handle through `aria-valuetext` while the handle sits on its tick.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CRangeSlider /&gt;](./api/#crangeslider)

# React Range Slider Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Range Slider component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## CRangeSlider

```jsx
import { CRangeSlider } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaLabel` | `string[] \| ((index: number, total: number) => string)` | - | Accessible names of the handles, so a screen reader can tell them apart: an array with one name per handle, or a function that returns the name of the handle at `index` out of `total`. Without it, two handles are named `"Minimum value"` and `"Maximum value"`, more handles `"Value {n}"`, and a single handle has no name of its own. `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` names the slider, which is a `group`; a single handle takes that name, followed by its own when it has one, or a `<label>` for its `id`. |
| `autoFocus` | `boolean` | - | Focuses the first thumb when the component mounts. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the `.form-range` wrapper of the slider. |
| `clickableTicks` | `boolean` | `true` | Pressing a tick moves the nearest handle to its value, and the handle follows the pointer until it is released. Set `false` to disable. |
| `defaultValue` | `number \| number[]` | - | The initial value(s) of an uncontrolled slider — read once on mount. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | `false` | Disables every handle. |
| `distance` | `number` | `0` | Keeps neighbouring handles at least this many units apart. |
| `hidden` | `boolean` | - | Hides the component. The attribute goes on the wrapper of the thumbs and the track. |
| `max` | `number` | `100` | Specifies the maximum value of the slider. |
| `min` | `number` | `0` | Specifies the minimum value of the slider. |
| `name` | `string \| string[]` | - | Name of each slider input, in order. An array maps one to one, and a shorter array leaves the remaining handles unnamed. A string is suffixed with the handle index, so `"price"` submits `price-0` and `price-1`. Without a name the handles are not submitted with the form. |
| `onChange` | `((value: number[]) => void)` | - | Called with the values of every handle when one of them changes. |
| `onInput` | `InputEventHandler<HTMLInputElement>` | - | Method called on every `input` event of a thumb. |
| `onValidationStateChange` | `((validationState: ValidationState \| undefined) => void)` | - | Callback fired with `undefined` when the user moves a handle, or the form is reset, while `validationState` is set. A given state is a verdict on the value it was given for; clear it here, so the slider shows only the validity you set on a handle, if any. |
| `step` | `number` | `1` | Specifies the interval between legal numbers in the slider. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `ticks` | `(number \| string \| { value?: number, label?: ReactNode, className?: string \| string[], style?: CSSProperties })[]` | - | Tick marks under the track. A number is a bare tick at that value; a string is a label placed by its position in the array, the first at `min` and the last at `max`; an object sets `value`, `label`, `className` and `style`, and without a `value` is placed by its position. |
| `tooltipClassName` | `string` | - | Classes for the value tooltips, for example a `theme-{color}` class, since a tooltip does not inherit the `theme` of the slider. |
| `tooltips` | `boolean \| "always"` | `true` | Shows the current value of each handle: `true` while the handle is hovered, dragged or focused, `'always'` at all times, `false` never. |
| `tooltipsFormat` | `((value: number) => ReactNode)` | - | Formats the tooltip content. A string it returns is also the `aria-valuetext` of the handle. |
| `track` | `boolean \| "fill"` | `fill` | Fills the track between the lowest and the highest handle, or up to a single handle. Set `false` to leave the track unfilled. |
| `validationState` | `'valid' \| 'invalid' \| string` | - | The validation state, rendered as the `is-{state}` class on the slider and its handles; `'invalid'` also sets `aria-invalid` on every handle and blocks the submit through the first one. Any custom state declared in the `$form-validation-states` Sass map is accepted. The user's next move of a handle asks to drop it through `onValidationStateChange`. |
| `value` | `number \| number[]` | - | The controlled value(s) of the slider — a single value or an array for several handles. Pair it with `onChange`; for the uncontrolled mode use `defaultValue` instead. |
| `vertical` | `boolean` | `false` | Stands the slider up: the value grows from the bottom, the tooltips sit at the start and the ticks at the end. |

# React Range Slider Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Range Slider component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

### CSS variables

The slider renders a [range](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/range/styling/), so it reads the range's tokens, declared on the `.form-range` that `className` and `style` land on: one setting styles both controls. `--cui-range-track-fill-bg` colours the band between the handles and `--cui-range-tick-*` the tick marks and their labels.

```scss
$form-range-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-range-track-width: 100%,
    --cui-range-track-height: .5rem,
    --cui-range-track-cursor: pointer,
    --cui-range-track-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg-2), var(--cui-bg-3)),
    --cui-range-track-border-radius: 1rem,
    --cui-range-track-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-inset),
    --cui-range-track-fill-bg: var(--cui-primary-base),
    --cui-range-track-disabled-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg-4), var(--cui-fg-3)),
    --cui-range-thumb-width: 1rem,
    --cui-range-thumb-height: var(--cui-range-thumb-width),
    --cui-range-thumb-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg),
    --cui-range-thumb-border: 0,
    --cui-range-thumb-border-radius: 1rem,
    --cui-range-thumb-box-shadow: 0 .1rem .25rem color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-black) 10%, transparent),
    --cui-range-thumb-active-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg-muted),
    --cui-range-thumb-disabled-bg: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-property: #{"background-color, border-color, box-shadow"},
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-duration: .15s,
    --cui-range-thumb-transition-timing: ease-in-out,
    --cui-range-thumb-focus-ring-width: var(--cui-focus-ring-width),
    --cui-range-tick-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-range-tick-height: .5rem,
    --cui-range-tick-minor-height: calc(var(--cui-range-tick-height) * .75),
    --cui-range-tick-bg: var(--cui-bg-4),
    --cui-range-tick-label-margin-top: .125rem,
    --cui-range-tick-label-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-range-tick-label-color: var(--cui-fg-2),
  ),
  $form-range-tokens
);
```

A vertical slider's height:

```scss
$form-range-vertical-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-range-vertical-height: 10rem,
  ),
  $form-range-vertical-tokens
);
```

`--cui-range-fill-start` and `--cui-range-fill` are not tokens: the component writes them from the lowest and the highest handle, and the CSS draws the band between them.

#### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-range-tick-label-color': '#333',
  '--cui-range-track-bg': '#f8f9fa',
}

return <CRangeSlider style={customVars} />
```
