## Disabled

Add the `disabled` boolean prop to any `<CButton>` component to make buttons look inactive. Disabled button has `pointer-events: none` applied to, disabling hover and active states from triggering.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonDisabledExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" disabled>
        Primary button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" disabled>
        Button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline" disabled>
        Primary button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" disabled>
        Button
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

Disabled buttons using the `<a>` component act a little different:

`<a>`s don't support the `disabled` attribute, so CoreUI has to add `.disabled` className to make buttons look inactive. CoreUI also has to add to the disabled button component `aria-disabled="true"` attribute to show the state of the component to assistive technologies.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonDisabled2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" disabled>
        Primary link
      </CButton>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="secondary" disabled>
        Link
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

The `.disabled` class uses `pointer-events: none` to try to disable the link functionality of `<a>`s, but that CSS property is not yet standardized. Besides, even in browsers that do support `pointer-events: none`, keyboard navigation remains unaffected, meaning that sighted keyboard users and users of assistive technologies will still be able to activate these links. So to be safe, we automatically add a `tabindex="-1"` attribute on disabled links (to prevent them from receiving keyboard focus) and use custom JavaScript to disable their functionality.

## Block buttons

Create buttons that span the full width of a parent—by using utilities.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlockExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Here we create a responsive variation, starting with vertically stacked buttons until the `md` breakpoint, where `.d-md-block` replaces the `.d-grid` class, thus nullifying the `gap-3` utility. Resize your browser to see them change.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock2Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 d-md-block">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton> <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

You can adjust the width of your block buttons with grid column width classes. For example, for a half-width "block button", use `.col-6`. Center it horizontally with `.mx-auto`, too.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock3Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 col-6 mx-auto">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Additional utilities can be used to adjust the alignment of buttons when horizontal. Here we've taken our previous responsive example and added some flex utilities and a margin utility on the button to right align the buttons when they're no longer stacked.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock4Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 d-md-flex justify-content-md-end">
      <CButton theme="primary" className="me-md-3">
        Button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Toggle states

Add the `toggle` boolean prop to create simple on/off toggle buttons. A toggle button flips the `.active` class and the `aria-pressed` attribute on click. Seed the initial state with `defaultActive`.

> Visually, these toggle buttons are identical to the [checkbox toggle buttons](https://coreui.io/react/docs/forms/checkbox/#checkbox-toggle-buttons). However, they are conveyed differently by assistive technologies: the checkbox toggles will be announced by screen readers as "checked"/"not checked" (since, despite their appearance, they are fundamentally still checkboxes), whereas these toggle buttons will be announced as "button"/"button pressed". The choice between these two approaches will depend on the type of toggle you are creating, and whether or not the toggle will make sense to users when announced as a checkbox or as an actual button.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonToggleExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div className="d-flex gap-1 mb-4">
        <CButton toggle>Toggle button</CButton>
        <CButton toggle defaultActive>
          Active toggle button
        </CButton>
        <CButton toggle disabled>
          Disabled toggle button
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <div className="d-flex gap-1">
        <CButton theme="primary" toggle>
          Toggle button
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary" toggle defaultActive>
          Active toggle button
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary" toggle disabled>
          Disabled toggle button
        </CButton>
      </div>
    </>
  )
}
```

Toggle links behave the same way:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonToggleLinkExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div className="d-flex gap-1 mb-4">
        <CButton as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle>
          Toggle link
        </CButton>
        <CButton as="a" href="#" role="button" toggle defaultActive>
          Active toggle link
        </CButton>
        <CButton as="a" role="button" toggle disabled>
          Disabled toggle link
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <div className="d-flex gap-1">
        <CButton as="a" theme="primary" href="#" role="button" toggle>
          Toggle link
        </CButton>
        <CButton as="a" theme="primary" href="#" role="button" toggle defaultActive>
          Active toggle link
        </CButton>
        <CButton as="a" theme="primary" role="button" toggle disabled>
          Disabled toggle link
        </CButton>
      </div>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The toggle works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the pressed state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultActive` | the button, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `active` | your component |

`defaultActive` seeds the uncontrolled toggle — the button flips itself from there, as the examples above do. Pass `active` and the button renders exactly what you pass: a click only fires `onClick`, so flip the state there, or nothing toggles.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonToggleControlledExample = () => {
  const [pressed, setPressed] = useState(false)

  return (
    <div className="d-flex align-items-center gap-3">
      <CButton theme="primary" toggle active={pressed} onClick={() => setPressed(!pressed)}>
        {pressed ? 'On' : 'Off'}
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" onClick={() => setPressed(false)}>
        Reset
      </CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

# React Button Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Button component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CButton

```jsx
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `active` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the active state for the component. With `toggle` it is the controlled active state of the toggle button. For the uncontrolled toggle use `defaultActive`; manage the controlled state from `onClick`. |
| `as` | `(ElementType & "symbol") \| (ElementType & "object") \| (ElementType & "button") \| (ElementType & "cite") \| (ElementType & "data") \| ... 175 more ...` | `button` | Component used for the root node. Either a string to use a HTML element or a component. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `color` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `defaultActive` | `boolean` | - | The initial active state of an uncontrolled toggle button — read once on mount. Ignored when `active` is set. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. |
| `href` | `string` | - | The href attribute specifies the URL of the page the link goes to. |
| `iconOnly` | `boolean` | - | Square the button for a lone icon - remember to give it an `aria-label`. |
| `link` | `boolean` | - | Render the button as a link. It behaves like a button but takes its color from the link color rather than from a theme, so `theme` and `variant` do not apply to it. |
| `role` | `string` | - | The role attribute describes the role of an element in programs that can make use of it, such as screen readers or magnifiers. |
| `shape` | `'rounded' \| 'rounded-top' \| 'rounded-end' \| 'rounded-bottom' \| 'rounded-start' \| 'rounded-circle' \| 'rounded-pill' \| 'rounded-0' \| 'rounded-1' \| 'rounded-2' \| 'rounded-3' \| string` | - | Select the shape of the component. |
| `size` | `"xs" \| "sm" \| "lg"` | - | Size the component extra small, small or large. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. Pair it with `variant` for the shape — a button is a shape plus a colour. The class may also sit on any ancestor, so theming a toolbar themes the buttons inside it. |
| `toggle` | `boolean` | - | Make the button behave as a toggle button. It manages its own active/pressed state, toggling it on click and reflecting it via the `aria-pressed` attribute. |
| `type` | `"button" \| "submit" \| "reset"` | `button` | Specifies the type of button. Always specify the type attribute for the `<button>` element. Different browsers may use different default types for the `<button>` element. |
| `variant` | `"ghost" \| "outline" \| "solid" \| "subtle"` | - | Set the shape of the button — how much ink it uses. Defaults to `solid` when `theme` is set. |

# React Button Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Button component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Button supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$button-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-btn-gap: var(--cui-btn-input-gap),
    --cui-btn-min-height: var(--cui-btn-input-min-height),
    --cui-btn-padding-y: var(--cui-btn-input-padding-y),
    --cui-btn-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-padding-x),
    --cui-btn-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-font-size),
    --cui-btn-font-weight: var(--cui-btn-input-font-weight),
    --cui-btn-line-height: var(--cui-btn-input-line-height),
    --cui-btn-white-space: nowrap,
    --cui-btn-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-bg: #{$btn-bg},
    --cui-btn-border-width: var(--cui-btn-input-border-width),
    --cui-btn-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-border-radius),
    --cui-btn-hover-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-hover-bg: #{$btn-hover-bg},
    --cui-btn-hover-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-active-bg: #{$btn-hover-bg},
    --cui-btn-active-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-color: #{$btn-color},
    --cui-btn-disabled-bg: #{$btn-bg},
    --cui-btn-disabled-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-shadow: inset 0 3px 5px color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-black) 12.5%, transparent),
    --cui-btn-disabled-opacity: var(--cui-btn-input-disabled-opacity),
    --cui-btn-transition-property: var(--cui-btn-input-action-transition-property),
    --cui-btn-transition-duration: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-duration),
    --cui-btn-transition-timing: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-timing)
  ),
  $button-tokens
);
```

`.btn-link` rewrites the ones that make it read as a link:

```scss
$button-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-btn-font-weight: var(--cui-font-weight-normal),
    --cui-btn-color: var(--cui-link-color),
    --cui-btn-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-hover-color: var(--cui-link-hover-color),
    --cui-btn-hover-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-hover-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-color: var(--cui-link-hover-color),
    --cui-btn-active-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-active-border-color: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-btn-disabled-bg: transparent,
    --cui-btn-disabled-border-color: transparent
  ),
  $button-link-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-btn-color': '#ffe484',
  '--cui-btn-bg': '#efefef',
}

return <CButton style={customVars}>{/* Button content */}</CButton>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$btn-color:                   var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-bg:                      var(--cui-bg-2) !default;
$btn-hover-bg:                var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-outline-color:           var(--cui-fg-2) !default;
$btn-outline-border-color:    var(--cui-border-color) !default;
$btn-outline-hover-color:     var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-outline-hover-bg:        var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-subtle-color:            var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-subtle-bg:               var(--cui-bg-2) !default;
$btn-subtle-hover-bg:         var(--cui-bg-3) !default;

$btn-ghost-color:             var(--cui-fg-2) !default;
$btn-ghost-hover-color:       var(--cui-fg-body) !default;
$btn-ghost-hover-bg:          var(--cui-bg-1) !default;
```

## Sass maps

`$button-sizes` lists the sizes that get a class. Each name generates `.btn-{size}` — plus the matching `.btn-group-{size}` selector — pointing the button's variables at the shared `--cui-btn-input-{size}-*` scale, so adding a name is enough once that scale defines it. Buttons inside an input group follow the group's own sizes, `$input-group-sizes`.

```scss
$button-sizes: defaults(
  ("xs", "sm", "lg"),
  $button-sizes
);
```

`$button-variants` holds every variant. Each entry names, per state, the theme token a button variable reads and the neutral value behind it; `disabled` repeats `base`. Add an entry and both spellings of the new variant are generated — the variant class and the `.btn-{variant}-{color}` class.

```scss
// Each entry names the theme token a button variable reads and the neutral
// value behind it, so the variant class alone is a grey button and any theme
// colour — from `.theme-*`, from a `.btn-*-{color}` class or from an ancestor —
// colours the whole set. `disabled` repeats `base`.
$button-variants: () !default;
$button-variants: defaults(
  (
    "solid": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("bg", $btn-bg),
        "border-color": ("bg", $btn-bg)
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-hover-bg)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-hover-bg)
      )
    ),
    "outline": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-outline-color),
        "bg": "transparent",
        "border-color": ("border", $btn-outline-border-color)
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-outline-hover-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-outline-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-outline-border-color)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-outline-hover-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-outline-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-outline-border-color)
      )
    ),
    "subtle": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-subtle", $btn-subtle-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("fg-emphasis", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-muted", $btn-subtle-hover-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("fg-emphasis", $btn-subtle-color),
        "bg": ("bg-muted", $btn-subtle-hover-bg),
        "border-color": "transparent"
      )
    ),
    "ghost": (
      "base": (
        "color": ("fg", $btn-ghost-color),
        "bg": "transparent",
        "border-color": "transparent"
      ),
      "hover": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-ghost-hover-color),
        "bg": ("hover", $btn-ghost-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("hover", $btn-ghost-hover-bg)
      ),
      "active": (
        "color": ("contrast", $btn-ghost-hover-color),
        "bg": ("active", $btn-ghost-hover-bg),
        "border-color": ("active", $btn-ghost-hover-bg)
      )
    )
  ),
  $button-variants
);
```

## Sass mixins

`button-variant()` turns one entry of that map into the button's variables.

```scss
@function btn-variant-value($value) {
  @if $value == "transparent" {
    @return transparent;
  }

  @if meta.type-of($value) == "list" {
    @return var(--cui-theme-#{list.nth($value, 1)}, #{list.nth($value, 2)});
  }

  @return var(--cui-theme-#{$value});
}

@mixin button-variant($variant) {
  $config: map.get($button-variants, $variant);

  @each $property, $value in map.get($config, "base") {
    --cui-btn-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
    --cui-btn-disabled-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
  }

  @each $state in ("hover", "active") {
    @each $property, $value in map.get($config, $state) {
      --cui-btn-#{$state}-#{$property}: #{btn-variant-value($value)};
    }
  }
}
```

## Sass loops

```scss
@each $variant, $config in $button-variants {
  .btn-#{$variant} {
    @include button-variant($variant);
  }
}
```

```scss
@each $size, $_ in $button-sizes {
  .btn-#{$size},
  .btn-group-#{$size} > :is(#{$btn-variant-selectors}) {
    --cui-btn-gap: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-gap);
    --cui-btn-min-height: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-min-height);
    --cui-btn-padding-y: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-y);
    --cui-btn-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-padding-x);
    --cui-btn-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-font-size);
    --cui-btn-line-height: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-line-height);
    --cui-btn-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-#{$size}-border-radius);
  }
}
```

### Deprecated color classes

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

The loop that generates the deprecated color classes, pointing each one at the matching theme color. It lives in the opt-in [`coreui-legacy.css`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/optimize/#v5-compatibility-css), not in `coreui.css`.

```scss
@each $color in map.keys($theme-colors) {
  $selectors: (string.unquote(".btn-#{$color}"));

  @each $variant, $_ in $button-variants {
    @if $variant != "solid" {
      $selectors: list.append($selectors, string.unquote(".btn-#{$variant}-#{$color}"), comma);
    }
  }

  #{$selectors} {
    @include theme-tokens($color);
  }
}
```

# React Bootstrap Button Component

> Learn how to use CoreUI’s React Button component with Bootstrap styling to build interactive, accessible, and responsive buttons for forms, tables, modals, and more.

## How to use React Bootstrap Button component

CoreUI provides a set of prebuilt React Button components styled with Bootstrap. Buttons signal actions to users and can initiate events both in the UI and behind the scenes.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary">Primary</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary">Secondary</CButton>
      <CButton theme="success">Success</CButton>
      <CButton theme="info">Info</CButton>
      <CButton theme="warning">Warning</CButton>
      <CButton theme="danger">Danger</CButton>
      <CButton theme="inverse">Inverse</CButton>
      <CButton link>Link</CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

> ## Disable text wrapping
> 
> To prevent text wrapping inside a button, apply the `.text-nowrap` class to the ``. Alternatively, set `$btn-white-space: nowrap` in Sass to apply it globally.
> 
> ## Button components
> 
> The `` component can render as a ``, ``, or `` element. When using it as an anchor for functionality (like toggles), add `role="button"` for accessibility.
> 
> ```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonComponentsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton as="a" theme="primary" href="#" role="button">
        Link
      </CButton>
      <CButton type="submit" theme="primary">
        Button
      </CButton>
      <CButton as="input" type="button" theme="primary" value="Input" />
      <CButton as="input" type="submit" theme="primary" value="Submit" />
      <CButton as="input" type="reset" theme="primary" value="Reset" />
    </>
  )
}
```
> 
> ## Outline buttons
> 
> Use `variant="outline"` to create buttons with a transparent background and colored border — a more subtle alternative to standard buttons.
> 
> ```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonOutlineExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">
        Primary
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline">
        Secondary
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="success" variant="outline">
        Success
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="info" variant="outline">
        Info
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="warning" variant="outline">
        Warning
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="danger" variant="outline">
        Danger
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="inverse" variant="outline">
        Inverse
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```
> 
> ## Ghost buttons
> 
> For minimal buttons with no background or border, use `variant="ghost"`. These are great for secondary actions.
> 
> ```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGhostExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" variant="ghost">
        Primary
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="ghost">
        Secondary
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="success" variant="ghost">
        Success
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="info" variant="ghost">
        Info
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="warning" variant="ghost">
        Warning
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="danger" variant="ghost">
        Danger
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="inverse" variant="ghost">
        Inverse
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```
> 
> 
> Some button styles use light text colors and should be placed on dark backgrounds to maintain contrast.

## Sizes

Create large or small buttons with the `size="lg"` or `size="sm"` props.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonSizesExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" size="lg">
        Large button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" size="lg">
        Large button
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonSizes2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" size="sm">
        Small button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" size="sm">
        Small button
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

You can also use CSS variables for fully custom sizes.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonSizes3Example = () => {
  const customVars = {
    '--cui-btn-padding-y': '.25rem',
    '--cui-btn-padding-x': '.5rem',
    '--cui-btn-font-size': '.75rem',
  } as React.CSSProperties

  return (
    <CButton theme="primary" size="sm" style={customVars}>
      Custom button
    </CButton>
  )
}
```

## Disabled

Disable any `<CButton>` by passing the `disabled` prop. This applies `pointer-events: none` and dims the button.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonDisabledExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" disabled>
        Primary button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" disabled>
        Button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline" disabled>
        Primary button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" disabled>
        Button
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

Disabling anchor elements (`<a>`) requires additional steps: CoreUI applies the `.disabled` class, adds `aria-disabled="true"`, and sets `tabindex="-1"`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonDisabled2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" disabled>
        Primary link
      </CButton>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="secondary" disabled>
        Link
      </CButton>
    </>
  )
}
```

These steps prevent users from interacting with disabled links via keyboard or mouse.

## Block buttons

To make buttons span the full width of their container, use Bootstrap's layout utilities like `.d-grid`, `.w-100`, and `.col-*`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlockExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Responsive layout: vertically stacked until the `md` breakpoint, where `.d-md-block` reverts to inline.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock2Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 d-md-block">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton> <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

You can also create column-based buttons using `.col-6` and center them with `.mx-auto`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock3Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 col-6 mx-auto">
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Use flex utilities and margin helpers to align buttons horizontally when they're no longer stacked.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonBlock4Example = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-grid gap-3 d-md-flex justify-content-md-end">
      <CButton theme="primary" className="me-md-3">
        Button
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
    </div>
  )
}
```

# React Button Group Component

> React button group component allows to group a series of buttons and power them with JavaScript.

## Examples

Wrap a series of `<CButton>` components in `<CButtonGroup>`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic example">
      <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Middle</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

> Ensure the correct role and provide a label}>
> For assistive technologies (ex. screen readers) to communicate that a series of buttons are grouped, a proper `role` attribute has to be provided. For button groups, this should be `role="group"`, while toolbars should have a `role="toolbar"`.
> 
> Besides, groups and toolbars should be provided an understandable label, as most assistive technologies will otherwise not declare them, despite the appearance of the specific role attribute. In the following examples provided here, we apply `aria-label`, but options such as `aria-labelledby` can also be used.

These classes can also be added to groups of links, as an alternative to the [`CNav`](./../navs-tabs/#base-nav) components.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroup2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary" active>
        Active link
      </CButton>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

### With links

These components can also be added to groups of links, as an alternative to the [`CNav` navigation components](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/navs-tabs/).

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupWithLinksExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic example with links">
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary" active aria-current="page">
        Active link
      </CButton>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
      <CButton as="a" href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

### Dividers

Add a divider between buttons with the `divider` property. Most useful when used with buttons that have the same theme color and a solid fill.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupDividersExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Divided button group">
        <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary" active>
          Active
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
      <CButtonGroup divider role="group" aria-label="Divided button group">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
    </>
  )
}
```

Works with vertical button groups, too.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupDividers2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButtonGroup vertical divider role="group" aria-label="Divided vertical button group">
        <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary" active>
          Active
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
      <CButtonGroup vertical divider role="group" aria-label="Divided vertical button group">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Theme variants

Set [`theme`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) on each button to give a whole group one color.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupThemeExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Secondary theme example">
      <CButton theme="secondary">Left</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary">Middle</CButton>
      <CButton theme="secondary">Right</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

You can mix and match button variants in a button group.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupMixedStylesExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic mixed styles example">
      <CButton theme="danger">Left</CButton>
      <CButton theme="warning">Middle</CButton>
      <CButton theme="success">Right</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

## Toggle buttons

Combine button-like checkbox and radio toggle buttons into a seamless looking button group.

### Checkbox

Checkbox toggle buttons can be grouped together. Any or all of the buttons can be checked.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButtonGroup, CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupCheckboxAndRadioExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic checkbox toggle button group">
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        id="btncheck1"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Checkbox 1"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        id="btncheck2"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Checkbox 2"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        id="btncheck3"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Checkbox 3"
      />
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

### Radio

By design, radio toggle button groups can only have one button checked at a time.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButtonGroup, CFormCheck } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupCheckboxAndRadio2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic checkbox toggle button group">
      <CFormCheck
        type="radio"
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        name="btnradio"
        id="btnradio1"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio 1"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        type="radio"
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        name="btnradio"
        id="btnradio2"
        autoComplete="off"
        label="Radio 2"
      />
      <CFormCheck
        type="radio"
        button={{ color: 'primary', variant: 'outline' }}
        name="btnradio"
        id="btnradio3"

## Button toolbar

Join sets of button groups into button toolbars for more complicated components. Use utility classes as needed to space out groups, buttons, and more.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup, CButtonToolbar } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonToolbarExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonToolbar role="toolbar" aria-label="Toolbar with button groups">
      <CButtonGroup className="me-3" role="group" aria-label="First group">
        <CButton theme="primary">1</CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary">2</CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary">3</CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary">4</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
      <CButtonGroup className="me-3" role="group" aria-label="Second group">
        <CButton theme="secondary">5</CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary">6</CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary">7</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
      <CButtonGroup className="me-3" role="group" aria-label="Third group">
        <CButton theme="info">8</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
    </CButtonToolbar>
  )
}
```

## Nesting

Put a `<CButtonGroup>` inside another `<CButtonGroup>` when you need dropdown menus combined with a series of buttons.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CButtonGroup,
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupNestingExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Button group with nested dropdown">
      <CButton theme="primary">1</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">2</CButton>
      <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
        <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownDivider />
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

## Vertical variation

Create a set of buttons that appear vertically stacked rather than horizontally. **Split button dropdowns are not supported here.**

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CButtonGroup,
  CCol,
  CFormCheck,
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
  CRow,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupVerticalExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRow>
      <CCol>
        <CButtonGroup vertical role="group" aria-label="Vertical button group">
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
        </CButtonGroup>
      </CCol>
      <CCol>
        <CButtonGroup vertical role="group" aria-label="Vertical button group">
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
            <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
            <CDropdownMenu>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownDivider />
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
            </CDropdownMenu>
          </CDropdown>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
            <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
            <CDropdownMenu>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownDivider />
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
            </CDropdownMenu>
          </CDropdown>
          <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
            <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
            <CDropdownMenu>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownDivider />
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
            </CDropdownMenu>
          </CDropdown>
          <CDropdown variant="btn-group">
            <CDropdownToggle theme="primary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
            <CDropdownMenu>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
              <CDropdownDivider />
              <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
            </CDropdownMenu>
          </CDropdown>
        </CButtonGroup>
      </CCol>
      <CCol>
        <CButtonGroup vertical role="group" aria-label="Vertical button group">
          <CFormCheck
            type="radio"
            button={{ color: 'danger', variant: 'outline' }}
            name="vbtnradio"
            id="vbtnradio1"
            autoComplete="off"
            label="Radio 1"
            defaultChecked
          />
          <CFormCheck
            type="radio"
            button={{ color: 'danger', variant: 'outline' }}
            name="vbtnradio"
            id="vbtnradio2"
            autoComplete="off"
            label="Radio 2"
          />
          <CFormCheck
            type="radio"
            button={{ color: 'danger', variant: 'outline' }}
            name="vbtnradio"
            id="vbtnradio3"
            autoComplete="off"
            label="Radio 3"
          />
        </CButtonGroup>
      </CCol>
    </CRow>
  )
}
```

# React Button Group Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Button Group component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CButtonGroup

```jsx
import { CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `divider` | `boolean` | - | Draw a separating line between the grouped buttons — for styles whose borders do not separate them, like solid or subtle. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "lg"` | - | Size the component small or large. |
| `vertical` | `boolean` | - | Create a set of buttons that appear vertically stacked rather than horizontally. Split button dropdowns are not supported here. |

## CButtonToolbar

```jsx
import { CButtonToolbar } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |

# React Bootstrap Button Group Component

> Learn how to group buttons using the React Bootstrap Button Group component from CoreUI. Create accessible, styled toolbars and button sets with ease.

## How to use React Bootstrap Button Group component

The React Bootstrap Button Group component allows you to group multiple buttons together into a single toolbar-like unit. Wrap a series of `<CButton>` components in a `<CButtonGroup>` to get started.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic example">
      <CButton theme="primary">Left</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Middle</CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary">Right</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

> Ensure the correct role and provide a label}>
> For assistive technologies (e.g. screen readers) to identify a set of buttons as grouped, use `role="group"` for button groups and `role="toolbar"` for toolbars.
> 
> Always include an accessible label using `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` to clarify the purpose of the group.

React Bootstrap Button Groups can also be applied to a group of links instead of using the [`CNav`](../../navs-tabs/#base-nav) component.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroup2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary" active>
        Active link
      </CButton>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
      <CButton href="#" theme="primary">
        Link
      </CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

## Mixed styles in React Bootstrap Button Groups

Combine buttons with different styles within a single group for more flexible UI designs.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CButtonGroup } from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupMixedStylesExample = () => {
  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic mixed styles example">
      <CButton theme="danger">Left</CButton>
      <CButton theme="warning">Middle</CButton>
      <CButton theme="success">Right</CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

## Outlined button styles

```html

  return (
    <CButtonGroup role="group" aria-label="Basic outlined example">

        Left

      <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">
        Middle
      </CButton>
      <CButton theme="primary" variant="outline">
        Right
      </CButton>
    </CButtonGroup>
  )
}
```

## Vertical React Bootstrap Button Groups

Stack buttons vertically using the vertical variation of React Bootstrap Button Group. Note: split dropdowns are not supported in vertical mode.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CButtonGroup,
  CCol,
  CFormCheck,
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
  CRow,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const ButtonGroupVerticalExample = () => {
  return (
    <CRow>
      <CCol>
        <CButtonGroup vertical role="group" aria-label="Vertical button group">
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>
        </CButtonGroup>
      </CCol>
      <CCol>
        <CButtonGroup vertical role="group" aria-label="Vertical button group">
          <CButton theme="primary">Button</CButton>

# React Calendar Component

> The React Calendar Component is a versatile, customizable tool for creating responsive calendars in React, supporting day, month, and year selection, and global locales.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Example

Explore the React Calendar component's basic usage through sample code snippets demonstrating its core functionality.

A calendar renders unadorned — it has no background, border, or padding of its own, so it takes the surface of whatever contains it. The examples below add `border` and `rounded` for that reason; a [card](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/card/) works just as well.

### Days

Select specific days using the React Calendar component. The example below shows basic usage.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const CalendarDaysExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar className="border rounded" locale="en-US" startDate="2024/02/13" />
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Weeks

Set the `selectionType` to `week` to enable selection of entire week. You can also add `showWeekNumber` to show week numbers.

Weeks are ISO 8601 weeks, which run from Monday to Sunday, and week selection treats them the way month selection treats months. When `firstDayOfWeek` starts the rows on another day, each row spans two weeks and stands for the one that holds most of its days: with Sunday first, the row from August 30 to September 5, 2026 is week 36, picks `2026W36` and gives its Monday, August 31. A week given as `startDate` or `endDate`, as a string or as any date inside it, selects that row, and the calendar opens on a page that shows it. `minDate` and `maxDate` count by whole weeks, so their weeks stay selectable, and `disabledDates` disables a week only when it disables every day of it.

CalendarWeeksExample

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const CalendarWeeksExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar
        className="border rounded"
        locale="en-US"
        selectionType="week"
        showWeekNumber
        startDate="2024W15"
        onStartDateChange={(date) => console.log(date)}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Disabled dates

The React Calendar component includes functionality to disable specific dates, such as weekends or holidays, using the `disabledDates` prop. It accepts:

- A single `Date` or an array of `Date` objects.
- A function or an array of functions that take a `Date` object as an argument and return a boolean indicating whether the date should be disabled.
- A mixed array of `Date` objects and functions.

In month, quarter and year selection a period can be picked unless it lies wholly before `minDate` or after `maxDate`, or `disabledDates` covers every day of it that the limits leave, and a range of periods is cleared only when it spans a period that `disabledDates` covers wholly.

Without a `calendarDate`, `startDate` or `endDate`, the calendar opens on today, or on the `minDate` or `maxDate` that today falls outside of, and that date takes the focus even when it cannot be picked.

To disable certain dates, you can provide them in an array. For date ranges, use nested arrays, where each inner array indicates a start date and an end date for that range:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const CalendarDisabledDatesExample = () => {
  const calendarDate = new Date(2022, 2, 1)
  const disabledDates = [
    [new Date(2022, 2, 4), new Date(2022, 2, 7)],
    new Date(2022, 1, 1),
    new Date(2022, 2, 1),
    new Date(2022, 2, 16),
    new Date(2022, 3, 16),
    [new Date(2022, 4, 2), new Date(2022, 4, 8)],
    [new Date(2022, 5, 1), new Date(2022, 6, 31)],
  ]
  const maxDate = new Date(2022, 12, 0)
  const minDate = new Date(2022, 1, 1)

  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar
        calendarDate={calendarDate}
        calendars={2}
        className="border rounded"
        disabledDates={disabledDates}
        locale="en-US"
        maxDate={maxDate}
        minDate={minDate}
        range
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Disabling weekends

You can disable weekends by passing a function to the `disabledDates` prop. Here's how to do it:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const disableWeekends = (date: Date) => {
  const day = date.getDay()
  return day === 0 || day === 6 // Disable Sundays (0) and Saturdays (6)
}

export const CalendarDisablingWeekendsExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar
        calendars={2}
        className="border rounded"
        disabledDates={disableWeekends}
        locale="en-US"
        range
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

In the example above:

- `disableWeekends` is a function that checks if a date falls on a Saturday (`6`) or a Sunday (`0`).
- The `disabledDates` prop is set to the `disableWeekends` function, which ensures that all weekends are disabled in the calendar.

This prop takes an array and applies custom logic to determine which dates should be disabled.

### Combining functions and specific dates

You can also combine specific dates and functions in the `disabledDates` array. For instance:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const disableWeekends = (date: Date) => {
  const day = date.getDay()
  return day === 0 || day === 6
}

export const CalendarCombiningFunctionsAndSpecificDatesExample = () => {
  const specificDates = [new Date(2024, 10, 25), new Date(2024, 11, 4), new Date(2024, 11, 12)] // Specific disabled dates

  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar
        calendarDate={new Date(2024, 10, 1)}
        calendars={2}
        className="border rounded"
        disabledDates={[disableWeekends, ...specificDates]}
        locale="en-US"
        range
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

In this example:

- `disableWeekends` disables weekends as before.
- `specificDates` is an array of specific dates to disable.
- The `disabledDates` prop combines both, allowing you to disable weekends and specific dates simultaneously.

## Locale

The CoreUI React Calendar allows users to display dates in non-English locales, making it suitable for international applications.

The navigation writes the month and the year in the order the locale does: the year first where the locale writes it first, as in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Hungarian or Lithuanian, the month first as in English or Polish.

### Auto

By default, the Calendar component uses the browser's default locale. However, you can easily configure it to use a different locale supported by the JavaScript Internationalization API. This feature helps create inclusive and accessible applications for a diverse audience.

With server-side rendering, pass `locale` explicitly: by default the server writes the text in its own locale and the browser in the reader's, and React reports a hydration mismatch when the two differ.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const CalendarAutoLocaleExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar className="border rounded" />
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Custom cell rendering

The React Calendar component provides powerful customization options through render props that allow you to completely control how calendar cells are displayed. These render functions are particularly useful when you need to add custom content, styling, or data to calendar cells.

### Render props

The component supports four render props, one for each view type:

- `renderDayCell={(date, meta) => ReactNode}` - Customize day cells in the days view
- `renderMonthCell={(date, meta) => ReactNode}` - Customize month cells in the months view
- `renderQuarterCell={(date, meta) => ReactNode}` - Customize quarter cells in the quarters view
- `renderYearCell={(date, meta) => ReactNode}` - Customize year cells in the years view

Each render function receives two parameters:

1. `date` - A JavaScript Date object representing the cell's date
2. `meta` - An object containing cell state information:
   - `isDisabled` - Whether the cell is disabled
   - `isInRange` - Whether the cell is within a selected range (range selection only)
   - `isSelected` - Whether the cell is selected; in a range only its start and end are, while `isInRange` covers them and every cell between
   - `label` - The cell's full name (`Wednesday, August 12, 2026`, `August 2026`, `Q3 2026`, `2026`)
   - For `renderDayCell` only:
     - `isInCurrentMonth` - Whether the day belongs to the current month
     - `isToday` - Whether the day is today, in its own month (the copy of today among an adjacent month's days is not)
     - In day selection, a day among an adjacent month's days carries the range like the month's own days when `selectAdjacentDays` is on; without it the day only fills the grid, the range is not drawn on it and `isInRange` is `false`
     - In day selection without `selectAdjacentDays`, a day among an adjacent month's days only fills the grid, so `isDisabled` is `true` and `isSelected` is `false` for it
     - In week selection, `isDisabled`, `isInRange` and `isSelected` describe the week row the day sits in, since the row is what the calendar picks and draws; `isInCurrentMonth` and `isToday` still describe the day

The render functions should return a React node (JSX) that will be displayed inside the cell.

A cell drawn by a render function gets no `aria-label` from the calendar, so its content is what a screen reader reads. Put `meta.label` in it, for example in a `visually-hidden` span next to the short visible text marked `aria-hidden="true"`, as the pricing example below does.

### Format options

In addition to custom rendering, you can control the display format of calendar elements using format props:

- `dayFormat` - Controls how day numbers are displayed (`'numeric'` or `'2-digit'`)
- `monthFormat` - Controls how month names are displayed (`'long'`, `'narrow'`, `'short'`, `'numeric'`, or `'2-digit'`)
- `yearFormat` - Controls how the year cells of the years view are displayed (`'numeric'` or `'2-digit'`)
- `weekdayFormat` - Controls how weekday names are displayed (number for character length, or `'long'`, `'narrow'`, `'short'`)

These format options use the JavaScript `Intl.DateTimeFormat` API and respect the `locale` prop. They apply to the cells of the grid, not to the navigation above it, which writes months and years in full.

### Pricing calendar with custom cells

This example demonstrates advanced usage of custom cell rendering to display pricing data across different calendar views. It uses `renderDayCell` to show daily prices, `renderMonthCell` to display monthly price ranges, and `renderYearCell` to show annual price ranges. The data is fetched from an external API and cached for performance.

```html
import React, { type ReactNode, useCallback, useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'
import { CCalendar } from '@coreui/react-pro'

type View = 'days' | 'months' | 'years'

interface PriceRange {
  min: number
  max: number
}

const toISODate = (date: Date) => date.toISOString().slice(0, 10)

const monthKey = (year: number, monthIndex: number) =>
  `${year}-${String(monthIndex + 1).padStart(2, '0')}-01`

const yearKey = (year: number) => `${year}-01-01`

const getDateRangeForView = (date: Date, view: View) => {
  const y = date.getFullYear()
  const m = date.getMonth()

  switch (view) {
    case 'days': {
      return { startDate: new Date(y, m, 1), endDate: new Date(y, m + 2, 0) }
    }
    case 'months': {
      return { startDate: new Date(y, 0, 1), endDate: new Date(y, 11, 31) }
    }
    case 'years': {
      const startYear = Math.floor(y / 12) * 12
      return { startDate: new Date(startYear, 0, 1), endDate: new Date(startYear + 11, 11, 31) }
    }
  }
}

const Cell = ({
  date,
  label,
  price,
  isSelected,
  isInCurrentMonth,
  view,
}: {
  date: ReactNode
  label: string
  price: ReactNode
  isSelected: boolean
  isInCurrentMonth?: boolean
  view?: View
}) => (
  <div className="py-1">
    <div aria-hidden="true">{date}</div>
    <span className="visually-hidden">{label}</span>
    <div
      className={
        isSelected ? 'fg-reset' : view === 'days' && !isInCurrentMonth ? 'fg-3 opacity-75' : 'fg-3'
      }
      style={{ fontSize: '0.75rem' }}
    >
      {price}
    </div>
  </div>
)

export const CalendarPricingWithCustomCellsExample = () => {
  const [calendarDate, setCalendarDate] = useState(() => new Date(2025, 0, 1))

  const [dayPrices, setDayPrices] = useState<Record<string, number>>({})
  const [monthRanges, setMonthRanges] = useState<Record<string, PriceRange>>({})
  const [yearRanges, setYearRanges] = useState<Record<string, PriceRange>>({})

  // request de-dupe
  const fetchedKeysRef = useRef(new Set<string>())
  const inFlightRef = useRef(new Set<string>())

  const fetchPricingData = useCallback(
    async (startDate: Date, endDate: Date, view: View, limit = 400) => {
      const start = toISODate(startDate)
      const end = toISODate(endDate)
      const requestKey = `${view}:${start}:${end}:${limit}`

      if (fetchedKeysRef.current.has(requestKey) || inFlightRef.current.has(requestKey)) {
        return
      }

      inFlightRef.current.add(requestKey)

      try {
        const res = await fetch(
          `https://apitest.coreui.io/demos/daily-rates.php?start_date=${start}&end_date=${end}&view=${view}&limit=${limit}`
        )
        const data = await res.json()

        fetchedKeysRef.current.add(requestKey)

        switch (view) {
          case 'days': {
            setDayPrices((prev) => ({ ...prev, ...data }))
            break
          }

          case 'months': {
            setMonthRanges((prev) => ({ ...prev, ...data }))
            break
          }

          default: {
            setYearRanges((prev) => ({ ...prev, ...data }))
            break
          }
        }
      } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching pricing data:', error)
      } finally {
        inFlightRef.current.delete(requestKey)
      }
    },
    []
  )

  const requestFor = useCallback(
    (date: Date, view: View) => {
      const { startDate, endDate } = getDateRangeForView(date, view)
      fetchPricingData(startDate, endDate, view)
    },
    [fetchPricingData]
  )

  useEffect(() => {
    requestFor(calendarDate, 'days')
  }, [calendarDate, requestFor])

  const onCalendarDateChange = useCallback(
    (date: Date, view: View) => {
      setCalendarDate(date)
      requestFor(date, view ?? 'days')
    },
    [requestFor]
  )

  const onViewChange = useCallback(
    (view: View) => {
      requestFor(calendarDate, view)
    },
    [calendarDate, requestFor]
  )

  return (
    <div className="d-flex justify-content-center">
      <CCalendar
        calendarDate={calendarDate}
        calendars={2}
        className="border rounded"
        locale="en-US"
        minDate={new Date(2022, 0, 1)}
        maxDate={new Date(2025, 11, 31)}
        range={true}
        renderDayCell={(date: Date, meta: any) => {
          const price = dayPrices[toISODate(date)]
          return (
            <Cell
              date={date.toLocaleDateString('en-US', { day: 'numeric' })}
              label={meta.label}
              price={price ? `$${price}` : '-'}
              isSelected={!!meta?.isSelected}
              isInCurrentMonth={!!meta?.isInCurrentMonth}
              view="days"
            />
          )
        }}
        renderMonthCell={(date: Date, meta: any) => {
          const range = monthRanges[monthKey(date.getFullYear(), date.getMonth())]
          return (
            <Cell
              date={date.toLocaleDateString('en-US', { month: 'short' })}
              label={meta.label}
              price={range ? `$${range.min}-$${range.max}` : '-'}
              isSelected={!!meta?.isSelected}
            />
          )
        }}
        renderYearCell={(date: Date, meta: any) => {
          const range = yearRanges[yearKey(date.getFullYear())]
          return (
            <Cell
              date={date.getFullYear()}
              label={meta.label}
              price={range ? `$${range.min}-$${range.max}` : '-'}
              isSelected={!!meta?.isSelected}
            />
          )
        }}
        onCalendarDateChange={onCalendarDateChange}
        onViewChange={onViewChange}
      />
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Accessibility

Keyboard navigation in the grid follows the [date picker dialog pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/dialog-modal/examples/datepicker-dialog/). The table is a `grid` of `gridcell` cells, which is what lets a cell report itself as selected: selected cells carry `aria-selected` (in week selection, the row), today carries `aria-current="date"`, a cell that cannot be picked carries `aria-disabled="true"` (a day outside `minDate` / `maxDate`, before year 1 or in `disabledDates`, a day among an adjacent month's days without `selectAdjacentDays`, and in week selection the row rather than its days), every day cell announces its full date with the weekday (`Wednesday, August 12, 2026`), and month, quarter and year cells are named by their text. With `range`, the grid of the view that picks the range is `aria-multiselectable`, and every day, week row or period between the two ends that can be picked carries `aria-selected` as well, so the ones in between are announced as selected; the months and years views of a day range only navigate, so there only the ends carry it. A cell drawn by a render function is named by its content; see [Render props](#render-props). In week selection the row that takes focus is named by the days it spans (`August 10 – 16, 2026`), after its week number when week numbers are shown (`Week 33, August 10 – 16, 2026`). Each grid is a composite with a single tab stop: <kbd>Tab</kbd> enters it once and leaves it, the keys below move inside it, and `tabindex="0"` sits on the selected date (in a range, an end the grid shows), else on the cell closest to the date the grid opens on, else wherever focus went last. Every cell that reaches into the days from the day of `minDate` to the day of `maxDate` can take the focus, times of day aside, also one that cannot be picked: the keys stop on it instead of skipping it, a screen reader announces it as unavailable, and <kbd>Enter</kbd> and <kbd>Space</kbd> do nothing there. Cells wholly outside those days, and in day selection the days of an adjacent month without `selectAdjacentDays`, carry no `tabindex`; a month, quarter or year counts as inside while any of its days is, and a week row while any day of the week it stands for is. When no panel has a cell that can take the focus, as when the calendar is given a page that lies wholly outside the limits, every grid itself takes the tab stop, also in markup rendered on the server, and the arrows move to the limit they point toward; a panel wholly outside the limits beside one that reaches into them has no tab stop of its own. A grid in which nothing can be picked, such as a page wholly outside the limits or one that `disabledDates` covers, points `aria-describedby` at a hidden element holding `ariaNothingToPickLabel` (`'Nothing on this page can be picked'`). The navigation buttons stay enabled at the limits: a page outside them can be shown, and it says so. Selectable cells and week rows are marked with `data-coreui-selectable`, which is the hook to use in your own CSS or scripts.

The month and year between the navigation arrows name the page the calendar shows, followed by a visually hidden `ariaNothingToPickLabel` when nothing on it can be picked. Turning a page is announced through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) in the polite live region of the page, or of the modal dialog around the calendar, such as the panel of a date picker: one message per panel that turned, naming the page, followed by `ariaNothingToPickLabel` when nothing on that page can be picked (`September 2026, Nothing on this page can be picked`). A day or a week row that holds focus already names its month and year, so a key that moves from it to another page names no page, and announces `ariaNothingToPickLabel` alone when nothing on the new page can be picked; another panel left with nothing to pick, by a turn or by a pick, is announced with its name. A month, quarter or year names only itself, so the page is announced from it as from a button. Nothing is announced while the calendar is hidden, and a newer turn cancels the messages of the previous one. In the years view the page is the range of years it shows, the same text as the grid's label. A pick is announced the same way, because focus stays on the cell and a screen reader does not read its `aria-selected` turning on: as `ariaSelectedDateAnnouncement` with the full name of what was picked (`Selected date: Wednesday, August 12, 2026`), and with `range` as `ariaSelectedRangeAnnouncement` whenever both ends are set after a pick, or as a date when they fall on the same day. The first pick of a range announces nothing. A date picker turns both messages off for the pick that closes its panel and names its toggle with the picked date instead, because a message added while focus goes back to the toggle is dropped by VoiceOver in Safari; a newer pick cancels a message that was not read yet. Activating the month or year button while it has focus opens the months or years view and moves focus to the month or year that panel showed, also when it cannot be picked, or to the panel's tab stop when it lies outside `minDate` / `maxDate`; holding <kbd>Enter</kbd> does not go on to pick it. In the years view the year button goes back to the view that picks the date; while it has focus, focus moves to the day, week, month or quarter that holds the start of the month the panel shows there, or to the panel's tab stop when that lies outside `minDate` / `maxDate`. The button is disabled when the years view is the one that picks (`selectionType="year"`). Picking a month or year in those views, with a click or with <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd>, opens the next view on that period, unless nothing in it can be picked, and moves focus to the first date of that panel inside `minDate` / `maxDate`, also when that date cannot be picked; when the panel lies wholly outside the limits, focus goes to the calendar's tab stop.

With `showWeekNumber`, each week number is a row header named with the locale's word for week and the number (`Week 36`, `Tydzień 36`), and the column header is that word, read by screen readers only unless `weekNumbersLabel` sets a visible one. In week selection the focused row's name starts with the same name, `Week 36, August 31 – September 6, 2026`. To name the week numbers yourself, give `ariaWeekNumberLabel` a function that takes the week number and returns its name (returning nothing keeps the default); keep the number in it, so a voice-control user can say what they see. The default puts the word before the number in every locale, so for a locale that writes it the other way round, such as `第36週`, pass the function.

### Keyboard support

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Arrow Right</kbd> / <kbd>Arrow Left</kbd> | Move focus to the next / previous day; crossing the edge of the grid moves to the adjacent month |
| <kbd>Arrow Down</kbd> / <kbd>Arrow Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous week |
| <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> | Move focus to the first / last day of the week inside `minDate` / `maxDate`, into the previous / next month when the week starts or ends there |
| <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Page Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous month, keeping the day number when the target month is long enough; a series of presses keeps the day it started from, so January 31 goes to February 28 and then March 31, also across a stop at `minDate` / `maxDate`; any other key or a click starts a new series |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>Page Up</kbd> | Move focus to the same day of the next / previous year, keeping the day of a series the same way; the other views turn as they do without Shift |
| <kbd>Tab</kbd> | Leave the grid; the calendar is one stop, so Tab never walks the dates |
| <kbd>Enter</kbd> / <kbd>Space</kbd> | Select the focused date; nothing happens on a date that cannot be picked |

The months, quarters, and years views answer to the same keys, with arrows moving by cell and row, <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> moving to the first / last cell of the row, and <kbd>Page Down</kbd> / <kbd>Page Up</kbd> moving by year (by the twelve years of a page in the years view). A jump never lands outside `minDate` / `maxDate`: focus stops on the limit, also when that date cannot be picked.

With `selectionType="week"` the row is what gets picked, so it is the tab stop and the arrows move between rows; <kbd>Home</kbd> and <kbd>End</kbd> move to the first and last week of the month.

A key from the table pressed with <kbd>Alt</kbd>, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> or <kbd>Cmd</kbd> is neither handled nor cancelled by the grid: focus stays where it is and the key stays free for the browser and assistive technology.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CCalendar /&gt;](./api/#ccalendar)
