# React Dialog Component

> React Dialog component built on the native <dialog> element — top layer rendering, blurred native backdrop, focus trapping, and accessible semantics out of the box.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

`<CDialog>` renders a popup on the native `<dialog>` element, so accessibility, focus management and the backdrop come from the browser rather than from a custom implementation. It carries the look Bootstrap 6 introduces under the same name — a centered floating panel over a blurred backdrop.

Dialog shares its behavior with [Modal](../modal/). Modal keeps the classic look and the v5 vocabulary; Dialog carries the new look and the `dialog-*` classes. Pick one — they are independent components, and **Modal is deprecated for removal in v7**.

What the native element provides:

- **Modal or non-modal** — `modal` (default `true`) promotes the dialog to the top layer with a backdrop and focus trapping; `modal={false}` leaves the page interactive.
- **A built-in backdrop** through the `::backdrop` pseudo-element. `backdrop="static"` locks clicks outside; `backdrop={false}` suppresses it visually.
- **Escape handling** closes the dialog; `keyboard={false}` disables it.
- **Accessibility** — focus is trapped inside a modal dialog and returned to the trigger on close, with no `role`, `aria-modal`, `aria-hidden` or `tabIndex` in the markup.
- **Animated open and close** — the exit transition, the `::backdrop` fade included, plays in every browser, because the dialog stays in the top layer until the transition ends.

## Example

Toggle a dialog by clicking the button below.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CDialog,
  CDialogBody,
  CDialogFooter,
  CDialogHeader,
  CDialogTitle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Dialog title</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>Woohoo, you are reading this text in a dialog!</CDialogBody>
        <CDialogFooter>
          <CButton theme="secondary" onClick={() => setShow(false)}>
            Close
          </CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Save changes</CButton>
        </CDialogFooter>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Slide animations

Dialogs fade in and out by default. `animation` picks a different entry: `"slide-down"` comes in from above, `"slide-up"` from below — and the exit reverses it. The value names the variant rather than the direction, so further ones are added to the stylesheet without touching the prop.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

type Animation = 'slide-up' | 'slide-down'

export const DialogSlideExample = () => {
  const [animation, setAnimation] = useState<Animation>('slide-down')
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  const open = (value: Animation) => {
    setAnimation(value)
    setShow(true)
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3">
        <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => open('slide-down')}>
          Slide down
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => open('slide-up')}>
          Slide up
        </CButton>
      </div>
      {/* The variant is held past the close, or the exit would reverse a different entry. */}
      <CDialog animation={animation} show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>{animation}</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>The exit reverses the entry.</CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Static backdrop

With `backdrop="static"` the dialog does not close on a click outside — it plays a scale bounce instead.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogStaticBackdropExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch static backdrop dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog backdrop="static" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Dialog title</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          Clicking outside plays a bounce instead of closing. Escape still closes it.
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Backdrop

The backdrop reads three tokens from `:root` — `--cui-backdrop-color`, `--cui-backdrop-opacity` and `--cui-backdrop-blur` — and every overlay component paints it the same way. A dialog defaults to a dark scrim; the drawer defaults to a translucent tint of the page. Pick the other look with the `backdropVariant` prop — a [backdrop preset](https://coreui.io/react/docs/helpers/backdrop/) on the component: `translucent` here, `scrim` on a drawer; `backdrop={false}` on either drops the layer altogether.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogBackdropExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog with a translucent backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDialog backdropVariant="translucent" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Translucent backdrop</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          The page behind stays readable through a light tint instead of a dark scrim.
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Scrolling long content

Add `scrollable` to scroll the dialog body while the header and footer stay put.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogScrollableExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch scrollable dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog scrollable show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Scrollable body</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          {Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, index) => (
            <p key={index}>
              Placeholder paragraph {index + 1} — the body scrolls while the header stays put.
            </p>
          ))}
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Toggle between dialogs

A trigger inside an open dialog can swap to another one — the backdrop stays up, so there is no flash between them. Drive both from one piece of state rather than closing the first and opening the second.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogToggleExample = () => {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState<'first' | 'second' | undefined>()

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setOpen('first')}>
        Open first dialog
      </CButton>

      <CDialog show={open === 'first'} onShowChange={(show) => !show && setOpen(undefined)}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>First dialog</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setOpen('second')}>
            Open second dialog
          </CButton>
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>

      <CDialog show={open === 'second'} onShowChange={(show) => !show && setOpen(undefined)}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Second dialog</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          <CButton theme="secondary" onClick={() => setOpen('first')}>
            Back to the first
          </CButton>
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Non-modal dialogs

Set `modal={false}` to show the dialog without the top layer — no backdrop, no focus trap, and the rest of the page stays interactive.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogNonModalExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch non-modal dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog modal={false} show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Non-modal</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          No backdrop, no focus trap — the rest of the page stays interactive and scrollable.
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Optional sizes

Dialogs have three optional sizes.

| Size | Prop | Dialog max-width |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small | `size="sm"` | `280px` |
| Default | — | `500px` |
| Large | `size="lg"` | `800px` |
| Extra large | `size="xl"` | `1140px` |

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

type Size = 'sm' | 'lg' | 'xl'

export const DialogSizesExample = () => {
  const [size, setSize] = useState<Size>('lg')
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  const open = (value: Size) => {
    setSize(value)
    setShow(true)
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3">
        {(['sm', 'lg', 'xl'] as const).map((value) => (
          <CButton key={value} theme="primary" onClick={() => open(value)}>
            {value} dialog
          </CButton>
        ))}
      </div>
      <CDialog size={size} show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Size {size}</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>Placeholder content for the dialog body.</CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Fullscreen dialog

Add `fullscreen` for a dialog that covers the viewport. Pass a breakpoint instead — `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl` or `2xl` — to cover it only below that width and keep the floating panel above it.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogFullscreenExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Fullscreen dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog fullscreen show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Fullscreen</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>The dialog covers the entire viewport.</CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Dark variant

Add `dark` and the dialog flips the tokens its own surface reads, so the dialog and everything in it — including the close button — turns dark on a light page.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogDarkExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Open dark dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog dark show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Dark dialog</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          The surface, the text and the dividers all read the flipped tokens.
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

The dialog works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the open state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the dialog, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the dialog requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, a click on the backdrop) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle — so you can watch the state without taking it over. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

### Uncontrolled

Give the dialog a starting point and let it close itself — dismiss gestures are handled internally.

```jsx
<CDialog defaultShow>
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the dialog renders exactly what you pass — dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange`, and nothing closes until you flip the prop. That makes confirm-before-close possible: instead of feeding a close request straight back, ask first.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CDialog,
  CDialogBody,
  CDialogFooter,
  CDialogHeader,
  CDialogTitle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DialogControlledExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)
  const [confirming, setConfirming] = useState(false)

  const handleShowChange = (nextShow: boolean) => {
    if (!nextShow) {
      setConfirming(true)
      return
    }

    setShow(nextShow)
  }

  const close = () => {
    setConfirming(false)
    setShow(false)
  }

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog
      </CButton>
      <CDialog show={show} onShowChange={handleShowChange}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Unsaved changes</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          {confirming
            ? 'Close without saving? Your changes will be lost.'
            : 'Try to close this dialog with Escape or a click on the backdrop — it will ask first.'}
        </CDialogBody>
        <CDialogFooter>
          {confirming ? (
            <>
              <CButton theme="secondary" onClick={() => setConfirming(false)}>
                Keep editing
              </CButton>
              <CButton theme="danger" onClick={close}>
                Discard and close
              </CButton>
            </>
          ) : (
            <CButton theme="primary" onClick={close}>
              Save and close
            </CButton>
          )}
        </CDialogFooter>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when closing has consequences — unsaved form input, an interrupted upload — or when the open state belongs to something else, like a route.

## Accessibility

The native `<dialog>` carries the semantics: a modal dialog traps focus, marks the rest of the page inert and returns focus to the trigger on close, and it is exposed as a dialog to assistive technology without any ARIA attribute of ours. Give the dialog an accessible name by pointing `aria-labelledby` at your `<CDialogTitle>`.

- [&lt;CDialogHeader /&gt;](./api/#cdialogheader)

# React Dialog Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Dialog component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CDialog

```jsx
import { CDialog } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean \| "slide-up" \| "slide-down"` | `true` | How the dialog comes in. Left out it fades in place, `false` turns the animation off, and a variant name picks one — the value names the variant, so further ones are added to the stylesheet rather than to this prop. |
| `backdrop` | `boolean \| "static"` | `true` | Apply a backdrop while the dialog is open. `'static'` keeps the dialog open on a backdrop click and bounces it instead. |
| `backdropVariant` | `"scrim" \| "translucent"` | - | Pick the backdrop's look: the dark scrim or the translucent tint of the page. Left out, the component keeps its own default. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `dark` | `boolean` | - | Flip the dialog to the dark color mode, whatever the page around it uses. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial open state of an uncontrolled dialog — read once on mount. |
| `fullscreen` | `boolean \| "sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl" \| "2xl"` | - | Cover the whole viewport — always with `true`, or only below the given breakpoint. |
| `keyboard` | `boolean` | `true` | Closes the dialog when escape key is pressed. |
| `modal` | `boolean` | `true` | Open the dialog modally, taking over the page. Set it to `false` for a dialog that leaves the rest of the page interactive. |
| `onClose` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired once the component has closed. |
| `onClosePrevented` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the dialog is shown, its backdrop is static and a click outside the dialog or an escape key press is performed with the keyboard option set to false. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the component requests to be shown. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the dialog requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, backdrop click) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the dialog stays as it is. |
| `scrollable` | `boolean` | - | Create a scrollable dialog that allows scrolling the dialog body. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the open state. When set, the dialog renders what `show` says and dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `size` | `"sm" \| "lg" \| "xl"` | - | Size the component small, large, or extra large. |
| `unmountOnClose` | `boolean` | `true` | By default the component is unmounted after close animation, if you want to keep the component mounted set this property to false. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the visibility of the dialog component. |

# React Dialog Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Dialog component with CSS variables and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Dialog supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$dialog-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-dialog-zindex: var(--cui-z-dialog),
    --cui-dialog-padding-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-width: 500px,
    --cui-dialog-margin: 1.75rem,
    --cui-dialog-color: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-dialog-bg: var(--cui-bg-body),
    --cui-dialog-border-color: var(--cui-border-color-translucent),
    --cui-dialog-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-dialog-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-7),
    --cui-dialog-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-lg),
    --cui-dialog-transition-property: #{"opacity, transform, visibility"},
    --cui-dialog-transition-duration: .3s,
    --cui-dialog-transition-timing: var(--cui-transition-timing-overlay),
    --cui-dialog-backdrop-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-backdrop-color) var(--cui-backdrop-opacity), transparent),
    --cui-dialog-backdrop-blur: var(--cui-backdrop-blur),
    --cui-dialog-header-padding-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-header-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-header-border-color: var(--cui-border-color-translucent),
    --cui-dialog-header-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-dialog-title-line-height: var(--cui-body-line-height),
    --cui-dialog-footer-padding-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-footer-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-dialog-footer-border-color: var(--cui-border-color-translucent),
    --cui-dialog-footer-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-dialog-footer-gap: .5rem,
    --cui-dialog-slide-distance: 3rem,
    --cui-dialog-scale-transform: scale(1.02),
  ),
  $dialog-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-dialog-bg': '#f8f9fa',
  '--cui-dialog-border-radius': '1rem',
}

return <CDialog style={customVars} />
```

The three optional sizes come from a map, so a size the map does not name is one entry rather than a new rule.

```scss
$dialog-sizes: () !default;
$dialog-sizes: defaults(
  (
    sm: 280px,
    lg: 800px,
    xl: 1140px,
  ),
  $dialog-sizes
);
```

# React Drawer Component

> React Drawer component built on the native <dialog> element — a floating side panel with top layer rendering, a native backdrop and accessible semantics out of the box.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

`<CDrawer>` is a panel that slides in from an edge of the viewport, built on the native `<dialog>` element. It carries the look Bootstrap 6 introduces under the same name — a floating, inset, rounded panel.

Drawer shares its behavior with [Offcanvas](../offcanvas/). Offcanvas keeps the classic look and the v5 vocabulary; Drawer carries the new look and the `drawer-*` classes. Pick one — they are independent components, and **Offcanvas is deprecated for removal in v7**.

## Example

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="start" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Drawer</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Content for the drawer goes here.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Placement

Drawers can slide in from any edge of the viewport — `placement` picks which one:

- `placement="start"` — left side of the viewport (shown above)
- `placement="end"` — right side of the viewport
- `placement="top"` — top of the viewport
- `placement="bottom"` — bottom of the viewport
- `fullscreen` — covers the viewport (minus the inset), and needs no placement

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CCloseButton,
  CDrawer,
  CDrawerBody,
  CDrawerHeader,
  CDrawerTitle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerPlacementEndExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Right drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Drawer right</CDrawerTitle>
          <CCloseButton onClick={() => setShow(false)} />
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Content for the drawer goes here.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
```

## Variants

`sheet` drops the inset and the rounded corners so the panel sits flush against the edge, `translucent` blurs what is behind it, `fitContent` sizes it to its content, and `fullscreen` covers the viewport.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

type Variant = 'sheet' | 'translucent' | 'fitContent' | 'fullscreen'

export const DrawerVariantsExample = () => {
  const [variant, setVariant] = useState<Variant>('sheet')
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  const open = (value: Variant) => {
    setVariant(value)
    setShow(true)
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap">
        {(['sheet', 'translucent', 'fitContent', 'fullscreen'] as const).map((value) => (
          <CButton key={value} theme="primary" onClick={() => open(value)}>
            {value}
          </CButton>
        ))}
      </div>
      <CDrawer placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow} {...{ [variant]: true }}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>{variant}</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Placeholder content for the drawer body.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Footer

Add a `<CDrawerFooter>` below the `<CDrawerBody>` for the panel's actions. It is a flex row that wraps and keeps its children spaced and vertically centered, so a row of buttons needs no utilities.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CDrawer,
  CDrawerBody,
  CDrawerFooter,
  CDrawerHeader,
  CDrawerTitle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerFooterExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle drawer with footer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Drawer with footer</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Placeholder content for the drawer body.</CDrawerBody>
        <CDrawerFooter>
          <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" onClick={() => setShow(false)}>
            Close
          </CButton>
          <CButton theme="primary">Save changes</CButton>
        </CDrawerFooter>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Backdrop presets

The backdrop reads `--cui-backdrop-color`, `--cui-backdrop-opacity` and `--cui-backdrop-blur`; a drawer defaults to a translucent tint of the page. For the dialog's dark scrim set `backdropVariant="scrim"`; the [presets](https://coreui.io/react/docs/helpers/backdrop/) work on every overlay component.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerBackdropScrimExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle drawer with a dark backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer backdropVariant="scrim" placement="start" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Dark backdrop</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>The scrim the dialog uses, on a drawer.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

### No backdrop

Set `backdrop={false}` to hide the backdrop while keeping the drawer modal — the panel still takes the top layer and traps focus, but nothing dims the page behind it. Pair it with `scroll` to make the drawer non-modal instead.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerNoBackdropExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Drawer without a backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer backdrop={false} placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>No backdrop</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Nothing dims the page, but focus is still trapped here.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Instant

Set `animation={false}` on a drawer that should appear and disappear at once, with no slide and no backdrop fade — it renders with `.drawer-instant`, and it applies to both directions.

### Dark

Add `dark` and the drawer flips the tokens its own surface reads, so the panel and everything in it — including the close button — turns dark on a light page.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerDarkExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Dark drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer dark placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Dark drawer</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>
          The surface, the text and the dividers all read the flipped tokens.
        </CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Body scrolling

A visible backdrop needs the top layer, so `scroll` alone only unlocks the page scroll. Pair it with `backdrop={false}` and the drawer opens **non-modally** — the page behind it stays interactive as well as scrollable.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerScrollingExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Enable body scrolling
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="start" scroll backdrop={false} show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Body scrolling</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>
          Without a backdrop the drawer opens non-modally, so the page behind it stays interactive
          and scrollable.
        </CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Static backdrop

With `backdrop="static"` the drawer does not close on a click outside — it plays a bounce instead.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerStaticBackdropExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle static drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="start" backdrop="static" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Static backdrop</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>Clicking outside plays a bounce instead of closing.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Responsive

`responsive` keeps the content in the page from the given breakpoint up, and turns it into a drawer below it. Once the window grows past the breakpoint, an open drawer asks to close through `onShowChange`: uncontrolled it closes, controlled it waits for `show` to change.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerResponsiveExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton className="d-lg-none" theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle responsive drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="start" responsive="lg" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Responsive drawer</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>
          Below <code>lg</code> this is a drawer; from <code>lg</code> up the content sits in the
          page.
        </CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

The drawer works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the open state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the drawer, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the drawer requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, a click on the backdrop) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

### Uncontrolled

Give the drawer a starting point and let it close itself.

```jsx
<CDrawer defaultShow placement="end">
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the drawer renders exactly what you pass — dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange`, so feed the change back, or nothing closes.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DrawerControlledExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Open drawer
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Controlled drawer</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>
          The drawer renders what the state says. Escape and the backdrop click land in
          <code> onShowChange</code>, and feeding them back is what closes the panel.
        </CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when the open state belongs to something else — a route, a filter panel toggled from a toolbar, a cart the whole page reads — or when closing should be intercepted first.

## Accessibility

The native `<dialog>` carries the semantics: a modal drawer traps focus, marks the rest of the page inert and returns focus to the trigger on close, without any ARIA attribute of ours. Give the drawer an accessible name by pointing `aria-labelledby` at your `<CDrawerTitle>`.

# React Drawer Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Drawer component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CDrawer

```jsx
import { CDrawer } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | How the drawer comes in. Left out it slides in from its placement; `false` turns the animation off. |
| `backdrop` | `boolean \| "static"` | `true` | Apply a backdrop while the drawer is open. `'static'` keeps it open on a backdrop click and bounces it instead. |
| `backdropVariant` | `"translucent" \| "scrim"` | - | Pick the backdrop's look: the dark scrim or the translucent tint of the page. Left out, the component keeps its own default. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `dark` | `boolean` | - | Flip the drawer to the dark color mode, whatever the page around it uses. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial open state of an uncontrolled drawer — read once on mount. |
| `fitContent` | `boolean` | - | Size the drawer to its content instead of the full edge. |
| `fullscreen` | `boolean` | - | Set the drawer to cover the entire user viewport. |
| `keyboard` | `boolean` | `true` | Closes the drawer when escape key is pressed. |
| `onClose` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired once the component has closed. |
| `onClosePrevented` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when a static backdrop or a disabled `keyboard` refuses a close request. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the component requests to be shown. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the drawer requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, backdrop click) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the drawer stays as it is. |
| `placement` | `"start" \| "end" \| "top" \| "bottom"` | - | The edge the drawer slides in from. A `fullscreen` drawer covers the viewport and needs none. |
| `responsive` | `boolean \| "sm" \| "md" \| "lg" \| "xl" \| "2xl"` | `true` | Hide the drawer outside the viewport from a specified breakpoint and down. |
| `scroll` | `boolean` | `false` | Allow the page behind the drawer to scroll. |
| `sheet` | `boolean` | - | Drop the inset and the rounded corners, so the drawer sits flush against the edge. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the open state. When set, the drawer renders what `show` says and dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `translucent` | `boolean` | - | Blur and saturate whatever is behind the drawer. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the visibility of the drawer component. |

# React Drawer Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Drawer component with CSS variables and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Drawer supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$drawer-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-drawer-inset: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-drawer-zindex: var(--cui-z-drawer),
    --cui-drawer-width: 400px,
    --cui-drawer-height: 30vh,
    --cui-drawer-sheet-width: 760px,
    --cui-drawer-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-drawer-padding-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-drawer-color: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-drawer-bg: var(--cui-bg-body),
    --cui-drawer-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-drawer-border-color: var(--cui-border-color-translucent),
    --cui-drawer-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-7),
    --cui-drawer-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-lg),
    --cui-drawer-transition-property: #{"transform, visibility"},
    --cui-drawer-transition-duration: .3s,
    --cui-drawer-transition-timing: var(--cui-transition-timing-overlay),
    --cui-drawer-title-line-height: var(--cui-body-line-height),
    --cui-drawer-body-gap: var(--cui-drawer-padding-y),
    --cui-drawer-footer-gap: .5rem,
    --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-bg-body),
    --cui-backdrop-opacity: 25%,
    --cui-drawer-backdrop-bg: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-backdrop-color) var(--cui-backdrop-opacity), transparent),
    --cui-drawer-backdrop-blur: var(--cui-backdrop-blur),
    --cui-drawer-scale-transform: scale(1.02),
  ),
  $drawer-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-drawer-width': '28rem',
  '--cui-drawer-inset': '1rem',
}

return <CDrawer placement="end" style={customVars} />
```

# React Context Menu Component

> React Context Menu opens a menu at the pointer on right-click or the keyboard's Menu key - built on the Menu component with the same items, submenus, keyboard navigation and dismissal.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

Context menus replace the browser's native menu on an element with a [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/). `<CContextMenu>` renders the trigger area; put the content in it and a `<CMenuContent>` next to it. A right-click (or <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> / the <kbd>Menu</kbd> key when the area has focus) opens the menu at the pointer, and every menu feature - items, icons, dividers, headers, submenus and the keyboard navigation - works unchanged.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CContextMenu, CMenuContent, CMenuDivider, CMenuItem } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const ContextMenuExample = () => {
  return (
    <CContextMenu className="border rounded-3 p-6 text-center fg-2" tabIndex={0}>
      Right-click anywhere in this area
      <CMenuContent>
        <CMenuItem>Copy</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuItem>Cut</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuItem>Paste</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuDivider />
        <CMenuItem theme="danger">Delete</CMenuItem>
      </CMenuContent>
    </CContextMenu>
  )
}
```

Context menus are built on a third party library, [Floating UI](https://floating-ui.com/), which keeps the menu inside the viewport: it flips above the pointer near the bottom edge and shifts sideways near the right one.

## Examples

### Submenus

Submenus work as in [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/#submenus): wrap a `<CMenuItem>` trigger and a nested `<CMenuContent>` in a `<CSubmenu>`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CContextMenu, CMenuContent, CMenuDivider, CMenuItem, CSubmenu } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const ContextMenuSubmenusExample = () => {
  return (
    <CContextMenu className="border rounded-3 p-6 text-center fg-2" tabIndex={0}>
      Right-click to see the submenus
      <CMenuContent>
        <CSubmenu>
          <CMenuItem>New</CMenuItem>
          <CMenuContent>
            <CMenuItem>Folder</CMenuItem>
            <CMenuItem>Text document</CMenuItem>
            <CMenuItem>Spreadsheet</CMenuItem>
          </CMenuContent>
        </CSubmenu>
        <CSubmenu>
          <CMenuItem>Sort by</CMenuItem>
          <CMenuContent>
            <CMenuItem>Name</CMenuItem>
            <CMenuItem>Date modified</CMenuItem>
            <CMenuItem>Size</CMenuItem>
          </CMenuContent>
        </CSubmenu>
        <CMenuDivider />
        <CMenuItem>Refresh</CMenuItem>
      </CMenuContent>
    </CContextMenu>
  )
}
```

### One menu for many rows

A context menu belongs to the `<CContextMenu>` area and opens for right-clicks anywhere inside it. Wrap the container - a table, a list, a file grid - rather than every row, and read the row from its own `onContextMenu` handler: the event bubbles to the area afterwards, which opens the menu. One menu, one component, no matter how many rows.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CContextMenu,
  CMenuContent,
  CMenuDivider,
  CMenuHeader,
  CMenuItem,
  CTable,
  CTableBody,
  CTableDataCell,
  CTableHead,
  CTableHeaderCell,
  CTableRow,
} from '@coreui/react-pro'

const files = [
  { name: 'Quarterly report.pdf', modified: '2 hours ago', size: '1.2 MB' },
  { name: 'Logo.svg', modified: 'Yesterday', size: '24 KB' },
  { name: 'Notes.txt', modified: '3 days ago', size: '2 KB' },
]

export const ContextMenuTableExample = () => {
  const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string>()

  return (
    <CContextMenu>
      <CTable hover>
        <CTableHead onContextMenu={(event) => event.preventDefault()}>
          <CTableRow>
            <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Name</CTableHeaderCell>
            <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Modified</CTableHeaderCell>
            <CTableHeaderCell scope="col">Size</CTableHeaderCell>
          </CTableRow>
        </CTableHead>
        <CTableBody>
          {files.map((file) => (
            <CTableRow key={file.name} onContextMenu={() => setSelected(file.name)}>
              <CTableDataCell>{file.name}</CTableDataCell>
              <CTableDataCell>{file.modified}</CTableDataCell>
              <CTableDataCell>{file.size}</CTableDataCell>
            </CTableRow>
          ))}
        </CTableBody>
      </CTable>
      <CMenuContent>
        <CMenuHeader>{selected}</CMenuHeader>
        <CMenuItem>Open</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuItem>Rename</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuItem>Download</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuDivider />
        <CMenuItem theme="danger">Delete</CMenuItem>
      </CMenuContent>
    </CContextMenu>
  )
}
```

A handler that calls `preventDefault()` keeps the menu closed and the browser's own menu away too - the right-click on the header row above opens nothing.

### Container

The menu is positioned with `position: fixed` at the pointer, so it escapes ancestors with `overflow: hidden` on its own. A `transform`, `filter` or `contain` on an ancestor turns that ancestor into the containing block for fixed elements and the menu drifts; render it through a portal with `portal` (or `container`) in that case.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CContextMenu, CMenuContent, CMenuItem } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const ContextMenuContainerExample = () => {
  return (
    <CContextMenu
      className="border rounded-3 p-6 text-center fg-2 overflow-hidden"
      portal
      style={{ transform: 'translateZ(0)' }}
      tabIndex={0}
    >
      Right-click inside a transformed, clipping container
      <CMenuContent>
        <CMenuItem>Still in the viewport</CMenuItem>
        <CMenuItem>Another action</CMenuItem>
      </CMenuContent>
    </CContextMenu>
  )
}
```

## Accessibility

Pointing devices are not the only way in: with focus on the area, <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> and the <kbd>Menu</kbd> key open the menu anchored to the element instead of the pointer. <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> is the Windows convention the [WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/menubar/) adopt for opening a context menu from the keyboard; the component handles the keys itself, so they work on macOS too, where no system shortcut exists and browsers never turn them into a `contextmenu` event. On Apple keyboards the function keys default to their media actions, so the shortcut is <kbd>Fn</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> unless the system is set to use them as standard function keys. Give a non-interactive area `tabIndex={0}` so keyboard users can reach it, and describe the gesture somewhere nearby - nothing in the markup announces that an element has a context menu.

Focus moves into the menu when it opens and returns to the area when it closes. Like [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/#accessibility), the component adds no `menuitem` roles on its own; add them yourself when the menu is a true application menu.

### Keyboard navigation

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd>, <kbd>Menu</kbd> | Open the context menu anchored to the focused area (<kbd>Fn</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F10</kbd> on Apple keyboards) |
| `↓` / `↑` | Navigate to next/previous menu item |
| `→` | Enter submenu (or `←` in RTL) |
| `←` | Exit submenu and return to parent (or `→` in RTL) |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Activate focused item or open submenu |
| `Esc` | Close the menu and return focus to the area |
| `Home` / `End` | Jump to first/last menu item |
| `Tab` | Move focus and close the menu |

# React Context Menu Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Context Menu component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## CContextMenu

```jsx
import { CContextMenu } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `autoClose` | `boolean \| "inside" \| "outside"` | `true` | Configures the auto close behavior: - `true` — closes on a click inside or outside the menu, - `'inside'` — closes on a click inside the menu only, - `'outside'` — closes on a click outside the menu only, - `false` — closes only on the Escape key. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the trigger area. |
| `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment \| (() => Element \| DocumentFragment \| null) \| null` | - | The element the panel is rendered into instead of `document.body`. Implies `portal`. Inside a modal dialog it goes into the dialog instead, because the rest of the page is inert. |
| `dark` | `boolean` | - | Renders the panel in the dark theme. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Keeps the menu closed and lets the browser's own menu through. |
| `offset` | `[number, number]` | `[0, 2]` | The distance of the panel from the pointer, as `[skidding, distance]`. |
| `onContextMenu` | `MouseEventHandler<HTMLDivElement>` | - | Callback fired on a right-click in the trigger area, also while `disabled` is set; a right-click inside the open menu does not reach it. Calling `event.preventDefault()` keeps both this menu and the browser menu closed for that click; the ContextMenu key and Shift+F10 open the menu without calling it. |
| `onHide` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the menu is hidden. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the menu is shown. |
| `placement` | `'top' \| 'top-start' \| 'top-end' \| 'bottom' \| 'bottom-start' \| 'bottom-end' \| 'left' \| 'left-start' \| 'left-end' \| 'right' \| 'right-start' \| 'right-end' \| string` | `bottom-start` | Where the panel opens relative to the pointer. It flips when that side of the viewport is short, and a logical `start` or `end` side resolves to the side the writing direction puts it on. |
| `portal` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders the panel through a portal. |

The menu itself is a [`<CMenuContent>`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/api/#cmenucontent) with the same items, headers, dividers and submenus as a [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/api/).

```scss
    --cui-menu-item-hover-color: var(--cui-menu-color, var(--cui-fg-body)),
```

```jsx

  </CContextMenu>
)
```

# React Dropdown Component

> React dropdown component allows you to toggle contextual overlays for displaying lists, links, and more html elements.

## Overview

Dropdowns are toggleable, contextual overlays for displaying lists of links and more.

> Since v6 the React Dropdown is a compatibility surface over the [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/) component — the props, class names and markup below keep working, and both share one engine underneath. **Dropdown may be removed in v7**, so prefer Menu for new work.

Dropdowns are built on a third party library, [Floating UI](https://floating-ui.com/), which provides dynamic positioning and viewport detection. Floating UI isn't used to position dropdowns in navbars though as dynamic positioning isn't required.

## Accessibility

The [<abbr title="Web Accessibility Initiative">WAI</abbr> <abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr>](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/) standard defines an actual [`role="menu"` widget](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria/#menu), but this is specific to application-like menus which trigger actions or functions. <abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr> menus can only contain menu items, checkbox menu items, radio button menu items, radio button groups, and sub-menus.

CoreUI's dropdowns, on the other hand, are designed to be generic and applicable to a variety of situations and markup structures. For instance, it is possible to create dropdowns that contain additional inputs and form controls, such as search fields or login forms. For this reason, beyond the `role="menu"` that `<CDropdownMenu>` renders, the component does not add the remaining `role` and `aria-` attributes required for true <abbr title="Accessible Rich Internet Applications">ARIA</abbr> menus (such as `role="menuitem"` on the items). Authors will have to include these more specific attributes themselves.

However, the component comes with built-in support for most standard keyboard menu interactions — you can move through individual `<CDropdownItem>` elements using the cursor keys and close the menu with the <kbd>ESC</kbd> key, without wiring up any listeners yourself.

## Examples

Bind the dropdown's toggle and the dropdown menu inside `<CDropdown>`, or different element that declares `position: relative;`. Dropdowns can be triggered from `<a>` or `<button>` elements to better fit your possible requirements.

### Single button

Here's how you can put them to work with either `<button>` elements:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownSingleButtonExample = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown>
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Dropdown button</CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

And with `<a>` elements:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownSingleButton2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown>
      <CDropdownToggle href="#" theme="secondary">
        Dropdown button
      </CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

The best part is you can do this with any button variant, too:

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownSingleButton3Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      {['primary', 'secondary', 'success', 'info', 'warning', 'danger'].map((color, index) => (
        <CDropdown variant="btn-group" key={index}>
          <CDropdownToggle theme={color}>{color}</CDropdownToggle>
          <CDropdownMenu>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownDivider />
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
          </CDropdownMenu>
        </CDropdown>
      ))}
    </>
  )
}
```

### Split button

Similarly, create split button dropdowns with virtually the same markup as single button dropdowns, but with the addition of boolean prop `split` for proper spacing around the dropdown caret.

We use this extra class to reduce the horizontal `padding` on either side of the caret by 25% and remove the `margin-left` that's attached for normal button dropdowns. Those additional changes hold the caret centered in the split button and implement a more properly sized hit area next to the main button.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CButton,
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownSplitButtonExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      {['primary', 'secondary', 'success', 'info', 'warning', 'danger'].map((color, index) => (
        <CDropdown variant="btn-group" key={index}>
          <CButton theme={color}>{color}</CButton>
          <CDropdownToggle theme={color} split />
          <CDropdownMenu>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownDivider />
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
          </CDropdownMenu>
        </CDropdown>
      ))}
    </>
  )
}
```

## Directions

> Directions are mirrored when using CoreUI in RTL, meaning `.dropstart` will appear on the right side.

### Centered

```html

  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownCenteredExample = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown variant="btn-group" direction="center">
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Centered dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

```html
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
            <CDropdownDivider />
            <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
          </CDropdownMenu>
        </CDropdown>
        <CButton theme="secondary">Small split button</CButton>
      </CButtonGroup>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Placement

_Added in 6.0.0._

The `direction` and `alignment` properties above pick one of six fixed positions. The `placement` property takes the same values the [Menu](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/menu/#placement) takes — physical (`top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`), logical (`start`, `end`, which mirror in RTL) and every `-start`/`-end` alignment — and it wins over `direction` and `alignment` when both are set. Breakpoint prefixes make it responsive: `bottom-start md:top-end` reads as bottom-start below `md` and top-end from `md` up.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownPlacementExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CDropdown placement="top-end" variant="btn-group">
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Top end</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>

      <CDropdown placement="bottom-start md:end-start" variant="btn-group">
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Bottom start, end from md</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
    </>
  )
}
```

Left unset, the placement follows `direction` and `alignment`. With `popper={false}`, or inside a navbar, the resolved placement is written onto the menu as `data-coreui-placement` and the stylesheet positions it from there, so the property works in static mode too.

## Menu items

Historically dropdown menu contents _had_ to be links, but that's no longer the case with v4. Now you can optionally use `<button>` elements in your dropdowns instead of just `<a>`s.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownMenuItemsExample = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown>
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem as="button">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem as="button">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem as="button">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem as="button">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

You can also create non-interactive dropdown items with `<CDropdownItemPlain>`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdownItem, CDropdownItemPlain, CDropdownMenu } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownMenuItems2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdownMenu>
      <CDropdownItemPlain>Dropdown item text</CDropdownItemPlain>
      <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
      <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
      <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
    </CDropdownMenu>
  )
}
```

### Active

In the following example we use `div` instead of `<CDropdownMenu>` to show `<CDropdownMenu>` content.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu } from '@coreui/react'

  return (
    <CDropdownMenu>

      <CDropdownItem href="#" active>
        Active link

      <CDropdownItem href="#">Another link</CDropdownItem>
```

```html
  )
}
```

## Menu alignment

By default, a dropdown menu is automatically positioned 100% from the top and along the left side of its parent. Add `aligment="end"` to right align the dropdown menu.

> Heads up! Dropdowns are positioned thanks to Popper.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownMenuAlignmentExample = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown alignment="end">
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Right-aligned menu example</CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

### Responsive alignment

An `alignment` object — `{ xs: 'start', lg: 'end' }` — becomes the responsive [placement](#placement) `bottom-start lg:bottom-end` and resolves the same way. Dynamic positioning is disabled for it: the menu carries the resolved placement as `data-coreui-placement` and the stylesheet positions it from there, at every viewport width.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownResponsiveAlignmentExample = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown alignment={{ xs: 'start', lg: 'end' }}>
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">
        Left-aligned but right aligned when large screen
      </CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownDivider,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownResponsiveAlignment2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CDropdown alignment={{ xs: 'end', lg: 'start' }}>
      <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">
        Right-aligned but left aligned when large screen
      </CDropdownToggle>
      <CDropdownMenu>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        <CDropdownDivider />
        <CDropdownItem href="#">Separated link</CDropdownItem>
      </CDropdownMenu>
    </CDropdown>
  )
}
```

The v5 classes `.dropdown-menu{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}{-start|-end}` are no longer rendered; they ship in `coreui-legacy.css` for markup that still uses them.

## Dropdown options

Use `offset` to displace the dropdown from its default position. The value is a string with two numbers separated by a comma, e.g. `offset={[10, 20]}`. Use `portal` property to render dropdowns in `body` instead of the parent element. This helps to avoid any overflow or z-index issues.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownOptionsExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex gap-1">
      <CDropdown offset={[10, 20]}>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Offset</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
      <CDropdown portal>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary" aria-controls="dropdownMenuInPortal">
          Portal
        </CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu id="dropdownMenuInPortal">
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
      <CDropdown reference="parent">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Reference</CButton>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary" split />
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
    </div>
  )
}
```

### Auto close behavior

By default, dropdowns are closed when clicking outside of the dropdown menu or the toggle button. You can change this behavior with the `autoClose` property. Set `autoClose` to: 

- `true` - Close on clicks inside or outside of the React.js dropdown menu.
- `false` - Disable auto-close; close manually by setting the `show={false}` (also not closed by `Escape`).
- `'inside'` - Close only when clicking inside the React.js dropdown menu.
- `'outside'` - Close only when clicking outside the React.js dropdown menu.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownOptionsAutoCloseBehaviorExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="d-flex gap-1">
      <CDropdown>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Default dropdown</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
      <CDropdown autoClose="inside">
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Clickable inside</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
      <CDropdown autoClose="outside">
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Clickable outside</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
      <CDropdown autoClose={false}>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Manual close</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The dropdown works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the open state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the dropdown, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the dropdown requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, an outside click, an item click) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

### Uncontrolled

Every example above is uncontrolled — the toggle manages the menu. `defaultShow` seeds it open on mount.

```jsx
<CDropdown defaultShow>
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the dropdown renders what you pass — the toggle and the dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange`, so feed the change back, or nothing moves. Here an external button drives the same state the dropdown's own gestures request changes to.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDropdown, CDropdownItem, CDropdownMenu, CDropdownToggle } from '@coreui/react'

export const DropdownControlledExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <div className="d-flex gap-3">
      <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" onClick={() => setShow(!show)}>
        {show ? 'Close the dropdown' : 'Open the dropdown'}
      </CButton>
      <CDropdown show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDropdownToggle theme="secondary">Dropdown button</CDropdownToggle>
        <CDropdownMenu>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Another action</CDropdownItem>
          <CDropdownItem href="#">Something else here</CDropdownItem>
        </CDropdownMenu>
      </CDropdown>
    </div>
  )
}
```

Use it when the open state belongs to something else — a keyboard shortcut, a tour step, or a control outside the dropdown like the button above.

# React Dropdown Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Dropdown component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CDropdown

```jsx
import { CDropdown } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `alignment` | `'start' \| 'end' \| { xs: 'start' \| 'end' } \| { sm: 'start' \| 'end' } \| { md: 'start' \| 'end' } \| { lg: 'start' \| 'end' } \| { xl: 'start' \| 'end'} \| { '2xl': 'start' \| 'end'}` | - | Specifies the alignment of the React Dropdown Menu within this React Dropdown. An object becomes a responsive `placement` — `{ xs: 'start', lg: 'end' }` reads as `'bottom-start lg:bottom-end'` — and turns dynamic positioning off. |
| `as` | `(ElementType & "symbol") \| (ElementType & "object") \| (ElementType & "div") \| (ElementType & "slot") \| (ElementType & "style") \| ... 175 more ...` | `div` | Determines the root node component (native HTML element or a custom React component) for the React Dropdown. |
| `autoClose` | `boolean \| "inside" \| "outside"` | `true` | Configures automatic closing behavior for the React Dropdown: - `true` - Close on clicks inside or outside of the React Dropdown Menu. - `false` - Disable auto-close; manually call `hide` or `toggle` (also not closed by `Escape`). - `'inside'` - Close only when clicking inside the React Dropdown Menu. - `'outside'` - Close only when clicking outside the React Dropdown Menu. |
| `className` | `string` | - | Adds custom classes to the React Dropdown root element. |
| `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment \| (() => Element \| DocumentFragment \| null) \| null` | - | Appends the React Dropdown Menu to a specific element. You can pass an HTML element or a function returning an element. Defaults to `document.body`. Inside a modal dialog it goes into the dialog instead, because the rest of the page is inert. |
| `dark` | `boolean` | - | Applies a darker color scheme to the React Dropdown Menu, often used within dark navbars. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial open state of an uncontrolled dropdown — read once on mount. |
| `direction` | `"center" \| "dropup" \| "dropup-center" \| "dropend" \| "dropstart"` | - | Specifies the direction of the React Dropdown. |
| `floatingConfig` | `Partial<ComputePositionConfig> \| ((defaultFloatingConfig: Partial<ComputePositionConfig>) => Partial<ComputePositionConfig>)` | - | Provides a custom Floating UI configuration or a function that returns a modified configuration for advanced positioning of the React Dropdown Menu. [Read more](https://floating-ui.com/docs/computePosition#options) |
| `offset` | `[number, number]` | `[0, 2]` | Defines x and y offsets ([x, y]) for the React Dropdown Menu relative to its target. |
| `onHide` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired right before the React Dropdown becomes hidden. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired immediately after the React Dropdown is displayed. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Dropdown requests an open-state change — a dismiss gesture (Escape, outside click, item click) or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the dropdown stays as it is. |
| `placement` | `'auto' \| 'auto-start' \| 'auto-end' \| 'top' \| 'top-start' \| 'top-end' \| 'bottom' \| 'bottom-start' \| 'bottom-end' \| 'left' \| 'left-start' \| 'left-end' \| 'right' \| 'right-start' \| 'right-end' \| 'start' \| 'start-start' \| 'start-end' \| 'end' \| 'end-start' \| 'end-end' \| string` | - | Where the React Dropdown Menu opens. It wins over `direction` and `alignment`; left unset, the menu follows them. A logical `start` or `end` side resolves to the side the writing direction puts it on, and breakpoint prefixes make the placement responsive — `'bottom-start md:top-end'` reads as bottom-start below `md` and top-end from `md` up. |
| `popper` | `boolean` | `true` | Enables or disables dynamic positioning for the React Dropdown Menu. When disabled, the menu is rendered statically and carries `data-coreui-popper="static"`. |
| `portal` | `boolean` | `false` | Renders the React Dropdown Menu using a React Portal, allowing it to escape the DOM hierarchy for improved positioning. |
| `reference` | `HTMLElement \| "parent" \| "toggle" \| RefObject<HTMLElement \| null>` | `toggle` | Sets the reference element for positioning the React Dropdown Menu. - `toggle` - The React Dropdown Toggle button (default). - `parent` - The React Dropdown wrapper element. - `HTMLElement` - A custom HTML element. - `React.RefObject` - A custom reference element. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the open state. When set, the dropdown renders what `show` says and dismiss gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `variant` | `"btn-group" \| "dropdown" \| "input-group" \| "nav-item"` | `dropdown` | Defines the visual variant of the React Dropdown |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Controls the visibility of the React Dropdown Menu: - `true` - Visible - `false` - Hidden |
