# React Popover Component

> Documentation and examples for adding React popovers, like those found in iOS, to any element on your site.

## Overview

Things to know when using the popover component:

- Zero-length `title` and `content` values render an empty popover, so always provide content.
- Popovers are appended to `document.body` by default. Use the `container` prop to append them to a different element when a parent's styles interfere with the popover (like in our input groups, button groups, etc).
- Triggering popovers on hidden elements will not work.
- Popovers for disabled elements must be triggered on a wrapper element.
- When triggered from anchors that wrap across multiple lines, popovers will be centered between the anchors' overall width. Use `.text-nowrap` on your `<a>`s to avoid this behavior.

Keep reading to see how popovers work with some examples.

## Examples

### Live demo

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverLiveExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover
      title="Popover title"
      content="And here’s some amazing content. It’s very engaging. Right?"
      placement="right"
    >
      <CButton theme="danger" size="lg">
        Click to toggle popover
      </CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

### Four directions

Four options are available: `top`, `end`, `bottom` and `start`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverFourDirectionsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CPopover content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="top">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover on top</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="end">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover at the end</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="bottom"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover on bottom</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="start"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover at the start</CButton>
      </CPopover>
    </>
  )
}
```

`start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL.

#### Deprecated physical names

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

`left` and `right` still work and behave exactly like `start` and `end` — they have always mirrored in RTL, so `right` never meant "the right side" there either. The logical names say that plainly; the physical ones are removed in v7.

### Responsive placement

Breakpoint prefixes make a placement responsive: `top md:end` reads as top below `md` and end from `md` up. The breakpoints are the Sass ones — `sm` 576px, `md` 768px, `lg` 1024px, `xl` 1280px, `2xl` 1536px. A bare placement with no prefix applies below the smallest one listed.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverResponsivePlacementExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover
      content="Top below md, right from md up."
      placement="top md:right"
      title="Responsive placement"
    >
      <CButton theme="secondary">Responsive placement</CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

### Custom popovers

You can customize the appearance of popovers using [CSS variables](./styling/#css-variables). We set a custom `style` to scope our custom appearance and use it to override some of the local CSS variables.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverCustomPopoversExample = () => {
  const customPopoverStyle = {
    '--cui-popover-max-width': '200px',
    '--cui-popover-border-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
    '--cui-popover-header-bg': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
    '--cui-popover-header-color': 'var(--cui-white)',
    '--cui-popover-body-padding-x': '1rem',
    '--cui-popover-body-padding-y': '.5rem',
  } as React.CSSProperties

  return (
    <CPopover
      content="This popover is themed via CSS variables."
      placement="right"
      title="Custom popover"
      style={customPopoverStyle}
    >
      <CButton theme="secondary">Custom popover</CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

### Dismiss on next click

Use the `focus` trigger to dismiss popovers on the user's next click of a different element than the toggle element. A press inside the popover itself does not dismiss it, so users can select its text or use the controls in it.

A shown popover can also be dismissed by pressing the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key. As with dropdown menus, a popover shown inside a dialog is dismissed on its own: the first <kbd>Escape</kbd> closes the popover and a subsequent one closes the dialog.

> #### Specific markup required for dismiss-on-next-click
> 
> For proper cross-browser and cross-platform behavior, you must use an `` element, _not_ a `` element, and you also must include a [`tabIndex`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Global_attributes/tabindex) attribute.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverDismissExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover
      content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
      placement="right"
      title="Dismissible popover"
      trigger="focus"
    >
      <CButton as="a" theme="danger" role="button" tabIndex={0}>
        Dismissible popover
      </CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

## Usage

> ### Making popovers work for keyboard and assistive technology users
> 
> To allow keyboard users to activate your popovers, you should only add them to HTML elements that are traditionally keyboard-focusable and interactive (such as links or form controls). Although arbitrary HTML elements (such as ``s) can be made focusable by adding the `tabIndex={0}` attribute, this will add potentially annoying and confusing tab stops on non-interactive elements for keyboard users, and most assistive technologies currently do not announce the popover's content in this situation. Additionally, do not rely solely on `hover` as the trigger for your popovers, as this will make them impossible to trigger for keyboard users.
> 
> While you can insert rich, structured React nodes with the `content` prop, we strongly recommend that you avoid adding an excessive amount of content. The way popovers currently work is that, once displayed, their content is tied to the trigger element with the `aria-describedby` attribute. As a result, the entirety of the popover's content will be announced to assistive technology users as one long, uninterrupted stream.
> 
> Additionally, while it is possible to also include interactive controls (such as form elements or links) in your popover, be aware that currently the popover does not manage keyboard focus order. When a keyboard user opens a popover, focus remains on the triggering element, and as the popover usually does not immediately follow the trigger in the document's structure, there is no guarantee that moving forward/pressing TAB will move a keyboard user into the popover itself. In short, simply adding interactive controls to a popover is likely to make these controls unreachable/unusable for keyboard users and users of assistive technologies, or at the very least make for an illogical overall focus order. In these cases, consider using a modal dialog instead.

### Disabled elements

Elements with the disabled attribute aren't interactive, meaning users cannot hover or click them to trigger a popover (or tooltip). As a workaround, you'll want to trigger the popover from a wrapper `<div>` or `<span>`, ideally made keyboard-focusable using `tabindex="0"`.

For disabled popover triggers, you may also prefer `trigger={['hover', 'focus']}` so that the popover appears as immediate visual feedback to your users as they may not expect to click on a disabled element.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverDisabledElementsExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover content="Disabled popover" placement="right" trigger={['hover', 'focus']}>
      <span className="d-inline-block" tabIndex={0}>
        <CButton theme="primary" disabled>
          Disabled button
        </CButton>
      </span>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The popover works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the visibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the popover, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the popover requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture, the Escape key or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

`onShowChange` is a request, not a report. To follow what is on screen, `onShow` and `onHide` fire when the popover starts showing or hiding (after `delay`, and only when the visibility actually changes), and `onShown` and `onHidden` once the transition has finished.

### Uncontrolled

Every example above is uncontrolled — the trigger gestures manage the popover. `defaultShow` seeds it visible on mount, and the gestures take over from there.

```jsx
<CPopover title="Popover" content="Shown on load" defaultShow>
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the popover renders what you pass — trigger gestures only call `onShowChange`. That is what a **pinned** popover needs: while the checkbox holds `show` true, clicking away only requests a change the page does not grant.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CCheckbox, CFormField, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverControlledExample = () => {
  const [pinned, setPinned] = useState(true)
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CFormField className="mb-4">
        <CCheckbox
          checked={pinned}
          id="popoverPinned"
          label="Pin the popover"
          onChange={(event) => setPinned(event.target.checked)}
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CPopover
        title="Pinned popover"
        content="While pinned, clicks and Escape only request a change — the page keeps it open."
        show={pinned || open}
        onShowChange={setOpen}
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Click me</CButton>
      </CPopover>
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when the visibility belongs to something else — an onboarding step, a hint anchored to a control — and feed `onShowChange` back for the parts you still want the gestures to drive, as the example does while unpinned.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CPopover /&gt;](./api/#cpopover)

# React Popover Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Popover component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CPopover

```jsx
import { CPopover } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Adds a fade transition animation to the React Popover. |
| `className` | `string` | - | Custom class name(s) for additional styling. |
| `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment \| (() => Element \| DocumentFragment \| null) \| null` | `document.body` | Defines the container element to which the React Popover is appended. Accepts: - A DOM element (`HTMLElement` or `DocumentFragment`) - A function that returns a single element - `null` (defaults to `document.body`) |
| `content` | `ReactNode` | - | Main content of the React Popover. It can be a string or any valid React node. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial visibility of an uncontrolled React Popover — read once on mount. |
| `delay` | `number \| { show: number; hide: number; }` | `0` | Delay (in milliseconds) before showing or hiding the React Popover. - If a number is provided, that delay applies to both "show" and "hide". - If an object is provided, use separate values for "show" and "hide". |
| `fallbackPlacements` | `'top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left' \| ('top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left')[]` | `['top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left']` | Specifies the fallback placements when the preferred `placement` cannot be met. |
| `floatingConfig` | `Partial<ComputePositionConfig> \| ((defaultFloatingConfig: Partial<ComputePositionConfig>) => Partial<ComputePositionConfig>)` | - | Allows customization of the Floating UI configuration for the React Popover. Can be an object or a function returning a modified configuration. [Learn more](https://floating-ui.com/docs/computePosition#options) |
| `offset` | `[number, number]` | `[0, 8]` | Offset of the React Popover relative to its toggle element, in the form `[x, y]`. |
| `onHidden` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Popover has finished its exit transition. |
| `onHide` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Popover starts hiding. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Popover starts showing. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Popover requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture (hover, focus, click), the Escape key or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the popover stays as it is. |
| `onShown` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Popover has finished its entry transition. |
| `placement` | `"auto" \| "top" \| "bottom" \| "right" \| "left" \| "end" \| "start" \| (string & {})` | `top` | Placement of the React Popover. Floating UI may override this based on available space. `start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL. `left` and `right` are their deprecated spellings and resolve identically. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the visibility. When set, the React Popover renders what `show` says (delays still apply as presentation) and trigger gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing changes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `title` | `ReactNode` | - | Title for the React Popover header. Can be a string or any valid React node. |
| `trigger` | `'hover' \| 'focus' \| 'click' \| ('hover' \| 'focus' \| 'click')[]` | `click` | Determines which events trigger the visibility of the React Popover. Can be a single trigger or an array of triggers. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Controls the visibility of the React Popover. - `true` shows the popover. - `false` hides the popover. |

# React Popover Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Popover component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Popover supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$popover-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-popover-zindex: var(--cui-z-popover),
    --cui-popover-max-width: 276px,
    --cui-popover-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-popover-bg: var(--cui-bg-body),
    --cui-popover-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-popover-border-color: var(--cui-border-color-translucent),
    --cui-popover-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-7),
    --cui-popover-inner-border-radius: calc(var(--cui-popover-border-radius) - var(--cui-popover-border-width)),
    --cui-popover-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow),
    --cui-popover-header-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-popover-header-padding-y: .5rem,
    --cui-popover-header-font-size: var(--cui-body-font-size),
    --cui-popover-header-color: var(--cui-heading-color),
    --cui-popover-header-bg: var(--cui-bg-1),
    --cui-popover-body-padding-x: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-popover-body-padding-y: var(--cui-spacer),
    --cui-popover-body-color: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-popover-arrow-width: 1rem,
    --cui-popover-arrow-height: .5rem,
    --cui-popover-arrow-border: var(--cui-popover-border-color),
    --cui-popover-transition-property: opacity,
    --cui-popover-transition-duration: .15s,
    --cui-popover-transition-timing: linear,
  ),
  $popover-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-popover-body-color': '#888',
  '--cui-popover-bg': '#f2f4f6',
}

return <CPopover style={customVars}>{/* Popover content */}</CPopover>
```

# React Bootstrap Popover Component

> Learn how to use the React Bootstrap Popover component from CoreUI to create interactive overlays for additional information, tooltips, or custom content.

## React Bootstrap Popover examples

The React Bootstrap Popover component lets you display small overlay content on hover, click, or focus. Use it for tooltips, inline help, or contextual info without cluttering the UI.

### Live demo

Trigger the React Bootstrap Popover on click.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverLiveExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover
      title="Popover title"
      content="And here’s some amazing content. It’s very engaging. Right?"
      placement="right"
    >
      <CButton theme="danger" size="lg">
        Click to toggle popover
      </CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

### Four directions

React Bootstrap Popovers support top, right, bottom, and left placement. Direction is automatically mirrored in RTL layouts.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverFourDirectionsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CPopover content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="top">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover on top</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="end">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover at the end</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="bottom"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover on bottom</CButton>
      </CPopover>
      <CPopover
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="start"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Popover at the start</CButton>
      </CPopover>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Custom popovers

Use inline `style` or CSS variables to override the popover's appearance.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverCustomPopoversExample = () => {
  const customPopoverStyle = {
    '--cui-popover-max-width': '200px',
    '--cui-popover-border-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
    '--cui-popover-header-bg': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
    '--cui-popover-header-color': 'var(--cui-white)',
    '--cui-popover-body-padding-x': '1rem',
    '--cui-popover-body-padding-y': '.5rem',
  } as React.CSSProperties

  return (
    <CPopover
      content="This popover is themed via CSS variables."
      placement="right"
      title="Custom popover"
      style={customPopoverStyle}
    >
      <CButton theme="secondary">Custom popover</CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

### Dismiss on next click

Use `trigger="focus"` to automatically hide the popover when clicking outside the element. A press inside the popover itself does not dismiss it, so users can select its text or use the controls in it.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverDismissExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover
      content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
      placement="right"
      title="Dismissible popover"
      trigger="focus"
    >
      <CButton as="a" theme="danger" role="button" tabIndex={0}>
        Dismissible popover
      </CButton>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

## Usage details

### Popovers on disabled elements

HTML elements with the `disabled` attribute cannot trigger popovers. Wrap them in a `<span>` or `<div>` and use `tabIndex="0"` to keep the element accessible. You can also use `trigger={['hover', 'focus']}` to ensure visual feedback.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CPopover } from '@coreui/react'

export const PopoverDisabledElementsExample = () => {
  return (
    <CPopover content="Disabled popover" placement="right" trigger={['hover', 'focus']}>
      <span className="d-inline-block" tabIndex={0}>
        <CButton theme="primary" disabled>
          Disabled button
        </CButton>
      </span>
    </CPopover>
  )
}
```

- [&lt;CPopover /&gt;](../api/#cpopover)

# React Progress Component

> Documentation and examples for using React progress bars featuring support for stacked bars, animated backgrounds, and text labels.

## Example

Progress components are built with two HTML elements, some CSS to set the width, and a few attributes. We don't use [the HTML5 `<progress>` element](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/progress), ensuring you can stack progress bars, animate them, and place text labels over them.

## Basic usage

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress value={0} />
      <CProgress value={25} />
      <CProgress value={50} />
      <CProgress value={75} />
      <CProgress value={100} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Labels

Add labels to your progress bars by placing text within the `<CProgressBar>`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressLabelsExample = () => {
  return <CProgress value={25}>25%</CProgress>
}
```

Please note that the default setting for the content within the `` is to be limited by the `overflow: hidden property`, preventing it from extending beyond the bar's boundaries. If the progress bar is shorter than its label, the content will be truncated and could be difficult to read. To modify this behavior, you can utilize the `.overflow-visible` class from the overflow utilities. However, it is important to specify a specific text color to ensure readability. It's worth noting that this approach currently does not consider color modes.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress, CProgressBar } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressLabels2Example = () => {
  return (
    <CProgress value={10}>
      <CProgressBar className="overflow-visible fg-black px-3" theme="success">
        Long label text for the progress bar, set to a dark color
      </CProgressBar>
    </CProgress>
  )
}
```

Since **v4.9.0** you can also use the `progressBarClassName` property directly on the `` component to achieve the same.

```jsx
<CProgress progressBarClassName="overflow-visible fg-black px-3" theme="success" value={10}>Long label text for the progress bar, set to a dark color</CProgress>
```

### Long labels

A `<CProgressBar>` clips what does not fit — it is `overflow: hidden` with `white-space: nowrap` — so a label wider than the bar is cut off rather than wrapped. Add [`overflow-visible`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/overflow/) to let it spill over the track instead.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress, CProgressBar } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressLongLabelsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress className="mb-4">
        <CProgressBar value={10}>Filling in your details</CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
      <CProgress>
        <CProgressBar className="overflow-visible" value={10}>
          Filling in your details
        </CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
    </>
  )
}
```

Spilling over comes at a cost: the label then sits on two backgrounds at once, so its color has to contrast with both the bar and the track. Where it cannot, put the label outside the progress bar instead.

## Height

We only set a `height` value on the `<CProgress>`, so if you change that value the inner `<CProgressBar>` will automatically resize accordingly.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressHeightExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress height={1} value={25} />
      <CProgress height={20} value={25} />
    </>
  )
}
```

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress, CProgressBar } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressHeight2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress height={1}>
        <CProgressBar value={25}></CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
      <CProgress height={20}>
        <CProgressBar value={25}></CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Backgrounds

Use `color` prop to change the appearance of individual progress bars.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressBackgroundsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress theme="success" value={25} />
      <CProgress theme="info" value={50} />
      <CProgress theme="warning" value={75} />
      <CProgress theme="danger" value={100} />
    </>
  )
}
```

Ensure that when you incorporate labels into progress bars featuring a custom background color, you also select an appropriate text color to ensure readability and maintain adequate contrast for the labels.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress, CProgressBar } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressBackgrounds2Example = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress theme="success" value={25}>
        <CProgressBar>25%</CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
      <CProgress theme="info" value={50}>
        <CProgressBar className="fg-black">50%</CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
      <CProgress theme="warning" value={75}>
        <CProgressBar className="fg-black">75%</CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
      <CProgress theme="danger" value={100}>
        <CProgressBar>100%</CProgressBar>
      </CProgress>
    </>
  )
}
```

Since **v4.9.0** you can also use the `progressBarClassName` property directly on the `` component to achieve the same.

```jsx
<CProgress theme="success" value={25}>25%</CProgress>
<CProgress theme="info" progressBarClassName="fg-black" value={50}>50%</CProgress>
<CProgress theme="warning" progressBarClassName="fg-black" value={75}>75%</CProgress>
<CProgress theme="danger" value={100}>100%</CProgress>
```

## Gradients

_Added in 6.0.0._

Set `--cui-progress-bar-bg-image` to paint the bar with a gradient instead of a flat colour. The image is sized to the bar, so the whole gradient is visible at any width and the label keeps the colour set by the theme. Set it in `style` on `<CProgress>`; the bar reads it from there.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressGradientExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress
        value={45}
        style={{
          '--cui-progress-bar-bg-image': 'linear-gradient(to right, #e6412c, #ffb400, #ffe25a)',
        }}
      />
      <CProgress
        value={70}
        style={{
          '--cui-progress-bar-bg-image':
            'linear-gradient(to right, var(--cui-info-base), var(--cui-success-base))',
        }}
      >
        70%
      </CProgress>
    </>
  )
}
```

Stripes are a second layer over the gradient, so `variant="striped"` and `animated` combine with it. Change the stripe pattern itself with `--cui-progress-bar-stripes`, or just its colour with `--cui-progress-bar-stripe-color`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressGradientStripedExample = () => {
  return (
    <CProgress
      animated
      value={65}
      variant="striped"
      style={{
        '--cui-progress-bar-bg-image': 'linear-gradient(to right, #e6412c, #ffb400, #ffe25a)',
      }}
    />
  )
}
```

## Multiple bars

Include multiple progress bars in a progress component if you need. In **v4.9.0**

> In version 4.9.0, we introduced a new `` component to more logically wrap multiple progress bars into a single stacked progress bar. The previous structure will continue to work until the next major version.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress, CProgressStacked } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressMultipleBarsExample = () => {
  return (
    <CProgressStacked>
      <CProgress value={15} />
      <CProgress theme="success" value={30} />
      <CProgress theme="info" value={20} />
    </CProgressStacked>
  )
}
```

**Previous markup**
```jsx
<CProgress>
  <CProgressBar value={15} />
  <CProgressBar theme="success" value={30} />
  <CProgressBar theme="info" value={20} />
</CProgress>
```

## Segmented

_Added in 6.0.0._

Add `segmented` to cut the track into a row of rounded segments. It is a CSS mask over the whole component, so the bar keeps its transition, theme, gradient and stripes; only the rendering changes. Segments are `--cui-progress-segment-min-width` wide (.25rem) and `--cui-progress-segment-gap` apart, as many as fit; set `segments` and the track holds at most that many, scaled to its width, with the gap staying put.

The component watches the track's width and fills whole segments only: `value` is turned into the number of segments it covers, rounded down, so the fill always ends on a segment's edge and a narrow screen shows fewer segments rather than thinner ones.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressSegmentedExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress
        height={48}
        segmented
        value={45}
        style={{
          '--cui-progress-bar-bg-image': 'linear-gradient(to right, #e6412c, #ffb400, #ffe25a)',
        }}
      />
      <CProgress segmented theme="success" value={70} />
      <CProgress
        height={24}
        segmented
        segments={20}
        theme="info"
        value={30}
        style={{ '--cui-progress-segment-gap': '.5rem' }}
      />
      <CProgress
        height={24}
        segmented
        theme="danger"
        value={30}
        style={{ '--cui-progress-segment-min-width': '1rem' }}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

The corners follow `--cui-progress-segment-border-radius`, `--cui-radius-2` by default, capped at half the segment and half the track height as `border-radius` would. Set it to `0px` for square segments, or anything in between; the value feeds the mask's `calc()`, so it has to be a length.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressSegmentedRadiusExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CProgress
        height={24}
        segmented
        segments={10}
        value={60}
        style={{ '--cui-progress-segment-border-radius': '0px' }}
      />
      <CProgress
        height={24}
        segmented
        segments={10}
        theme="warning"
        value={60}
        style={{ '--cui-progress-segment-border-radius': 'var(--cui-radius-5)' }}
      />
    </>
  )
}
```

## On a colored surface

Add the `white` property to draw the bar in the current text color and the track as a faint tint of it. That way a progress bar sitting on a solid or brand-colored surface takes its colors from the text around it rather than needing a color of its own.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react'

export const ProgressWhiteExample = () => {
  return <CProgress white value={50} />
}
```

## Grouping bars

Related bars need no component of their own — [stacks](https://coreui.io/react/docs/helpers/stacks/) and [spacing utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/margin/) lay them out. Put a label column beside a `vstack` of bars to compare several series against the same baseline.

```html
import React from 'react'

export const ProgressGroupingExample = () => {
  return (
    <div className="hstack gap-4">
      <span className="fg-2 small flex-shrink-0" style={{ width: '100px' }}>
        Title
      </span>
      <div className="vstack gap-1">
        <CProgress height={4}>
          <CProgressBar theme="info" value={34} aria-label="First series" />
        </CProgress>
        <CProgress height={4}>
          <CProgressBar theme="danger" value={78} aria-label="Second series" />
        </CProgress>
      </div>
    </div>
  )
}
```

# React Progress Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Progress component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CProgress

```jsx
import { CProgress } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animated` | `boolean` | - | Use to animate the stripes right to left via CSS3 animations. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the component. |
| `color` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `height` | `number` | - | Sets the height of the component. If you set that value the inner `<CProgressBar>` will automatically resize accordingly. |
| `progressBarClassName` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the `<CProgressBar/>` component. |
| `segmented` | `boolean` | - | Cuts the track into a row of rounded segments and fills whole segments only. Set `segments` to cap how many, otherwise as many as fit above `--cui-progress-segment-min-width`. |
| `segments` | `number` | - | The most segments a segmented track holds; fewer are drawn when they would get narrower than `--cui-progress-segment-min-width`. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `value` | `number` | - | The percent to progress the ProgressBar (out of 100). |
| `variant` | `"striped"` | - | Set the progress bar variant to optional striped. |
| `white` | `boolean` | - | Change the default color to white. |

```jsx
import { CProgressBar } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `value` | `number` | `0` | The percent to progress the ProgressBar. |
| `variant` | `"striped"` | - | Set the progress bar variant to optional striped. |

# React Progress Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Progress component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Progress supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$progress-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-progress-height: 1rem,
    --cui-progress-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-progress-bg: var(--cui-bg-2),
    --cui-progress-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-5),
    --cui-progress-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-inset),
    --cui-progress-bar-color: var(--cui-primary-contrast),
    --cui-progress-bar-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg),
    --cui-progress-bar-bg-image: none,
    --cui-progress-bar-stripes: linear-gradient(45deg, var(--cui-progress-bar-stripe-color) 25%, transparent 25%, transparent 50%, var(--cui-progress-bar-stripe-color) 50%, var(--cui-progress-bar-stripe-color) 75%, transparent 75%, transparent),
    --cui-progress-bar-stripe-color: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-white) 15%, transparent),
    --cui-progress-bar-transition: width .6s ease,
    --cui-progress-bar-animation: progress-bar-stripes 1s linear infinite,
  ),
  $progress-tokens
);
```

`segmented` adds the segment geometry:

```scss
$progress-segmented-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-progress-segment-gap: .25rem,
    --cui-progress-segment-min-width: .25rem,
    --cui-progress-segment-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-2),
  ),
  $progress-segmented-tokens
);

// Unset by default: the plugin then packs as many segments as fit above the minimum width
@if $progress-segments != null {
  $progress-segmented-tokens: map.set($progress-segmented-tokens, --cui-progress-segments, $progress-segments);
}
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-progress-bar-color': '#888',
  '--cui-progress-bar-bg': '#f2f4f6',
}

return <CProgress style={customVars}>...</CProgress>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$progress-segments:                    null !default;

$progress-contrast-track-opacity:      20% !default;
```

## Keyframes

Used for creating the CSS animations for `.progress-bar-animated`.

```scss
@if $enable-transitions {
  @keyframes progress-bar-stripes {
    0% { background-position-x: var(--cui-progress-height), 0; }
  }
}
```

The React Bootstrap Progress component helps you visually represent progress or completion rates in tasks, processes, or downloads. These bars are fully customizable with colors, labels, sizes, and animations.

# React Scrollspy Component

> Automatically update the navigation based on scroll position to indicate which section is currently active in the viewport.

## How it works

_Added in 6.0.0._

`<CScrollspy>` watches the sections you list by id and hands the id of the current one to its children — the navigation stays yours, controlled through the `active` property like everywhere else in React. It is best used with a [nav component](../navs-tabs/) or [list group](../list-group/), but any anchor elements in the page work the same way. Here's how it works.

- To start, scrollspy requires two things: a navigation, list group, or a simple set of links, plus a scrollable container. The scrollable container can be the viewport or a custom element with a set `height` and `overflow-y: scroll`.
- List the section ids in `ids`, in document order, and pass the scrollable element through `containerRef` when it is not the viewport. If there is no focusable element inside the container, be sure to also include `tabIndex={0}` to ensure keyboard access.
- As you scroll the container, the function-as-children form receives the id of the active section, and `onActivate` fires whenever it changes. Ids must resolve to an element in the DOM, otherwise they're ignored — a link `<a href="#home">` needs something like `<div id="home">` among the sections.
- Sections are looked up when the component mounts and whenever `ids` or `containerRef` change; a section added later is picked up once `ids` changes.

### Detection

The component watches every section with an [`IntersectionObserver`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/IntersectionObserver) and decides which one is current from a single rule: an invisible **activation line** drawn across the scroll container, `topMargin` below its top edge (`12%` of the container's height by default). The result depends only on where the container is scrolled to, never on which direction it got there.

- **The active section is the lowest one whose top edge has moved up to or above the activation line.** When several sections are visible at once, the one you have scrolled furthest into wins.
- **Between two sections nothing changes.** While the gap between one section's end and the next heading crosses the line, the previous id stays active instead of the navigation going blank.
- **Above the first section the first id is active**, so the navigation is never empty once the container has content.
- **At the bottom of the container the last id is active**, even when the last section is too short for its top edge to ever reach the line.

Move the line with `topMargin` — a percentage of the container's height or a pixel value, for example `96px` to put it just below a sticky navbar; a pixel line is recomputed when the window resizes. To take over the observer's root box entirely, set `rootMargin` instead; when both are given, `rootMargin` wins. See the [API](#api).

### Scrollable containers and keyboard access

If you're making a scrollable container (other than the viewport), be sure to have a `height` set and `overflow-y: scroll;` applied to it—alongside `tabIndex={0}` to ensure keyboard access.

## Examples

### Navbar

Scroll the area below the navbar and watch the active state change. Open the dropdown and watch the dropdown items be highlighted as well — the toggle lights up whenever any of its items is the active one.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
  CNav,
  CNavItem,
  CNavLink,
  CNavbar,
  CNavbarBrand,
} from '@coreui/react'
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const copy =
  'This is some placeholder content for the scrollspy page. Note that as you scroll down the page, the appropriate navigation link is highlighted.'

export const ScrollspyNavbarExample = () => {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
  const dropdownIds = new Set(['spyNavHeading3', 'spyNavHeading4', 'spyNavHeading5'])

  return (
    <CScrollspy
      ids={['spyNavHeading1', 'spyNavHeading2', ...dropdownIds]}
      containerRef={containerRef}
    >
      {(activeId) => (
        <>
          <CNavbar className="bg-3 px-4">
            <CNavbarBrand href="#">Navbar</CNavbarBrand>
            <CNav variant="pills">
              <CNavItem>
                <CNavLink href="#spyNavHeading1" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading1'}>
                  First
                </CNavLink>
              </CNavItem>
              <CNavItem>
                <CNavLink href="#spyNavHeading2" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading2'}>
                  Second
                </CNavLink>
              </CNavItem>
              <CDropdown variant="nav-item">
                <CDropdownToggle
                  link
                  className={activeId && dropdownIds.has(activeId) ? 'active' : undefined}
                >
                  Dropdown
                </CDropdownToggle>
                <CDropdownMenu>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading3" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading3'}>
                    Third
                  </CDropdownItem>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading4" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading4'}>
                    Fourth
                  </CDropdownItem>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading5" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading5'}>
                    Fifth
                  </CDropdownItem>
                </CDropdownMenu>
              </CDropdown>
            </CNav>
          </CNavbar>
          <div
            className="overflow-auto p-4"
            style={{ maxHeight: '14rem' }}
            ref={containerRef}
            tabIndex={0}
          >
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading1">First heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading2">Second heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading3">Third heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading4">Fourth heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading5">Fifth heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
          </div>
        </>
      )}
    </CScrollspy>
  )
}
```

### Nested nav

Scrollspy also works with nested `<CNav>`s. The component reports one active id, so parent activation is yours to derive — a small map from parent to its section ids keeps the group's link lit while any of its children is active. Scroll the area next to the navbar and watch the active state change.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CNav, CNavLink } from '@coreui/react'
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const copy =
  'This is some placeholder content for the scrollspy page. Note that as you scroll down the page, the appropriate navigation link is highlighted.'

const groups: Record<string, string[]> = {
  spyItem1: ['spyItem1', 'spyItem1-1', 'spyItem1-2'],
  spyItem2: ['spyItem2'],
  spyItem3: ['spyItem3', 'spyItem3-1', 'spyItem3-2'],
}

export const ScrollspyNestedExample = () => {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
  const parentOf = (id: string | null) =>
    id ? Object.keys(groups).find((parent) => groups[parent].includes(id)) : undefined

  return (
    <CScrollspy ids={Object.values(groups).flat()} containerRef={containerRef}>
      {(activeId) => (
        <div className="row">
          <div className="col-4">
            <CNav className="flex-column" variant="pills">
              <CNavLink href="#spyItem1" active={parentOf(activeId) === 'spyItem1'}>
                Item 1
              </CNavLink>
              <CNav className="flex-column ms-4" variant="pills">
                <CNavLink href="#spyItem1-1" active={activeId === 'spyItem1-1'}>
                  Item 1-1
                </CNavLink>
                <CNavLink href="#spyItem1-2" active={activeId === 'spyItem1-2'}>
                  Item 1-2
                </CNavLink>
              </CNav>
              <CNavLink href="#spyItem2" active={parentOf(activeId) === 'spyItem2'}>
                Item 2
              </CNavLink>
              <CNavLink href="#spyItem3" active={parentOf(activeId) === 'spyItem3'}>
                Item 3
              </CNavLink>
              <CNav className="flex-column ms-4" variant="pills">
                <CNavLink href="#spyItem3-1" active={activeId === 'spyItem3-1'}>
                  Item 3-1
                </CNavLink>
                <CNavLink href="#spyItem3-2" active={activeId === 'spyItem3-2'}>
                  Item 3-2
                </CNavLink>
              </CNav>
            </CNav>
          </div>
          <div
            className="col-8 overflow-auto"
            style={{ maxHeight: '16rem' }}
            ref={containerRef}
            tabIndex={0}
          >
            <h4 id="spyItem1">Item 1</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h5 id="spyItem1-1">Item 1-1</h5>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h5 id="spyItem1-2">Item 1-2</h5>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyItem2">Item 2</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyItem3">Item 3</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h5 id="spyItem3-1">Item 3-1</h5>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h5 id="spyItem3-2">Item 3-2</h5>
            <p>{copy}</p>
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </CScrollspy>
  )
}
```

### List group

Scrollspy also works with `<CListGroup>`s. Scroll the area next to the list group and watch the active state change.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CListGroup, CListGroupItem } from '@coreui/react'
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const copy =
  'This is some placeholder content for the scrollspy page. Note that as you scroll down the page, the appropriate navigation link is highlighted.'

export const ScrollspyListGroupExample = () => {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
  const ids = ['spyList1', 'spyList2', 'spyList3', 'spyList4']

  return (
    <CScrollspy ids={ids} containerRef={containerRef}>
      {(activeId) => (
        <div className="row">
          <div className="col-4">
            <CListGroup>
              {ids.map((id, index) => (
                <CListGroupItem as="a" key={id} href={`#${id}`} active={activeId === id}>
                  Item {index + 1}
                </CListGroupItem>
              ))}
            </CListGroup>
          </div>
          <div
            className="col-8 overflow-auto"
            style={{ maxHeight: '16rem' }}
            ref={containerRef}
            tabIndex={0}
          >
            {ids.map((id, index) => (
              <React.Fragment key={id}>
                <h4 id={id}>Item {index + 1}</h4>
                <p>{copy}</p>
              </React.Fragment>
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </CScrollspy>
  )
}
```

### Simple anchors

Scrollspy is not limited to nav components and list groups, so it will work with any `<a>` anchor elements in the current document. Scroll the area and watch the highlighted link change.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'

  'This is some placeholder content for the scrollspy page. Note that as you scroll down the page, the appropriate navigation link is highlighted.'

      {(activeId) => (
        <div className="row">
          <div className="col-4">

              {ids.map((id, index) => (
                <a
                  key={id}
                  href={`#${id}`}
                  className={activeId === id ? 'p-1 rounded bg-subtle-primary' : 'p-1 rounded'}

                  Item {index + 1}
                </a>
              ))}

          </div>
          <div
            className="col-8 overflow-auto"
            style={{ maxHeight: '16rem' }}
            ref={containerRef}
            tabIndex={0}
          >
            {ids.map((id, index) => (
              <React.Fragment key={id}>
                <h4 id={id}>Item {index + 1}</h4>
                <p>{copy}</p>
              </React.Fragment>
            ))}
          </div>
        </div>
      )}
    </CScrollspy>

}
```

# React Scrollspy Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Scrollspy component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CScrollspy

```jsx
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode \| ((activeId: string \| null) => ReactNode)` | - | Render prop or plain children. The function form receives the id of the currently active section (without the `#`), or `null`. |
| `containerRef` | `RefObject<HTMLElement \| null>` | - | Ref to the scrollable container holding the sections. Defaults to the viewport. |
| `ids` | `string[]` | - | Ids of the sections to observe, in document order. |
| `onActivate` | `((id: string \| null) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the active section changes. |
| `rootMargin` | `string \| null` | - | Raw IntersectionObserver `rootMargin`. When set it takes precedence over `topMargin` and is passed straight to the observer. |
| `threshold` | `number[]` | `[0]` | Intersection observer thresholds. |
| `topMargin` | `string` | `12%` | Position of the activation line, measured from the top of the scroll root. The active section is the deepest one whose top has scrolled to or above it. Accepts a percentage (`12%`) or pixels (`96px`, e.g. below a sticky navbar). |

# React Bootstrap Scrollspy Component

> Learn how to highlight the section currently in view using CoreUI's React Scrollspy component styled to match Bootstrap navigation.

## How to use React Bootstrap Scrollspy component

Use CoreUI's `<CScrollspy>` to keep Bootstrap-styled navigation in sync with the reader's scroll position. List the section ids in `ids`, pass a `containerRef` when the sections scroll inside their own container, and read the active id from the children function to control the `active` state of your links.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import {
  CDropdown,
  CDropdownItem,
  CDropdownMenu,
  CDropdownToggle,
  CNav,
  CNavItem,
  CNavLink,
  CNavbar,
  CNavbarBrand,
} from '@coreui/react'
import { CScrollspy } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const copy =
  'This is some placeholder content for the scrollspy page. Note that as you scroll down the page, the appropriate navigation link is highlighted.'

export const ScrollspyNavbarExample = () => {
  const containerRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null)
  const dropdownIds = new Set(['spyNavHeading3', 'spyNavHeading4', 'spyNavHeading5'])

  return (
    <CScrollspy
      ids={['spyNavHeading1', 'spyNavHeading2', ...dropdownIds]}
      containerRef={containerRef}
    >
      {(activeId) => (
        <>
          <CNavbar className="bg-3 px-4">
            <CNavbarBrand href="#">Navbar</CNavbarBrand>
            <CNav variant="pills">
              <CNavItem>
                <CNavLink href="#spyNavHeading1" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading1'}>
                  First
                </CNavLink>
              </CNavItem>
              <CNavItem>
                <CNavLink href="#spyNavHeading2" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading2'}>
                  Second
                </CNavLink>
              </CNavItem>
              <CDropdown variant="nav-item">
                <CDropdownToggle
                  link
                  className={activeId && dropdownIds.has(activeId) ? 'active' : undefined}
                >
                  Dropdown
                </CDropdownToggle>
                <CDropdownMenu>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading3" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading3'}>
                    Third
                  </CDropdownItem>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading4" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading4'}>
                    Fourth
                  </CDropdownItem>
                  <CDropdownItem href="#spyNavHeading5" active={activeId === 'spyNavHeading5'}>
                    Fifth
                  </CDropdownItem>
                </CDropdownMenu>
              </CDropdown>
            </CNav>
          </CNavbar>
          <div
            className="overflow-auto p-4"
            style={{ maxHeight: '14rem' }}
            ref={containerRef}
            tabIndex={0}
          >
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading1">First heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading2">Second heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading3">Third heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading4">Fourth heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
            <h4 id="spyNavHeading5">Fifth heading</h4>
            <p>{copy}</p>
          </div>
        </>
      )}
    </CScrollspy>
  )
}
```

# React Search Button Component

> React search button component for keyboard-aware search entry points, command palettes, modals, and offcanvas panels.

## Overview

The CoreUI React Search Button component is a trigger element designed for search entry points and command-style actions. It behaves like a regular button on click, but it can also react to a configurable keyboard shortcut such as `meta+/` or `ctrl+/`.

- Use it as a standalone trigger for a custom search UI.
- Pair it with React state to open a modal, offcanvas, or command palette.
- Shortcut keys are rendered automatically.
- Displayed shortcut keys react to keyboard interaction and receive an `.active` state while pressed.

## Basic example

Use `` as the entry point for a controlled search interface. Use `onTrigger` as the main activation callback for both direct interaction and keyboard shortcuts.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CBadge,
  CFormInput,
  CListGroup,
  CListGroupItem,
  CModal,
  CModalBody,
  CModalHeader,
  CModalTitle,
  CSearchButton,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const SearchButtonExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CSearchButton
        onTrigger={() => setShow(true)}
        aria-label="Open search dialog"
        aria-controls="search-button-modal"
        shortcut="meta+/,ctrl+/"
      />
      <CModal show={show} onShowChange={setShow} aria-labelledby="search-button-modal-title">
        <CModalHeader>
          <CModalTitle id="search-button-modal-title" className="w-100">
            <CFormInput type="search" placeholder="Search" aria-label="Search" />
          </CModalTitle>
        </CModalHeader>
        <CModalBody>
          <p className="fg-2 small mb-3">Recent searches</p>
          <CListGroup flush>
            <CListGroupItem
              as="button"
              type="button"
              className="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center"
            >
              CoreUI components overview
              <CBadge theme="secondary" shape="rounded-pill">
                Open
              </CBadge>
            </CListGroupItem>
            <CListGroupItem
              as="button"
              type="button"
              className="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center"
            >
              Modal dialog examples
              <CBadge theme="secondary" shape="rounded-pill">
                Open
              </CBadge>
            </CListGroupItem>
            <CListGroupItem
              as="button"
              type="button"
              className="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center"
            >
              Sidebar navigation customization
              <CBadge theme="secondary" shape="rounded-pill">
                Open
              </CBadge>
            </CListGroupItem>
          </CListGroup>
        </CModalBody>
      </CModal>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Custom shortcut

Configure the shortcut with the `shortcut` prop. On macOS, the component prefers the `meta` variant for the visible label. On Windows and Linux, it prefers the `ctrl` variant.

> Shortcuts such as `meta+f`, `ctrl+f`, `meta+s`, or `ctrl+s` can override native browser or system shortcuts. Prefer safer combinations such as `meta+/` and `ctrl+/` unless replacing the default behavior is intentional.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CAlert, CSearchButton } from '@coreui/react'

export const SearchButtonCustomShortcutExample = () => {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0)

  return (
    <div>
      <CSearchButton
        placeholder="Command palette"
        shortcut="meta+i,ctrl+i"
        onTrigger={() => setCount((value) => value + 1)}
        aria-label="Open command palette"
      />
      <CAlert theme="info" className="mt-4 mb-0">
        Triggered {count} {count === 1 ? 'time' : 'times'} with click or shortcut.
      </CAlert>
    </div>
  )
}
```

## Launch an offcanvas

The component works naturally with controlled React state and also supports a dedicated `onTrigger` callback. This demo uses `meta+shift+o` / `ctrl+shift+o` to avoid colliding with other live examples on the page.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import {
  CCloseButton,
  CFormInput,
  COffcanvas,
  COffcanvasBody,
  COffcanvasHeader,
  COffcanvasTitle,
  CSearchButton,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const SearchButtonOffcanvasExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CSearchButton
        onTrigger={() => setShow(true)}
        shortcut="meta+shift+o,ctrl+shift+o"
        aria-label="Open search panel"
        aria-controls="search-button-offcanvas"
      />

      <COffcanvas id="search-button-offcanvas" placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <COffcanvasHeader>
          <COffcanvasTitle>Search panel</COffcanvasTitle>
          <CCloseButton className="fg-reset" onClick={() => setShow(false)} />
        </COffcanvasHeader>
        <COffcanvasBody>
          <CFormInput
            type="search"
            className="mb-4"
            placeholder="Search..."
            aria-label="Search in panel"
          />
          <p className="mb-0">Use this space for filters, recent searches, or command shortcuts.</p>
        </COffcanvasBody>
      </COffcanvas>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Keyboard behavior

### When the configured shortcut is pressed

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Enter` / `Space` on a focused search button | Trigger the component activation callback |
| Configured shortcut, e.g. `⌘/` / `Ctrl+/` | Trigger the component activation callback |
| Modifier key inside the visible shortcut | Add `.active` to the corresponding `.search-button-key` while pressed |
| Final key inside the visible shortcut | Add `.active` to the corresponding `.search-button-key` while pressed |

### Keyboard state behavior

| Interaction | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| Matching shortcut on `keydown` | Optionally prevents the browser's default behavior and calls `onTrigger` |
| Plain typing inside `input`, `textarea`, `select`, or `contenteditable` | Does not trigger the component without `meta` or `ctrl` |
| `keyup` after a shortcut key press | Removes `.active` from the rendered shortcut keys |
| Browser window `blur` | Clears all active shortcut key states |
| Multiple configured shortcuts | The component listens to all configured shortcuts and renders the platform-preferred one in the UI |

## Accessibility

Accessibility is an important part of the Search Button design. The component includes built-in behaviors that help preserve expected keyboard interaction and reduce conflicts with assistive technologies, but accessible results still depend on choosing the right markup and shortcut combinations.

### Built-in accessibility behavior

- Native button semantics are preserved because `<CSearchButton>` renders a `<button type="button">` by default.
- Rendered `.search-button-keys` are treated as visual hints only and are hidden from assistive technologies.
- Plain typing inside editable fields does not trigger the component unless the shortcut also includes `meta` or `ctrl`.
- The component keeps standard button keyboard behavior such as `Enter` and `Space`.

### Author responsibilities

- Choose shortcuts carefully and avoid overriding common browser or system shortcuts unless that behavior is intentional and clearly communicated.
- Make sure the visible button label clearly describes the action, for example `Search`, `Open search`, or `Command palette`.
- Mark decorative icons as `aria-hidden="true"` when you provide a custom `icon`.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the component.

- [&lt;CSearchButton /&gt;](./api/#csearchbutton)

# React Search Button Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Search Button component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CSearchButton

```jsx
import { CSearchButton } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `children` | `ReactNode` | - | Content to customize the full button body. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. A disabled button also ignores its keyboard shortcut. |
| `icon` | `ReactNode` | - | Custom icon displayed before the placeholder text. |
| `onTrigger` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the component is activated by click or keyboard shortcut. |
| `placeholder` | `ReactNode` | `Search` | Placeholder content rendered inside `.search-button-placeholder`. |
| `preventDefault` | `boolean` | `true` | Prevent the browser's default behavior when the configured shortcut matches. |
| `shortcut` | `string` | `meta+/,ctrl+/` | Comma-separated shortcut list. The component matches all configured shortcuts and renders the platform-preferred one. |

# React Search Button Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Search Button component with CSS variables and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Search Button uses local CSS variables on `.search-button` for enhanced real-time customization. Values for the CSS variables are set via Sass, so Sass customization is still supported, too.

```scss
$search-button-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-search-button-height: var(--cui-btn-input-min-height),
    --cui-search-button-padding-x: var(--cui-btn-input-padding-x),
    --cui-search-button-font-size: var(--cui-btn-input-font-size),
    --cui-search-button-font-weight: var(--cui-btn-input-font-weight),
    --cui-search-button-color: var(--cui-fg-2),
    --cui-search-button-bg: var(--cui-btn-input-bg),
    --cui-search-button-border-width: var(--cui-btn-input-border-width),
    --cui-search-button-border-color: var(--cui-btn-input-border-color),
    --cui-search-button-border-radius: var(--cui-btn-input-border-radius),
    --cui-search-button-box-shadow: var(--cui-btn-input-box-shadow),
    --cui-search-button-transition-property: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-property),
    --cui-search-button-transition-duration: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-duration),
    --cui-search-button-transition-timing: var(--cui-btn-input-transition-timing),
    --cui-search-button-focus-color: var(--cui-btn-input-focus-color),
    --cui-search-button-focus-bg: var(--cui-btn-input-focus-bg),
    --cui-search-button-focus-border-color: var(--cui-btn-input-focus-border-color),
    --cui-search-button-icon-size: 1.125rem,
    --cui-search-button-keys-gap: .25rem,
    --cui-search-button-key-width: 1.5rem,
    --cui-search-button-key-height: 1.5rem,
    --cui-search-button-key-padding-inline: .25rem,
    --cui-search-button-key-font-size: .75rem,
    --cui-search-button-key-bg: var(--cui-bg-2),
    --cui-search-button-key-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-3),
    --cui-search-button-key-active-bg: var(--cui-bg-3),
    --cui-search-button-placeholder-margin-inline: .55rem 2rem,
  ),
  $search-button-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-search-button-bg': 'var(--cui-tertiary-bg)',
  '--cui-search-button-color': 'var(--cui-body-color)',
  '--cui-search-button-border-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
}

return (
  <CSearchButton
    placeholder="Search docs"
    onTrigger={() => {}}
    style={customVars}
  />
)
```

```html
  CFormInput,
  COffcanvas,
  COffcanvasBody,
  COffcanvasHeader,
  COffcanvasTitle,
  CSearchButton,
} from '@coreui/react'

export const SearchButtonOffcanvasExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CSearchButton
        onTrigger={() => setShow(true)}
        shortcut="meta+shift+o,ctrl+shift+o"
        aria-label="Open search panel"
        aria-controls="search-button-offcanvas"
      />

      <COffcanvas id="search-button-offcanvas" placement="end" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <COffcanvasHeader>
          <COffcanvasTitle>Search panel</COffcanvasTitle>
          <CCloseButton className="fg-reset" onClick={() => setShow(false)} />
        </COffcanvasHeader>
        <COffcanvasBody>
          <CFormInput
            type="search"
            className="mb-4"
            placeholder="Search..."
            aria-label="Search in panel"
          />
          <p className="mb-0">Use this space for filters, recent searches, or command shortcuts.</p>
        </COffcanvasBody>
      </COffcanvas>
    </>
  )
}
```

# React Sidebar Component

## How it works

Here's what you need to know before getting started with the React Sidebar component:

- `CSidebar` renders the `.sidebar` container.
- On mobile devices, the sidebar is hidden by default. Control it with the `show` prop.
- On desktop devices, the sidebar is shown by default. Hide it with `show={false}` — see [Controlled and uncontrolled](#controlled-and-uncontrolled).
- Use `narrow` to switch the sidebar to the narrow variant.
- Use `unfoldable` to switch the sidebar to the narrow-unfoldable variant.
- `CSidebarNav` renders `.sidebar-nav` and supports nested groups through `CNavGroup`.
- For accessibility, prefer semantic elements such as `nav`, or add `role="navigation"` when using `as="div"` on `CSidebarNav`.

## Supported content

Sidebar comes with built-in support for a handful of sub-components. Choose from the following as needed:

- `<CSidebarHeader>` for an optional header.
- `<CSidebarBrand>` for your company, product, or project name.
- `<CSidebarNav>` for a full-height and lightweight navigation, including nested groups.
- `<CSidebarFooter>` for an optional footer.
- `<CSidebarToggler>` for toggling the sidebar state.

## Examples

Below is a more complete sidebar example shown by default on desktop devices. It combines several optional features in a single demo, including narrow visibility helpers, tree navigation, nested groups, a custom group indicator, badges, and a footer menu.

### Narrow sidebar

Add the `narrow` prop to make the sidebar narrow.

Use `.d-sidebar-narrow` to show content only in the narrow state and `.d-sidebar-narrow-none` to hide content in the narrow state. These utility classes replace older brand-specific visibility helpers.

```html
import React from 'react'
import {
  CSidebar,
  CSidebarBrand,
  CSidebarHeader,
  CSidebarNav,
  CNavItem,
  CTooltip,
} from '@coreui/react'

import CIcon from '@coreui/icons-react'
import { cilCart, cilCloudDownload, cilSpeedometer } from '@coreui/icons'

export const SidebarNarrowExample = () => {
  return (
    <CSidebar className="border-end" narrow>
      <CSidebarHeader className="border-bottom">
        <CSidebarBrand>
          <svg
            role="img"
            aria-label="CoreUI Logo Signet"
            width="88"
            height="32"
            xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
            xmlnsXlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"
            viewBox="0 0 102 115"
          >
            <g style={{ fill: 'currentColor' }}>
              <path d="M96 24.124 57 1.608a12 12 0 0 0-12 0L6 24.124a12.034 12.034 0 0 0-6 10.393V79.55a12.033 12.033 0 0 0 6 10.392l39 22.517a12 12 0 0 0 12 0l39-22.517a12.033 12.033 0 0 0 6-10.392V34.517a12.034 12.034 0 0 0-6-10.393ZM94 79.55a4 4 0 0 1-2 3.464l-39 22.517a4 4 0 0 1-4 0L10 83.014a4 4 0 0 1-2-3.464V34.517a4 4 0 0 1 2-3.464L49 8.536a4 4 0 0 1 4 0l39 22.517a4 4 0 0 1 2 3.464V79.55Z"></path>
              <path d="M74.022 70.071h-2.866a4 4 0 0 0-1.925.494L51.95 80.05 32 68.531V45.554l19.95-11.519 17.29 9.455a4 4 0 0 0 1.919.49h2.863a2 2 0 0 0 2-2v-2.71a2 2 0 0 0-1.04-1.756L55.793 27.02a8.04 8.04 0 0 0-7.843.09L28 38.626a8.025 8.025 0 0 0-4 6.929V68.53a8 8 0 0 0 4 6.928l19.95 11.519a8.043 8.043 0 0 0 7.843.088l19.19-10.532a2 2 0 0 0 1.038-1.753v-2.71a2 2 0 0 0-2-2Z"></path>
            </g>
          </svg>
        </CSidebarBrand>
      </CSidebarHeader>
      <CSidebarNav>
        <CTooltip content="Nav item" placement="right">
          <CNavItem href="#">
            <CIcon customClassName="nav-icon" icon={cilSpeedometer} />
          </CNavItem>
        </CTooltip>
        <CTooltip content="Nav item" placement="right">
          <CNavItem href="#">
            <CIcon customClassName="nav-icon" icon={cilSpeedometer} />
          </CNavItem>
        </CTooltip>
        <CTooltip content="Download" placement="right">
          <CNavItem href="https://coreui.io">
            <CIcon customClassName="nav-icon" icon={cilCloudDownload} />
          </CNavItem>
        </CTooltip>
        <CTooltip content="Get CoreUI PRO" placement="right">
          <CNavItem href="https://coreui.io/pricing/">
            <CIcon customClassName="nav-icon" icon={cilCart} />
          </CNavItem>
        </CTooltip>
      </CSidebarNav>
    </CSidebar>
  )
}
```
