# React Toast Component

> Push notifications to your visitors with a toast, a lightweight and easily customizable alert message.

React toasts are lightweight notifications designed to mimic the push notifications that have been popularized by mobile and desktop operating systems. They’re built with flexbox, so they’re easy to align and position.

## Overview

Things to know when using the toast plugin:

- Toasts are opt-in for performance reasons, so **you must initialize them yourself**.
- Toasts will automatically hide if you do not specify `autohide: false`.

## Examples

### Basic

To encourage extensible and predictable toasts, we recommend a header and body. Toast headers use `display: flex`, allowing easy alignment of content thanks to our margin and flexbox utilities.

Toasts are as flexible as you need and have very little required markup. At a minimum, we require a single element to contain your "toasted" content and strongly encourage a dismiss button.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/react'

export const ToastExample = () => {
  return (
    <CToast animation={false} autohide={false} defaultShow>
      <CToastHeader closeButton>
        <svg
          className="rounded me-3"
          width="20"
          height="20"
          xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
          preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
          focusable="false"
          role="img"
        >
          <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
        </svg>
        <div className="fw-bold me-auto">CoreUI for React.js</div>
        <small>7 min ago</small>
      </CToastHeader>
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
  )
}
```

### Translucent

Add the `translucent` property to let the background through the toast and blur it. The header thins out with it, so the whole toast reads as one surface.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/react'

export const ToastTranslucentExample = () => {
  return (
    <CToast autohide={false} defaultShow translucent>
      <CToastHeader closeButton>

          className="rounded me-3"
          width="20"
          height="20"

          preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
          focusable="false"
          role="img"
        >
          <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
        </svg>
        <div className="fw-bold me-auto">CoreUI for React.js</div>
        <small>7 min ago</small>
      </CToastHeader>
      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
```
```html
  )
}
```

### Custom content

Customize your toasts by removing sub-components, tweaking them with [utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/api/), or by adding your own markup. Here we've created a simpler toast by removing the default `<CToastHeader>`, adding a custom hide icon from [CoreUI Icons](https://coreui.io/icons/), and using some [flexbox utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/flex/) to adjust the layout.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastClose } from '@coreui/react'

export const ToastCustomContentExample = () => {
  return (
    <CToast autohide={false} defaultShow className="align-items-center">
      <div className="d-flex">
        <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
        <CToastClose className="me-3 m-auto" />
      </div>
    </CToast>
  )
}
```

Alternatively, you can also add additional controls and components to toasts.

```html
import React from 'react'

          focusable="false"
          role="img"
        >
          <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
        </svg>
        <div className="fw-bold me-auto">CoreUI for React.js</div>

      <CToastBody>Hello, world! This is a toast message.</CToastBody>
    </CToast>
```

## Toaster

_Added in 6.0.0._

`createToaster()` builds a store of toasts outside the React tree and `<CToaster toaster={toaster}>` renders whatever it holds, so a notification can be added from anywhere — an event handler, a data layer, a route loader — with a placed container, a visible-toasts limit, stacking and screen-reader priority. See the [toaster component](../toaster/).

## Placement

Place toasts with the `<CToaster>` component. The `placement` option of `createToaster()` — or the component's own `placement` prop, which wins over it — fixes the toast container to one of nine positions through the `.toast-container-{placement}` classes: for example `top-end` pins toasts to the upper end corner, a common position for notifications, inset from the edge by `--cui-toast-container-inset` (`--cui-spacer-5` by default). Toasts added to the same toaster stack automatically. If you're only ever going to show one toast at a time, you can also position a single `<CToast>` yourself with our [position utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/position/).

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end' })

export const ToastPlacementExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton
        theme="primary"
        onClick={() =>
          toaster.add({
            title: 'CoreUI for React.js',
            description: 'Hello, world! This is a toast message.',
          })
        }
      >
        Show toast in the top right corner
      </CButton>
      <CToaster toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The toast works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the visibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the toast, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the toast requests a visibility change — the close button, the autohide timer or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

### Uncontrolled

Seed the toast with `defaultShow` and let it manage itself — the autohide timer and the close button dismiss it internally.

```jsx
<CToast defaultShow>
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the toast renders exactly what you pass — in controlled mode the autohide timer only fires `onShowChange`, it never closes the toast itself. The same goes for the close button, so the page below stays open through both.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CToast, CToastBody, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/react'

export const ToastControlledExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)
  const [requested, setRequested] = useState<boolean | null>(null)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton
        theme="primary"
        onClick={() => {
          setShow(!show)
          setRequested(null)
        }}
      >
        {show ? 'Hide toast' : 'Show toast'}
      </CButton>
      <CToast className="mt-4" delay={3000} show={show} onShowChange={setRequested}>
        <CToastHeader closeButton>
          <div className="fw-bold me-auto">Controlled toast</div>
        </CToastHeader>
        <CToastBody>
          The autohide timer and the close button only request a change — this page ignores both.
        </CToastBody>
      </CToast>
      {show && requested === false && (
        <p className="fg-2 mt-3">The toast asked to close, and the page kept it open.</p>
      )}
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when the visibility belongs to something else — an operation whose progress the toast reports — or when a dismissal needs to be intercepted rather than obeyed. This is how `<CToaster>` renders the toasts of a store: each one is controlled by its `open` flag, and the close button and the autohide timer go through `toaster.close(id)`.

## Accessibility

Toasts are meant to be brief interruptions for your visitors or users. To assist those using screen readers and similar assistive technologies, `<CToast>` renders as an [`aria-live` region](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Accessibility/ARIA/ARIA_Live_Regions) with `role="alert"`, `aria-live="assertive"`, and `aria-atomic="true"`. Changes to live regions, such as showing or updating a toast, are automatically announced by screen readers without moving the user's focus or interrupting the user. `aria-atomic="true"` ensures the entire toast is announced as a single, unfragmented unit, rather than just announcing what changed — this prevents issues if only part of the toast is updated or if the same toast appears again later. If the information is critical to the process, such as a list of form errors, use the [alert component](../alert/) instead of a toast.

You should adjust the `role` and `aria-live` level based on the content: the defaults suit important messages like errors, while for less urgent notifications you should pass `role="status"` and `aria-live="polite"` to the toast, which override the defaults. A toast rendered from a [toaster](../toaster/) carries no live role at all: the store announces it through the [live regions of the page](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages), and `priority` picks the polite or the assertive one.

Note that the live region must exist in the markup *before* the toast is generated or updated for assistive technologies to reliably announce it. Since `<CToast>` mounts its element only when shown, for critical messages consider keeping a permanently rendered wrapper with the `aria-live` attribute around your toasts — or use the [toaster](../toaster/), which announces through the live regions of the page.

As the content changes, remember to adjust the `delay` prop so users have enough time to read the toast.

When using `autohide={false}`, you must add a close button (for example `<CToastHeader closeButton>` or `<CToastClose>`) to let users dismiss the toast.

While technically it's possible to add focusable or actionable controls, such as additional buttons or links, to your toast, you should avoid doing this with autohiding toasts. Even if you set a long `delay`, keyboard and assistive technology users might find it hard to reach the toast in time to act because toasts don't receive focus when they appear. If you absolutely need to have additional controls, we recommend using a toast with `autohide={false}`.

# React Toast Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Toast component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CToast

```jsx
import { CToast } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Apply a CSS fade transition to the toast. Set it to `false` to show and hide the toast instantly, which adds the `.toast-instant` class. |
| `autohide` | `boolean` | `true` | Auto hide the toast. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `color` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial visibility of an uncontrolled toast — read once on mount. |
| `delay` | `number` | `5000` | Delay hiding the toast (ms). |
| `onClose` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the toast has finished its exit transition. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the toast starts showing. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the toast requests a visibility change — the close button, the autohide timer or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the toast stays as it is. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the visibility. When set, the toast renders what `show` says and the close button or the autohide timer only call `onShowChange` — nothing closes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `theme` | `'primary' \| 'secondary' \| 'success' \| 'danger' \| 'warning' \| 'info' \| 'inverse' \| string` | - | Sets the color context of the component to one of CoreUI’s themed colors. |
| `translucent` | `boolean` | - | Let the background through the toast and blur it. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the visibility of component. |

## CToastHeader

```jsx
import { CToastHeader } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaCloseLabel` | `string` | - | Sets the `aria-label` of the close button. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `closeButton` | `boolean` | - | Automatically add a close button to the header. |

## CToastBody

```jsx
import { CToastBody } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |

## CToastClose

```jsx
import { CToastClose } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aria-label` | `string` | `'Close'` | Sets the `aria-label` attribute of the close button. |
| `as` | `(ElementType & string) \| (ElementType & ComponentClass<any, any>) \| (ElementType & FunctionComponent<any>)` | - | Component used for the root node. Either a string to use a HTML element or a component. |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Toggle the disabled state for the component. |

# React Toast Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Toast component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Toast supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$toast-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-toast-zindex: var(--cui-z-toast),
    --cui-toast-padding-x: .75rem,
    --cui-toast-padding-y: .5rem,
    --cui-toast-spacing: #{$container-padding-x},
    --cui-toast-max-width: #{350px},
    --cui-toast-color: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-toast-bg: #{$toast-background-color},
    --cui-toast-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-toast-border-color: #{$toast-border-color},
    --cui-toast-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-7),
    --cui-toast-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow),
    --cui-toast-header-color: var(--cui-fg-3),
    --cui-toast-header-bg: #{$toast-background-color},
    --cui-toast-header-border-color: #{$toast-border-color},
    --cui-toast-font-size: .875rem,
    --cui-toast-slide: .5rem,
    --cui-toast-transition-property: #{"opacity, translate, display"},
    --cui-toast-transition-duration: #{.3s},
    --cui-toast-transition-timing: #{ease-out},
  ),
  $toast-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-toast-spacing': '2rem',
  '--cui-toast-color': '#f2f3f4',
}

return <CToast style={customVars}>{/* Toast content */}</CToast>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$toast-background-color:            var(--cui-bg-body) !default;
$toast-border-color:                var(--cui-border-color-translucent) !default;
```

# React Bootstrap Toast Component

> Learn how to create lightweight, customizable toast notifications using CoreUI’s React components styled with Bootstrap.

## How to use React Bootstrap Toast component

Use CoreUI's React toast notifications styled like Bootstrap to provide lightweight, dismissible alerts for your application. Toasts can include headers, body content, icons, or be customized entirely.

### Basic usage

Toasts support headers and body content. Use the `autohide` prop to configure automatic dismissal behavior.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CToast, CToastBody, CToastHeader } from '@coreui/react'

export const ToastExample = () => {
  return (
    <CToast animation={false} autohide={false} defaultShow>
      <CToastHeader closeButton>
        <svg
          className="rounded me-3"
          width="20"
          height="20"
          xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"
          preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice"
          focusable="false"
          role="img"
        >
          <rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#007aff"></rect>
        </svg>

        <small>7 min ago</small>
      </CToastHeader>
```

# React Toaster Component

> Create toast notifications from anywhere in a React app: a store keyed by id with add, update, close and promise, a placed container, a visible-toasts limit and screen-reader priority.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

`createToaster()` builds a store of [toasts](../toast/) outside the React tree, so a notification can be added from anywhere — an event handler, a data layer, a route loader — and `<CToaster toaster={toaster}>` renders whatever the store holds, keyed by id. Create the store once, next to the component tree rather than inside it, and keep the instance: `add()` returns the id, `update()` rewrites a toast in place, `close()` hides one or all of them, and `promise()` follows an asynchronous operation through its loading, success and error states.

```jsx
const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end', limit: 3 })

const id = toaster.add({ title: 'Saved', description: 'Your changes are live.', theme: 'success' })
toaster.update(id, { description: 'Done' })
toaster.close(id)
```

`<CToaster>` renders the container the `placement` option pins to the viewport, in a portal on `document.body`; pass `portal={false}` to keep it where it is written and place it yourself. The container is a `region` landmark named by `ariaLabel` (`Notifications` by default), so users of assistive technology can navigate to it.

Inside the container — in a `render` body, or in children of `<CToaster>` — `useToaster()` returns the store, so an action can close or update the toast it belongs to without a reference to the module-level instance.

## Live example

Two toasters, each with its container in a top corner of the viewport: a list on the end side and a [stack](#stacking) on the start side. Every other example on this page renders its container inside the example with `portal={false}`, so its toasts stay put.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end' })
const stacked = createToaster({ limit: 6, placement: 'top-start', stack: true })

export const ToasterLiveExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton
        theme="primary"
        onClick={() =>
          toaster.add({
            title: 'CoreUI for React.js',
            description: 'Hello, world! This is a toast message.',
          })
        }
      >
        Add a toast
      </CButton>
      <CButton
        theme="secondary"
        onClick={() =>
          stacked.add({
            title: 'CoreUI for React.js',
            description: 'Hello, world! This one joins a stack.',
          })
        }
      >
        Add to the stack
      </CButton>
      <CToaster toaster={toaster} />
      <CToaster toaster={stacked} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Title, description and theme

A toast is a plain options object. `title` renders the header with a close button, `description` the body; a toast without a title puts the close button in the body. `theme` adds the `theme-{color}` class, `priority: 'high'` has screen readers announce the toast right away instead of when they are idle, `timeout` overrides the toaster's default (`0` keeps the toast until it is closed) and `dismissible: false` drops the close button.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterContentExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap mb-4">
        <CButton
          theme="primary"
          onClick={() => toaster.add({ title: 'Saved', description: 'Your changes are live.' })}
        >
          Title and description
        </CButton>
        <CButton
          theme="secondary"
          onClick={() => toaster.add({ description: 'Copied to the clipboard' })}
        >
          Description only
        </CButton>
        <CButton
          theme="danger"
          onClick={() =>
            toaster.add({
              title: 'Payment failed',
              description: 'The card was declined.',
              theme: 'danger',
              priority: 'high',
            })
          }
        >
          Themed, high priority
        </CButton>
        <CButton
          theme="secondary"
          variant="outline"
          onClick={() =>
            toaster.add({
              title: 'Read me',
              description: 'This one stays until you close it.',
              dismissible: false,
            })
          }
        >
          Not dismissible
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

Any React node works as a title or description; for a body of your own, pass `render` — it receives the toast object and replaces the default header and body. Only the string parts reach the screen reader, so keep the message itself in `title` and `description`.

## Updating a toast

Passing an `id` that already exists updates that toast instead of adding a second one, and bumps its `updateKey`, so a "Draft saved" toast clicked twice stays a single toast. `update()` does the same for a toast whose id you kept, and accepts a function of the current toast when the change depends on it: `toaster.update(id, previous => ({ description: previous.data.step + 1 }))`. A toast that is already closing is not reused: adding its `id` again removes it at once and adds a new toast, which takes the newest place in the container.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterUpdateExample = () => {
  const saves = useRef(0)

  const saveDraft = () => {
    saves.current += 1
    toaster.add({
      id: 'draft',
      title: 'Draft saved',
      description: `Saved ${saves.current} time${saves.current === 1 ? '' : 's'}`,
    })
  }

  const upload = () => {
    const id = toaster.add({ title: 'Uploading…', description: '0 %' })
    let progress = 0

    const interval = setInterval(() => {
      progress += 25
      toaster.update(id, { description: `${progress} %` })

      if (progress !== 100) {
        return
      }

      clearInterval(interval)
      toaster.update(id, { title: 'Uploaded', theme: 'success' })
    }, 500)
  }

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 flex-wrap mb-4">
        <CButton theme="primary" onClick={saveDraft}>
          Save draft
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary" onClick={upload}>
          Upload with progress
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Promises

`promise()` adds a toast in the `loading` state and updates it when the promise settles: `success` receives the resolved value, `error` the rejection. Each state is a description node, a full options object, or a function returning either.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterPromiseExample = () => {
  const save = () => {
    const request = new Promise<string>((resolve, reject) => {
      setTimeout(
        () => (Math.random() > 0.3 ? resolve('3 files') : reject(new Error('Network error'))),
        2000
      )
    })

    toaster
      .promise(request, {
        loading: 'Saving…',
        success: (files) => `Saved ${files}`,
        error: (error) => ({
          title: 'Not saved',
          description: (error as Error).message,
          priority: 'high',
        }),
      })
      .catch(() => {})
  }

  return (
    <>
      <CButton className="mb-4" theme="primary" onClick={save}>
        Save
      </CButton>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Action

`action` renders a button in the body; its `onClick` receives the click event and the toast object, so an undo can rewrite the same toast.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterActionExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CButton
        className="mb-4"
        theme="primary"
        onClick={() =>
          toaster.add({
            description: 'Message archived',
            action: {
              label: 'Undo',
              onClick: (_event, toast) =>
                toaster.update(toast.id, { description: 'Message restored', action: null }),
            },
          })
        }
      >
        Archive message
      </CButton>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Limit

`limit` caps how many toasts are visible at once. The newest stay on screen; older ones sink away from the edge and fade, remain in the DOM with `inert` and `data-coreui-limited`, and rise back in as the visible ones go away. `limit: 0` shows everything.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ limit: 2, timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterLimitExample = () => {
  const count = useRef(0)

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
        <CButton
          theme="primary"
          onClick={() => {
            count.current += 1
            toaster.add({ title: `Toast ${count.current}`, description: 'Only two stay visible.' })
          }}
        >
          Add a toast
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" onClick={() => toaster.close()}>
          Close all
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Stacking

With `stack: true` the toasts sit on top of each other: the newest in front at full size, the ones behind it scaled down by `--cui-toast-stack-scale` per step and receding towards a vanishing depth. The first toast behind peeks out by `--cui-toast-stack-peek` and every further one by that strip times the scale ratio, so the corners of the stack line up like a deck of cards seen in perspective. Only the front toast's timer runs; the ones behind wait their turn and start counting when they reach the front, so the stack empties from the front. Hovering or focusing the container spreads the stack into a list; leaving it folds the stack back. The stack takes the place of the flow layout; `limit` decides how many toasts it holds. Folded, the deck shows the front toast and two behind it (`--cui-toast-stack-visible`); spreading it reveals every toast within the limit.

```html
import React, { useRef } from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ limit: 0, stack: true, timeout: 0 })

export const ToasterStackExample = () => {
  const count = useRef(0)

  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
        <CButton
          theme="primary"
          onClick={() => {
            count.current += 1
            toaster.add({
              title: `Toast ${count.current}`,
              description:
                count.current % 2 ? 'Hover or focus the stack to spread it out.' : 'A shorter one.',
            })
          }}
        >
          Add a toast
        </CButton>
        <CButton theme="secondary" variant="outline" onClick={() => toaster.close()}>
          Close all
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <CToaster className="position-relative" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

The component keeps the geometry in tokens the CSS reads: `--cui-toast-stack-index`, `--cui-toast-stack-before` (the height of the toasts in front) and `--cui-toast-height` on each toast, `--cui-toast-stack-count`, `--cui-toast-stack-front-height` and `--cui-toast-stack-heights` on the container. Style the stack by these — the `data-coreui-stack-index` and `data-coreui-stack-hidden` attributes mark a toast's place in it.

A stack works in every placement: it grows away from the edge it is pinned to, so at the bottom the newest toast is the lowest one and the stack peeks upward.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const placements = [
  'top-start',
  'top-center',
  'top-end',
  'middle-start',
  'middle-center',
  'middle-end',
  'bottom-start',
  'bottom-center',
  'bottom-end',
] as const

const toasters = placements.map((placement) => createToaster({ limit: 0, placement, stack: true }))

export const ToasterPlacementStackExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div
        className="d-grid gap-3"
        style={{ gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(3, 1fr)', maxWidth: '30rem' }}
      >
        {placements.map((placement, index) => (
          <CButton
            key={placement}
            theme="secondary"
            variant="outline"
            onClick={() =>
              toasters[index].add({
                title: `${placement} · ${toasters[index].getToasts().length + 1}`,
                description: 'Hover the stack to spread it.',
              })
            }
          >
            {placement}
          </CButton>
        ))}
      </div>
      {toasters.map((toaster, index) => (
        <CToaster key={placements[index]} toaster={toaster} />
      ))}
    </>
  )
}
```

## Motion

A toast slides in from beyond the container's edge while it fades in — from the side in the `start` and `end` placements, from above in `top-center` and from below in `bottom-center` — and leaves the way it came, so the entry and the exit read as one gesture. `middle-center` sits in the middle of the screen with no edge to come from, so its toasts only fade. While a toast leaves, the ones behind it glide into the freed space; when a new one arrives, they make room the same way. `enter` picks another edge for the entry and `leave` for the exit — a `top-end` toaster can drop its toasts in from above and still send them out sideways. `start` and `end` are logical: they follow the direction the container sits in, so under `dir="rtl"` they change sides along with the placement. All of it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.

```jsx
const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'top-end', enter: 'top', leave: 'end' })
```

### Instant

A toast with `instant: true` skips all of it — no slide, no fade, no glide of its neighbours, no stack transition — and so does every toast when the user prefers reduced motion: the stylesheet emits no transitions under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` and the component skips its position animations, so toasts appear, move and vanish in place.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const toaster = createToaster({ timeout: 3000 })

export const ToasterInstantExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div className="hstack gap-3 mb-4">
        <CButton
          theme="primary"
          onClick={() =>
            toaster.add({
              title: 'Instant',
              description: 'No slide, no fade, no glide.',
              instant: true,
            })
          }
        >
          Add an instant toast
        </CButton>
        <CButton
          theme="secondary"
          onClick={() =>
            toaster.add({ title: 'Animated', description: 'Slides in and glides the others.' })
          }
        >
          Add an animated toast
        </CButton>
      </div>
      <CToaster className="position-static" portal={false} toaster={toaster} />
    </>
  )
}
```

## Placement

`placement` pins the container to the viewport with one of the nine [`.toast-container-{block}-{inline}`](../toast/#placement) classes: `top`, `middle` or `bottom` × `start`, `center` or `end`. In the `top` placements a new toast is rendered first, in the others last, so the newest always sits closest to the edge. The `placement` prop of `<CToaster>` wins over the store's option when you need the same store in another spot.

Each button below adds a toast through a toaster placed at that spot, so you can see where a toast enters from: from the side in the `start` and `end` columns, from above in `top-center` and from below in `bottom-center`, while `middle-center` fades in place.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react'

const placements = [
  'top-start',
  'top-center',
  'top-end',
  'middle-start',
  'middle-center',
  'middle-end',
  'bottom-start',
  'bottom-center',
  'bottom-end',
] as const

const toasters = placements.map((placement) => createToaster({ placement }))

export const ToasterPlacementExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <div
        className="d-grid gap-3"
        style={{ gridTemplateColumns: 'repeat(3, 1fr)', maxWidth: '30rem' }}
      >
        {placements.map((placement, index) => (
          <CButton
            key={placement}
            theme="secondary"
            variant="outline"
            onClick={() =>
              toasters[index].add({
                title: placement,
                description: 'Slides in from the nearest edge.',
              })
            }
          >
            {placement}
          </CButton>
        ))}
      </div>
      {toasters.map((toaster, index) => (
        <CToaster key={placements[index]} toaster={toaster} />
      ))}
    </>
  )
}
```

## Accessibility

The container is a `region` landmark named by `ariaLabel` (`Notifications` by default), so screen-reader users can jump to it through landmark navigation. Every toast is read through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) when it is added or updated: the string parts of its `title` and `description` go to the polite live region of the page, or to the assertive one with `priority: 'high'`, as a message of their own, so toasts raised together are each announced instead of the last one overwriting the others. The store sends the message once and it belongs to the page, not to `<CToaster>`, so a container mounted again on the same store, for example after a route change, does not add the messages of older toasts again, a toast added together with a route change is announced once, and while a modal dialog is open the message goes to a region inside the dialog. Updating or removing a toast takes its message out of the region. Only that text is announced, never the close button or the action, and the toast element itself carries no live role. A toast added while a modal dialog plays its closing transition, or from the modal's `onClose`, is announced on the page half a second after the dialog has closed, once the page is back for the screen reader; [Announcing messages](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) has the measurements. The close button `<CToaster>` renders is named by `ariaCloseLabel` (`Close` by default); set it once for the whole toaster in a translated interface, and name the close button of a `render` body yourself. `normal`, the default, waits until the user is idle, unless the toast is added together with a `high` one, which takes both to the assertive region; keep `high` for the few messages that should interrupt, such as a failed save (WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages).

Auto-hiding is a time limit on reading, which WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable asks you to let the user turn off, adjust or extend. Timers stop while the pointer or focus is inside the container (`pauseOnHover`), so a spread stack or a toast being read does not disappear mid-way, and the default `timeout` is the toaster's to set for the whole app. A toast with an action, or one the user must act on, should not hide on its own: give it `timeout: 0`, so keyboard and screen-reader users can reach the button. Toasts never take focus.

## Usage

Create a toaster once — at module scope, not inside a component — and render it wherever the app is mounted.

```jsx
import { CToaster, createToaster } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const toaster = createToaster({ placement: 'bottom-end', limit: 3 })

export const App = () => (
  <>
    <Routes />
    <CToaster toaster={toaster} />
  </>
)
```

### Options

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaCloseLabel` | string | `'Close'` | Accessible name of the close button `<CToaster>` renders in every toast; a `render` body names its own. |
| `ariaLabel` | string | `'Notifications'` | Accessible name of the container's `region` landmark. |
| `enter` | string | `'auto'` | Edge a toast slides in from: `'start'`, `'end'`, `'top'` or `'bottom'`. `'start'` and `'end'` are logical and follow the direction the container sits in. `'auto'` follows the placement — the side in the `start` and `end` columns, above in `top-center`, below in `bottom-center`, and no slide at all in `middle-center`. |
| `leave` | string | `'auto'` | Edge a toast slides out to, taking the same values as `enter`. `'auto'` is the edge it came in from. |
| `limit` | number | `3` | How many toasts stay visible; the oldest beyond it are hidden and `inert` until a slot frees. `0` disables the limit. |
| `pauseOnHover` | boolean | `true` | Pause every toast's timer while the pointer or focus is inside the container, and resume when it leaves. Each toast still pauses on its own hover and focus. |
| `placement` | string | `'top-end'` | Corner or edge of the viewport for the container: `top`, `middle` or `bottom` × `start`, `center` or `end`. Toasts in the `top` placements are rendered first, in the others last, so the newest always sits closest to the edge. |
| `stack` | boolean | `false` | Stack the toasts on top of each other, newest in front, and spread them out on hover or focus. |
| `timeout` | number | `5000` | Default time (ms) before a toast hides. `0` keeps toasts until they are closed. |

An unknown `placement`, `enter` or `leave` throws a `TypeError` when the store is created.

### Toast options

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `action` | object, null | — | `{ label, onClick(event, toast) }` renders a button in the body. |
| `className` | string | — | Extra classes on the `.toast`. |
| `data` | object | — | Anything you want to read back from the toast object later, e.g. in `update(id, previous => …)`. |
| `description` | ReactNode | — | Body of the toast. |
| `dismissible` | boolean | `true` | Render the close button. |
| `id` | string | generated | Stable id; adding with an existing id updates that toast in place, unless it is already closing, in which case a new toast replaces it. |
| `instant` | boolean | `false` | Skip the fade (`.toast-instant`). |
| `onClose` | function | — | Called when the toast starts closing, with the toast object. |
| `onRemove` | function | — | Called after the toast left the store, with the toast object. |
| `priority` | string | `'normal'` | Which live region announces the toast, as in [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages): `'normal'` the polite one, `'high'` the assertive one, which also takes the normal toasts added together with it. |
| `render` | function | — | `(toast) => ReactNode` renders the body of the toast in place of `title` and `description`. |
| `theme` | string | — | Adds `theme-{color}`. |
| `timeout` | number | toaster's `timeout` | Time (ms) before this toast hides; `0` keeps it. |
| `title` | ReactNode | — | Header of the toast, with the close button next to it. |
| `translucent` | boolean | `false` | Adds `.toast-translucent`. |

### Methods

| Method | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `add(options)` | Adds a toast and returns its id. With an `id` that already exists it behaves like `update`, unless that toast is already closing. |
| `update(id, options)` | Rewrites the toast in place and increments its `updateKey`. `options` may be a function receiving the current toast object and returning the changes. |
| `close(id?)` | Starts closing the toast; it leaves the store once its exit transition ends. Without an id, closes every toast. |
| `remove(id)` | Drops the toast from the store without an exit transition. `<CToaster>` calls it once the transition has ended. |
| `promise(promise, { loading, success, error })` | Adds a toast in the `loading` state and updates it when the promise settles: `success` gets the resolved value, `error` the rejection. Each state is a description node or a full options object, or a function returning either. Returns the promise. |
| `pause()` / `resume()` | Stop and restart every toast's timer; `pauseOnHover` calls these for the container. |
| `getToasts()` | The toast objects in insertion order, each with `id`, `updateKey`, `limited`, `open`, `order` and the options it was created with. |
| `subscribe(listener)`, `getSnapshot()` | The store contract `<CToaster>` reads through `useSyncExternalStore`; `getSnapshot()` lists the toasts in rendering order. `getPaused()` is read the same way. |
| `useToaster()` | The store of the surrounding `<CToaster>`, for content rendered inside it. |

### Events

The store reports per toast instead of on the container: `onClose` fires when a toast starts closing and `onRemove` once it has left the store. Both receive the toast object, so a handler can tell which toast it was without keeping the id.

## Customizing

### CSS variables

The toaster renders regular toasts, so their tokens apply — see the [toast CSS variables](../toast/styling/#css-variables). Four are its own: `--cui-toast-container-inset` on the container sets the distance from the viewport edge, `--cui-toast-translate` on the container is where a toast enters from and leaves to, overridden separately by `--cui-toast-enter-translate` and `--cui-toast-leave-translate` (the `enter` and `leave` options write those; set them yourself for any other offset), `--cui-toast-inline-sign` on the container is the `1` or `-1` those inline offsets are multiplied by, which is how `start` and `end` follow the direction, and `--cui-toast-limited-translate` on a toast sets where a toast over the limit sinks to.

```scss
--cui-toast-zindex: var(--cui-z-toast);
--cui-toast-container-inset: #{var(--cui-spacer-5)};
--cui-toast-inline-sign: 1;
--cui-toast-max-width: #{350px};
--cui-toast-spacing: #{$container-padding-x};
--cui-toast-transition-duration: #{.3s};
--cui-toast-transition-timing: #{ease-out};
```

The stack's peek, scale step and folded count are tokens on `.toast-container-stack`:

```scss
.toast-container-stack {
  --cui-toast-stack-peek: .75rem;
  --cui-toast-stack-scale: .1;
  // Every toast behind is scaled by the same ratio again and pushed towards a vanishing depth,
  // so the corners of the stack line up and each strip is the previous one times the ratio
  --cui-toast-stack-visible: 3;
  --cui-toast-stack-ratio: calc(1 - var(--cui-toast-stack-scale));
  --cui-toast-stack-depth: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height) + var(--cui-toast-stack-peek) / var(--cui-toast-stack-scale));
  --cui-toast-stack-last: calc(min(var(--cui-toast-stack-count), var(--cui-toast-stack-visible)) - 1);

  width: var(--cui-toast-max-width);
  max-width: 100%;
  height: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-last))) + var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height) * pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-last)));
  pointer-events: auto;
  @include transition-props(height, var(--cui-toast-transition-duration), var(--cui-toast-transition-timing));

  > .toast {
    position: absolute;
    inset-block-start: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index))));
    inset-inline: 0;
    z-index: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-count) - var(--cui-toast-stack-index));
    height: var(--cui-toast-stack-front-height);
    margin-block-end: 0;
    overflow: hidden;
    transform-origin: top center;
    scale: pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index));

    &:not(.toast-instant) {
      @include transition-props(
        #{"opacity, translate, display, inset-block-start, height, scale"},
        var(--cui-toast-transition-duration),
        var(--cui-toast-transition-timing),
        allow-discrete
      );

      > * {
        @include transition-props(opacity, var(--cui-toast-transition-duration), var(--cui-toast-transition-timing));
      }
    }
  }

  > .toast:not([data-coreui-stack-index="0"]) {
    --cui-toast-leave-translate: 0 0;
    --cui-toast-limited-translate: 0 0;

    > * {
      opacity: 0;
    }
  }

  > .toast[data-coreui-stack-hidden] {
    pointer-events: none;
    opacity: 0;
  }

  &:is(:hover, :focus-within) {
    height: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-heights) + (var(--cui-toast-stack-count) - 1) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));

    > .toast {
      inset-block-start: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-before) + var(--cui-toast-stack-index) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));
      height: var(--cui-toast-height);
      scale: 1;

      > * {
        opacity: 1;
      }
    }

    > .toast[data-coreui-stack-hidden]:not([data-coreui-limited]) {
      pointer-events: auto;
      opacity: 1;
    }
  }
}

.toast-container-bottom-start.toast-container-stack,
.toast-container-bottom-center.toast-container-stack,
.toast-container-bottom-end.toast-container-stack {
  > .toast {
    inset-block-start: auto;
    inset-block-end: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-depth) * (1 - pow(var(--cui-toast-stack-ratio), var(--cui-toast-stack-index))));
    transform-origin: bottom center;

    &:not(.toast-instant) {
      @include transition-props(
        #{"opacity, translate, display, inset-block-end, height, scale"},
        var(--cui-toast-transition-duration),
        var(--cui-toast-transition-timing),
        allow-discrete
      );
    }
  }

  &:is(:hover, :focus-within) > .toast {
    inset-block-end: calc(var(--cui-toast-stack-before) + var(--cui-toast-stack-index) * var(--cui-toast-spacing));
  }
}
```

### Sass variables

```scss
$toast-background-color:            var(--cui-bg-body) !default;
$toast-border-color:                var(--cui-border-color-translucent) !default;
```

# React Toaster Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Toaster component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CToaster

```jsx
import { CToaster } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `className` | `string` | - | A string of all className you want applied to the base component. |
| `placement` | `'top-start' \| 'top-center' \| 'top-end' \| 'middle-start' \| 'middle-center' \| 'middle-end' \| 'bottom-start' \| 'bottom-center' \| 'bottom-end' \| string` | - | Describes the placement of your component. Defaults to the placement of `toaster`. |
| `portal` | `boolean` | - | Render the container in a React Portal on `document.body`. Defaults to `true` whenever a placement pins the container to the viewport — set it to `false` to keep the container where it is written, for a toaster scoped to a part of the page. |
| `toaster` | `Toaster` | - | The store created with `createToaster()` whose toasts the component renders. Without it the component is a plain container for the `CToast` children. |

# React Tooltip Component

> Documentation and examples for adding React Tooltips.

## Overview

Things to keep in mind when using the tooltip component:

- Tooltips with empty `content` render an empty box, so always provide content.
- Tooltips are appended to `document.body` by default. Use the `container` prop to append them to a different element when a parent's styles interfere with the tooltip (like in our input groups, button groups, etc.).
- Tooltips cannot be triggered on hidden elements.
- Tooltips for disabled elements need to be activated on a wrapper element.
- When triggered by hyperlinks that span multiple lines, tooltips will be centered. Use `.text-nowrap` on your `<a>` elements to avoid this behavior.

Got all that? Great, let's see how they work with some examples.

## Examples

### Tooltips on links

Hover over the links below to see tooltips:

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CLink, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipOnLinksExample = () => {
  return (
    <p className="fg-2">
      Tight pants next level keffiyeh
      <CTooltip content="Tooltip text">
        <CLink> you probably </CLink>
      </CTooltip>
      haven&#39;t heard of them. Photo booth beard raw denim letterpress vegan messenger bag
      stumptown. Farm-to-table seitan, mcsweeney&#39;s fixie sustainable quinoa 8-bit american
      apparel
      <CTooltip content="Tooltip text">
        <CLink> have a </CLink>
      </CTooltip>
      terry richardson vinyl chambray. Beard stumptown, cardigans banh mi lomo thundercats. Tofu
      biodiesel williamsburg marfa, four loko mcsweeney&#39;s cleanse vegan chambray. A really
      ironic artisan
      <CTooltip content="Tooltip text">
        <CLink> whatever keytar </CLink>
      </CTooltip>
      scenester farm-to-table banksy Austin
      <CTooltip content="Tooltip text">
        <CLink> twitter handle </CLink>
      </CTooltip>
      freegan cred raw denim single-origin coffee viral.
    </p>
  )
}
```

### Custom tooltips

You can customize the appearance of tooltips using [CSS variables](./styling/#css-variables). We set a custom `style` to scope our custom appearance and use it to override some of the local CSS variables.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipCustomExample = () => {
  const customTooltipStyle = {
    '--cui-tooltip-bg': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
  } as React.CSSProperties

  return (
    <CTooltip
      content="This top tooltip is themed via CSS variables."
      placement="top"
      style={customTooltipStyle}
    >
      <CButton theme="secondary">Custom tooltip</CButton>
    </CTooltip>
  )
}
```

### Theme variants

A tooltip reads the `.theme-{color}` slots, so a [theme class](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/components/#theme-variants) on the tip colors its surface and picks the contrasting text. Pass it through `className`; without one the tip keeps its default look, the page's foreground color.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipThemeVariantsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CTooltip className="theme-primary" content="Primary tooltip">
        <CButton variant="outline">Primary</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip className="theme-secondary" content="Secondary tooltip">
        <CButton variant="outline">Secondary</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip className="theme-success" content="Success tooltip">
        <CButton variant="outline">Success</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip className="theme-danger" content="Danger tooltip">
        <CButton variant="outline">Danger</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Directions

Hover over the buttons below to see the four directions: `top`, `end`, `bottom` and `start`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipDirectionsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="top">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip on top</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus." placement="end">
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip at the end</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="bottom"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip on bottom</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="start"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip at the start</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
    </>
  )
}
```

`start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL.

#### Deprecated physical names

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

`left` and `right` still work and behave exactly like `start` and `end` — they have always mirrored in RTL, so `right` never meant "the right side" there either. The logical names say that plainly; the physical ones are removed in v7.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipDeprecatedDirectionsExample = () => {
  return (
    <>
      <CTooltip
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="right"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip on right</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
      <CTooltip
        content="Vivamus sagittis lacus vel augue laoreet rutrum faucibus."
        placement="left"
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip on left</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Responsive placement

Breakpoint prefixes make a placement responsive: `top md:end` reads as top below `md` and end from `md` up. The breakpoints are the Sass ones — `sm` 576px, `md` 768px, `lg` 1024px, `xl` 1280px, `2xl` 1536px. A bare placement with no prefix applies below the smallest one listed.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipResponsivePlacementExample = () => {
  return (
    <CTooltip content="Top below md, right from md up." placement="top md:right">
      <CButton theme="secondary">Responsive placement</CButton>
    </CTooltip>
  )
}
```

### Tooltips with HTML content

The `content` prop accepts any valid React node, so you can insert styled elements like `<em>`, `<strong>`, or `<u>` directly inside the tooltip. This is useful when you want to emphasize certain words, add inline formatting, or even insert icons.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipHtmlExample = () => {
  return (
    <CTooltip
      content={
        <>
          <em>Tooltip</em> <u>with</u> <b>HTML</b>
        </>
      }
    >
      <CButton theme="secondary">Tooltip with HTML</CButton>
    </CTooltip>
  )
}
```

### Tooltips on SVG elements

SVG elements do not support the `title` attribute the way HTML elements do, but `<CTooltip>` doesn't need it — wrap the SVG (or a link containing it) in the component like any other trigger. Since tooltips are appended to `document.body` by default, positioning stays correct even when SVGs are nested inside complex layouts.

Using tooltips with SVGs is a great way to enhance accessibility and interactivity for icon-based UIs or data visualizations without modifying the structure of your SVGs.

## Usage

A shown tooltip can be dismissed by pressing the <kbd>Escape</kbd> key, and a hover- or focus-triggered tooltip stays open while the pointer or focus is over the trigger or the tip itself — so users can reach interactive content inside it. It hides when the pointer leaves both. A focus-triggered tooltip also stays open after a press inside it, for example to select its text, and hides on the next click outside or when focus moves elsewhere. Together these satisfy the [WCAG 1.4.13 "Content on Hover or Focus"](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/content-on-hover-or-focus.html) success criterion (dismissable, hoverable, persistent).

### Disabled elements

Elements with the disabled attribute aren’t interactive, meaning users cannot focus, hover, or click them to trigger a tooltip (or popover). As a workaround, you’ll want to trigger the tooltip from a wrapper `<div>` or `<span>`, ideally made keyboard-focusable using `tabindex="0"`.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CButton, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipDisabledElementsExample = () => {
  return (
    <CTooltip content="Disabled tooltip" trigger={['hover', 'focus']}>
      <span className="d-inline-block" tabIndex={0}>
        <CButton theme="primary" disabled>
          Disabled button
        </CButton>
      </span>
    </CTooltip>
  )
}
```

## Controlled and uncontrolled

_Added in 6.0.0._

The tooltip works either way, and the prop you reach for is what picks the mode.

| | prop | who owns the visibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled | `defaultShow` | the tooltip, from that starting point |
| Controlled | `show` | your component |

`onShowChange` fires in **both** modes whenever the tooltip requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture (hover, focus, click), the Escape key or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. The deprecated `visible` prop keeps its old behavior and is ignored when `defaultShow` or `show` is set.

`onShowChange` is a request, not a report. To follow what is on screen, `onShow` and `onHide` fire when the tooltip starts showing or hiding (after `delay`, and only when the visibility actually changes), and `onShown` and `onHidden` once the transition has finished.

### Uncontrolled

Every example above is uncontrolled — the trigger gestures manage the tooltip. `defaultShow` seeds it visible on mount, and the gestures take over from there.

```jsx
<CTooltip content="Shown on load" defaultShow>
```

### Controlled

Pass `show` and the tooltip renders what you pass — trigger gestures only call `onShowChange` (the `delay` still applies as presentation). That is what a **pinned** tooltip needs: while the checkbox holds `show` true, hovering away only requests a change the page does not grant.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CCheckbox, CFormField, CTooltip } from '@coreui/react'

export const TooltipControlledExample = () => {
  const [pinned, setPinned] = useState(true)
  const [hovered, setHovered] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CFormField className="mb-4">
        <CCheckbox
          checked={pinned}
          id="tooltipPinned"
          label="Pin the tooltip"
          onChange={(event) => setPinned(event.target.checked)}
        />
      </CFormField>
      <CTooltip
        content="Pinned tooltips stay put."
        show={pinned || hovered}
        onShowChange={setHovered}
      >
        <CButton theme="secondary">Hover me</CButton>
      </CTooltip>
    </>
  )
}
```

Use it when the visibility belongs to something else — an onboarding step, a validation hint that must stay put — and feed `onShowChange` back for the parts you still want the gestures to drive, as the example does while unpinned.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CTooltip /&gt;](./api/#ctooltip)

# React Tooltip Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Tooltip component and discover how to effectively utilize its props for customization.

## CTooltip

```jsx
import { CTooltip } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `animation` | `boolean` | `true` | Enables or disables the CSS fade transition for the React Tooltip. |
| `className` | `string` | - | Adds a custom class name to the React Tooltip container. Useful for overriding default styles or applying additional design choices. |
| `container` | `Element \| DocumentFragment \| (() => Element \| DocumentFragment \| null) \| null` | `document.body` | Appends the React Tooltip to a specific element instead of the default `document.body`. You may pass: - A DOM element (`HTMLElement` or `DocumentFragment`) - A function that returns a single element - `null` |
| `content` | `ReactNode` | - | Content to be displayed within the React Tooltip. Can be a string or any valid React node. |
| `defaultShow` | `boolean` | - | The initial visibility of an uncontrolled React Tooltip — read once on mount. |
| `delay` | `number \| { show: number; hide: number; }` | `0` | The delay (in milliseconds) before showing or hiding the React Tooltip. - If provided as a number, the delay is applied to both "show" and "hide". - If provided as an object, it should have distinct "show" and "hide" values. |
| `fallbackPlacements` | `'top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left' \| ('top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left')[]` | `['top', 'right', 'bottom', 'left']` | Array of fallback placements for the React Tooltip to use when the preferred placement cannot be achieved. These placements are tried in order. |
| `floatingConfig` | `Partial<ComputePositionConfig> \| ((defaultFloatingConfig: Partial<ComputePositionConfig>) => Partial<ComputePositionConfig>)` | - | Customize the Floating UI configuration used to position the React Tooltip. Pass either an object or a function returning a modified config. [Learn more](https://floating-ui.com/docs/computePosition#options) |
| `offset` | `[number, number]` | `[0, 6]` | Adjusts the offset of the React Tooltip relative to its target. Expects a tuple `[x-axis, y-axis]`. |
| `onHidden` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Tooltip has finished its exit transition. |
| `onHide` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Tooltip starts hiding. |
| `onShow` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Tooltip starts showing. |
| `onShowChange` | `((show: boolean) => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Tooltip requests a visibility change — a trigger gesture (hover, focus, click), the Escape key or, in uncontrolled mode, any internal toggle. In controlled mode update `show` yourself, or the tooltip stays as it is. |
| `onShown` | `(() => void)` | - | Callback fired when the React Tooltip has finished its entry transition. |
| `placement` | `"auto" \| "top" \| "bottom" \| "right" \| "left" \| "end" \| "start" \| (string & {})` | `top` | Initial placement of the React Tooltip. Note that Floating UI middleware may alter this placement automatically if there's insufficient space in the chosen position. `start` and `end` are logical: they follow the reading direction, so `end` is the right side in LTR and the left side in RTL. `left` and `right` are their deprecated spellings and resolve identically. Breakpoint prefixes make it responsive: `top md:end` reads as top below `md` and end from `md` up. The breakpoints are the Sass ones — `sm`, `md`, `lg`, `xl`, `2xl`. |
| `show` | `boolean` | - | Control the visibility. When set, the React Tooltip renders what `show` says (delays still apply as presentation) and trigger gestures only call `onShowChange` — nothing changes until the parent flips the prop. |
| `trigger` | `'hover' \| 'focus' \| 'click' \| ('hover' \| 'focus' \| 'click')[]` | `['hover', 'focus']` | Determines the events that toggle the visibility of the React Tooltip. Can be a single trigger or an array of triggers. |
| `visible` | `boolean` | - | Controls the visibility of the React Tooltip. - `true` to show the tooltip. - `false` to hide the tooltip. |


---

# React Tooltip Component Styling

> Learn how to customize the React Tooltip component with CSS classes, variables, and Sass for flexible styling and seamless integration into your design.

## CSS variables

React Tooltip supports CSS variables for easy customization. These variables are set via Sass but allow direct overrides in your stylesheets or inline styles.

```scss
$tooltip-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-tooltip-zindex: var(--cui-z-tooltip),
    --cui-tooltip-max-width: 200px,
    --cui-tooltip-padding-x: calc(var(--cui-spacer) * .75),
    --cui-tooltip-padding-y: calc(var(--cui-spacer) * .375),
    --cui-tooltip-font-size: var(--cui-font-size-sm),
    --cui-tooltip-color: #{$tooltip-color},
    --cui-tooltip-bg: var(--cui-fg-body),
    --cui-tooltip-border-radius: var(--cui-radius-5),
    --cui-tooltip-opacity: .95,
    --cui-tooltip-arrow-width: .8rem,
    --cui-tooltip-arrow-height: .4rem,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-property: opacity,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-duration: .15s,
    --cui-tooltip-transition-timing: linear,
  ),
  $tooltip-tokens
);
```

### How to use CSS variables

```jsx
const customVars = {
  '--cui-tooltip-color': '#888',
  '--cui-tooltip-bg': '#f2f4f6',
}

return <CTooltip style={customVars}>{/* Tooltip content */}</CTooltip>
```

## Sass variables

_Deprecated in 6.0.0._

Sass variables set these defaults at build time and are removed in v7. The CSS variables above reach the same values without recompiling, and can be set on a single element.

```scss
$tooltip-color:                     var(--cui-bg-body) !default;
```

# React Transfer Component

> Two lists side by side and four buttons that move values between them — the selection or everything at once: a select-all header with a counter, an optional per-list search, a one-way mode and an announcement of every move.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## Overview

_Added in 6.0.0._

A transfer moves values between two lists — what is available on the left, what has been chosen on the right. It is two [list boxes](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/) and a column of buttons: each list runs in `multiple` selection mode with the checkbox indicator, each button is enabled while it has something to move, and a move takes the values from one list to the other.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { label: 'List item 2', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
  { label: 'List item 4', value: '4' },
  { label: 'List item 5', value: '5' },
]

export const TransferExample = () => {
  return <CTransfer defaultValue={['5']} items={items} />
}
```

Everything inside a list is the list box's: the options and their values, the selection, the arrow keys, the typeahead and the select-all button. `CTransfer` owns what happens between the lists, so nothing here is a second implementation of the same behavior — read the [List box](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/) page for the parts a list is made of.

`items` is what both lists are made of, each entry a `value` plus a `label` and, if you want them, a `description` and `disabled`. The target list holds the values of `value` / `defaultValue`, in the order they were chosen; the source list holds the rest, in the order `items` gives them.

"All" is the same scope the select-all button works on — the visible, enabled options — so with a search running, the all button moves what the search left behind and nothing more.

`CTransfer` is a renderer over `useTransfer()`, which owns the two lists, the two selections, the two queries and the moves. Call the hook directly to build a surface of your own.

The transfer caps how tall a list gets — `--cui-transfer-list-max-height` puts a `max-height` and `overflow-y: auto` on the options, so a long list scrolls inside its own box instead of stretching the row.

## Controlled value

`value` is the target list, so the transfer is controlled by the values it has chosen. `onChange` reports the next value and what the move was — `direction` is the list the options landed in, `moved` the values that crossed. Leave `value` out and pass `defaultValue` for the uncontrolled mode.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Ada', value: 'ada' },
  { label: 'Grace', value: 'grace' },
  { label: 'Linus', value: 'linus' },
]

export const TransferControlledExample = () => {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<string[]>(['grace'])

  return (
    <>
      <CTransfer items={items} onChange={(next) => setValue(next)} value={value} />
      <div className="mt-4">On call: {value.join(', ') || 'nobody'}</div>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Search

`search` is the [list box's own search](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/#search), put above each of the two lists: it hides the options that do not match, which takes them out of the navigation, out of the counter and out of the select-all scope, while the selection survives.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Apple', value: 'apple' },
  { label: 'Apricot', value: 'apricot' },
  { label: 'Banana', value: 'banana' },
  { label: 'Blueberry', value: 'blueberry' },
  { label: 'Cherry', value: 'cherry' },
  { label: 'Cranberry', value: 'cranberry' },
]

export const TransferSearchExample = () => {
  return <CTransfer items={items} search />
}
```

The search matches an option's label, or its `textValue` when it carries one — the description is left out of the match. `searchPlaceholder` is the placeholder of both fields and the first half of each field's accessible name, and `onSearch` reports every query with the list it belongs to, so the two fields can be watched from one callback.

### External search

`search="external"` filters nothing: the lists show whatever `items` holds, and the query is only reported through `onSearch` — the fetching and the filtering are yours, as on the [list box](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/#external-search). `value` outlives a change of `items`: a value still in the new set stays in the target in its own order, and a value that's gone leaves both lists. Keep the chosen items in the set you hand back and the target holds still while the source is refetched.

`loading` covers the wait. Pass `true` to mark both lists, or `{ source: true }` / `{ target: true }` to mark the one that is waiting: its options are marked `aria-busy` and a row with `loadingLabel` shows below them, while they stay usable.

```html
import React, { useEffect, useRef, useState } from 'react'
import { CTransfer, useDebouncedCallback } from '@coreui/react-pro'
import type { TransferDirection, TransferItem } from '@coreui/react-pro'

type UserRecord = {
  first_name: string
  id: number
  last_name: string
}

export const TransferExternalSearchExample = () => {
  const [items, setItems] = useState<TransferItem[]>([])
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false)
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('')
  const [value, setValue] = useState<string[]>([])
  const chosen = useRef<string[]>([])

  const handleSearch = useDebouncedCallback((side: TransferDirection, next: string) => {
    if (side === 'source') {
      setQuery(next)
    }
  }, 300)

  useEffect(() => {
    const getUsers = async () => {
      setLoading(true)
      try {
        const response = await fetch(
          `https://apitest.coreui.io/demos/users?first_name=${query}&limit=20`
        )
        const result = await response.json()
        const records: TransferItem[] = result.records.map((record: UserRecord) => ({
          label: `${record.first_name} ${record.last_name}`,
          value: String(record.id),
        }))

        setItems((previous) => [
          ...previous.filter((item) => chosen.current.includes(item.value)),
          ...records.filter((item) => !chosen.current.includes(item.value)),
        ])
      } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching users:', error)
        setItems((previous) => previous.filter((item) => chosen.current.includes(item.value)))
      } finally {
        setLoading(false)
      }
    }

    getUsers()
  }, [query])

  return (
    <CTransfer
      items={items}
      loading={{ source: loading }}
      onChange={(next) => {
        chosen.current = next
        setValue(next)
      }}
      onSearch={handleSearch}
      search="external"
      searchPlaceholder="Search users..."
      sourceTitle="Users"
      targetTitle="Invited"
      value={value}
    />
  )
}
```

## One way

`oneWay` takes the return trip away: both buttons that move back are gone, `moveToSource()` and `moveAllToSource()` refuse, and a value that has been chosen stays chosen.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { label: 'List item 2', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
]

export const TransferOneWayExample = () => {
  return <CTransfer items={items} oneWay />
}
```

## Titles

`sourceTitle` and `targetTitle` name the two lists. The title is the label of the list's select-all button, its accessible name, and the destination named in the move announcement. `selectedLabel` builds each list's counter text — a function `(count, total) => string`, or a string in which `{count}` and `{total}` are replaced.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'Ada', value: 'ada' },
  { label: 'Grace', value: 'grace' },
  { label: 'Linus', value: 'linus' },
]

export const TransferTitlesExample = () => {
  return (
    <CTransfer
      items={items}
      selectedLabel={(count, total) => `${count}/${total} picked`}
      sourceTitle="Team"
      targetTitle="On call"
    />
  )
}
```

## Descriptions

An option is the list box's, so `description` adds a second line here too — and the search matches on the label, not on the description.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { description: 'See the contents of a file', label: 'Read', value: 'read' },
  { description: 'Change the contents of a file', label: 'Write', value: 'write' },
  { description: 'Give someone else access', label: 'Share', value: 'share' },
]

export const TransferDescriptionsExample = () => {
  return <CTransfer items={items} />
}
```

Pass `renderItem` to render an option yourself. It takes the option and its index, and the option it hands you carries the `hidden` the search left behind — pass it on, or the filter stops showing.

## Disabled items

`disabled` on an entry of `items` takes the option out of the keyboard order and out of every selection method, so it never moves: not through a move button, and not through `moveToTarget()` or `moveToSource()` with the value in hand. `disabled` on the transfer does the same for all of it: both lists go quiet and every button is disabled.

```html
import React from 'react'
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'

const items = [
  { label: 'List item 1', value: '1' },
  { disabled: true, label: 'List item 2 — locked', value: '2' },
  { label: 'List item 3', value: '3' },
]

export const TransferDisabledExample = () => {
  return <CTransfer items={items} />
}
```

## Accessibility

Each list is a listbox of its own with the title as its accessible name, and the select-all button carries the state of its list in `aria-pressed` — all of that comes from [List box](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/#accessibility), keyboard included: the arrows, <kbd>Home</kbd>, <kbd>End</kbd>, <kbd>Space</kbd>, <kbd>Shift</kbd> ranges, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> + <kbd>A</kbd> and the typeahead all work inside the list that has the focus.

What the transfer adds is the crossing. Each move button is named — `ariaMoveToTargetLabel`, `ariaMoveToSourceLabel`, `ariaMoveAllToTargetLabel`, `ariaMoveAllToSourceLabel` — and is disabled while it has nothing to move, so the keyboard never lands on a button that would do nothing. The chevrons are decorative, so the name is all a screen reader gets.

The move happens away from the focus, and the button that did it usually turns off in the process — a list with nothing selected left. Rather than dropping the focus on the document, the component puts it on the first option that just arrived.

Every move, either way, adds a message of its own to the live region of the page through [`announce()`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/screen-readers/#announcing-messages) once it is applied, so a move that a controlled `value` refuses is not announced and the same move made twice is announced twice: `ariaMovedAnnouncement` is `'{count} moved to {title}'` by default, with `{title}` the destination's title. `{count}` and `{title}` are replaced wherever they appear, so the sentence can be reordered for a translation.

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `Tab` | Move between the select-all button, the search field, the options and the move buttons |
| `↓` / `↑` | Move the highlight inside the focused list |
| `Space` | Toggle the highlighted option |
| `Shift` + `↓` / `↑` | Extend the selection inside the focused list |
| `Ctrl` / `Cmd` + `A` | Select every visible, enabled option of the focused list |
| `Enter` / `Space` | Move the selection when the focus is on a move button |

## Customizing

### CSS variables

The transfer reads its own set of CSS variables, declared on `.transfer`. Set them on a single transfer to restyle it without recompiling:

```css
--cui-transfer-gap
--cui-transfer-actions-gap
--cui-transfer-list-min-height
--cui-transfer-list-max-height
```

The lists carry the [list box](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/list-box/#css-variables) variables on top of these, so the padding, the colors and the option states are set there.

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CTransfer /&gt;](./api/#ctransfer)
