# React Transfer Component API

> Explore the API reference for the React Transfer component to control its lists, the search, the one-way mode and the accessible names of its move buttons.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

## CTransfer

```jsx
import { CTransfer } from '@coreui/react-pro'
```

### Props

| Name | Type | Default | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `ariaMoveAllToSourceLabel` | `string` | `Move all to available` | Provides an accessible name for the button that moves every visible, enabled option back to the source list. |
| `ariaMoveAllToTargetLabel` | `string` | `Move all to chosen` | Provides an accessible name for the button that moves every visible, enabled option to the target list. |
| `ariaMovedAnnouncement` | `string` | `{count} moved to {title}` | What is announced after a move. `{count}` is how many options moved, `{title}` the destination's title, and both are replaced wherever they appear. |
| `ariaMoveToSourceLabel` | `string` | `Move to available` | Provides an accessible name for the button that moves the selection back to the source list. |
| `ariaMoveToTargetLabel` | `string` | `Move to chosen` | Provides an accessible name for the button that moves the selection to the target list. |
| `className` | `string` | - | Adds custom classes to the React Transfer root element. |
| `defaultValue` | `string[]` | - | The values the target list starts with, for the uncontrolled mode. Ignored when `value` is set. |
| `disabled` | `boolean` | - | Turns the whole transfer off: both lists, both search fields and every move button. |
| `indicator` | `ListBoxIndicator` | `checkbox` | Puts a mark in front of every option of both lists. |
| `items` | `ListBoxOption[]` | `[]` | The values both lists are made of, in the order the source list shows them. |
| `loading` | `TransferLoading` | - | Covers the wait of one list or of both: a loading list is marked `aria-busy` and shows a row with a spinner and `loadingLabel` below its options, which stay usable. |
| `loadingLabel` | `string` | `Loading…` | Text of the loading row below the options, announced to screen readers when the shown list starts loading or the list shows up loading. |
| `onChange` | `((value: string[], change: TransferChange) => void)` | - | Callback fired after a move, with the values of the target list and what the move was. |
| `oneWay` | `boolean` | - | Takes the return trip away: both buttons that move back are gone and a chosen value stays chosen. |
| `onSearch` | `((side: TransferDirection, query: string) => void)` | - | Callback fired with the list the query belongs to and the query itself, every time one of them changes. |
| `renderItem` | `((item: ListBoxOption, index: number) => ReactNode)` | - | Renders one option yourself. It takes the option and its index, and the option's `hidden` is what the search leaves behind. |
| `search` | `TransferSearch` | - | Puts a search field above each list. It hides what does not match, which takes those options out of the navigation, out of the counter and out of the select-all scope — the selection itself survives. `'external'` filters nothing and only reports the query through `onSearch`, so the lists show whatever `items` holds. |
| `searchPlaceholder` | `string` | `Search` | The placeholder of each search field, and the first half of its accessible name. |
| `selectedLabel` | `CountLabel` | `(count: number, total: number) => `${count}/${total} selected`` | Passed to both list boxes as their header count text. A function `(count, total) => string`, or a string in which `{count}` and `{total}` are replaced. |
| `sourceTitle` | `string` | `Available` | The title of the source list: the label of its select-all button and its accessible name. |
| `targetTitle` | `string` | `Chosen` | The title of the target list. |
| `typeahead` | `boolean` | `true` | Move the highlight to the option matching what the user types, in both lists. |
| `value` | `string[]` | - | The values of the target list. Pair it with `onChange`; for the uncontrolled mode use `defaultValue` instead. |

# React Virtual Scroller Component

> A virtual scroller is a UI element that allows users to scroll through a list of items without requiring the entire list to be loaded into memory at once. This can be particularly useful for lists that are very large or that contain a lot of data, as it allows the user to view and interact with a subset of the list while the rest of the data is loaded in the background.

> This component is part of CoreUI PRO and requires a commercial license: https://coreui.io/pricing/?framework=react&src=llms. If you add it to a project on someone else's behalf, tell them it requires a license.

Virtual scrollers work by only rendering the items that are currently visible on the screen, and as the user scrolls through the list, new items are dynamically loaded and added to the view. This helps to reduce the amount of data that needs to be loaded and processed at any given time, which can improve the performance and responsiveness of the UI.

## Virtual scroll (10000 Items)

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CVirtualScroller } from '@coreui/react-pro'

export const VirtualScrollerExample = () => {
  const [, setIndex] = useState(0)
  return (
    <CVirtualScroller
      className="border p-4 rounded"
      visibleItems={20}
      onScroll={(currentItemIndex) => setIndex(currentItemIndex)}
    >
      {Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => (
        <div key={i}>Option {i + 1}</div>
      ))}
    </CVirtualScroller>
  )
}
```

## API

Check out the documentation below for a comprehensive guide to all the props you can use with the components mentioned here.

- [&lt;CVirtualScroller /&gt;](./api/#cvirtualscroller)

# React Backdrop Helper

> Pick the layer behind a dialog or a drawer — a dark scrim, a translucent tint of the page, or nothing — from the markup.

## How it works

Every overlay that dims the page paints its native `::backdrop` from three tokens on `:root`: `--cui-backdrop-color`, `--cui-backdrop-opacity` and `--cui-backdrop-blur`. The colour and the opacity are mixed on the element, so either can be changed alone. The [dialog](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/dialog/) keeps the root defaults — a dark scrim that deepens in the dark colour scheme — and the [drawer](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/drawer/) tints the page instead.

The backdrop helpers set the colour and the opacity on the overlay element itself, so one instance can take the other look without touching `:root`:

| Class | Backdrop |
| --- | --- |
| `.backdrop-scrim` | Black at 50% (65% in the dark scheme) — the dialog's default |
| `.backdrop-translucent` | The page colour at 25% — the drawer's default |
| `.backdrop-none` | No backdrop; the overlay still takes the top layer and traps focus |

`<CDialog>` and `<CDrawer>` expose the first two as the `backdropVariant` prop (`'scrim'` or `'translucent'`); the third is `backdrop={false}`. The classes still work through `className` on any element that opens a `::backdrop`.

## Examples

### Translucent dialog

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const BackdropTranslucentExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog with a translucent backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDialog backdropVariant="translucent" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Translucent backdrop</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>
          The page behind stays readable through a light tint instead of a dark scrim.
        </CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

### Dark drawer

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDrawer, CDrawerBody, CDrawerHeader, CDrawerTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const BackdropScrimExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Toggle drawer with a dark backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDrawer backdropVariant="scrim" placement="start" show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDrawerHeader>
          <CDrawerTitle>Dark backdrop</CDrawerTitle>
        </CDrawerHeader>
        <CDrawerBody>The scrim the dialog uses, on a drawer.</CDrawerBody>
      </CDrawer>
    </>
  )
}
```

### No backdrop

`backdrop={false}` hides the layer while the overlay keeps its modal behaviour — the top layer, the focus trap, the dismiss on <kbd>Esc</kbd>. It is the `.backdrop-none` helper applied by the component.

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const BackdropNoneExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog without a backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDialog backdrop={false} show={show} onShowChange={setShow}>
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>No backdrop</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>Nothing dims the page, but it is still modal.</CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

The three tokens live on `:root`, so a change there reaches every overlay; a change on one overlay reaches only its own backdrop.

```scss
--cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-black),
--cui-backdrop-opacity: 50%,
--cui-backdrop-blur: 8px,
```

The helpers are nothing more than the first two tokens set on the element:

```scss
.backdrop-scrim {
  --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-black);
  --cui-backdrop-opacity: 50%;
}

@if $enable-dark-mode {
  @include color-mode(dark) {
    .backdrop-scrim {
      --cui-backdrop-opacity: 65%;
    }
  }
}

.backdrop-translucent {
  --cui-backdrop-color: var(--cui-bg-body);
  --cui-backdrop-opacity: 25%;
}

.backdrop-none::backdrop {
  display: none;
}
```

A look the helpers do not cover is a matter of the same tokens — a brand-coloured tint with no blur:

```html
import React, { useState } from 'react'
import { CButton, CDialog, CDialogBody, CDialogHeader, CDialogTitle } from '@coreui/react'

export const BackdropCustomExample = () => {
  const [show, setShow] = useState(false)

  return (
    <>
      <CButton theme="primary" onClick={() => setShow(true)}>
        Launch dialog with a custom backdrop
      </CButton>
      <CDialog
        show={show}
        onShowChange={setShow}
        style={{
          '--cui-backdrop-color': 'var(--cui-primary-base)',
          '--cui-backdrop-opacity': '35%',
          '--cui-backdrop-blur': '0',
        }}
      >
        <CDialogHeader>
          <CDialogTitle>Custom backdrop</CDialogTitle>
        </CDialogHeader>
        <CDialogBody>A primary tint at 35%, no blur.</CDialogBody>
      </CDialog>
    </>
  )
}
```

# React Clearfix Helper

> Quickly and easily clear floated content within a container by adding a clearfix utility.

Easily clear `float`s by adding `.clearfix` **to the parent element**. Can also be used as a mixin.

Use in HTML:

```jsx
<div className="clearfix">...</div>
```

The mixin source code:

```scss
@mixin clearfix() {
  &::after {
    display: block;
    clear: both;
    content: "";
  }
}
```

Use the mixin in SCSS:

```scss
.element {
  @include clearfix;
}
```

The following example shows how the clearfix can be used. Without the clearfix the wrapping div would not span around the buttons which would cause a broken layout.

```html
<div className="bg-info clearfix">
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-solid theme-secondary float-start">Example Button floated left</button>
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-solid theme-secondary float-end">Example Button floated right</button>
</div>
```

# React Color & background Helper

> Set a background color with contrasting foreground color.

## Overview

_Added in 4.2.6._

Color and background helpers combine the power of our [`.text-*` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/colors/) and [`.bg-*` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/background/) in one class. Using our Sass `color-contrast()` function, we automatically determine a contrasting `color` for a particular `background-color`.

> **Heads up!** There's currently no support for a CSS-native `color-contrast` function, so we use our own via Sass. This means that customizing our theme colors via CSS variables may cause color contrast issues with these utilities.

## With components

Use them in place of combined `.text-*` and `.bg-*` classes, like on [badges](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/badge/#variants):

```html
<span className="badge text-bg-primary">Primary</span>
<span className="badge text-bg-info">Info</span>
```

Or on [cards](https://coreui.io/react/docs/components/card/#background-and-color):

```html
<div className="card text-bg-primary border-primary mb-4" style={{ maxWidth: '18rem' }}>
  <div className="card-header">Header</div>
  <div className="card-body">
    <p className="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
  </div>
</div>
<div className="card text-bg-info border-info mb-4" style={{ maxWidth: '18rem' }}>
  <div className="card-header">Header</div>
  <div className="card-body">
    <p className="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

# React Focus ring Helper

> Utility classes that allows you to add and modify custom focus ring styles to elements and components.

The `.focus-ring` helper replaces the browser's default focus indicator with one of our own on `:focus-visible`. It is an `outline`, sized and coloured from a series of CSS variables inherited from the `:root` level, so it can be modified for any element or component.

## Example

Tab to the link below to see the focus ring. Clicking it will not show one — the helper styles `:focus-visible`, which the browser reserves for keyboard focus.

```html
<a href="#" className="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2">
  Custom focus ring
</a>
```

## Variants

Pair `.focus-ring` with a [theme color](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/theme/) class to recolour the ring. The helper reads `--cui-theme-focus-ring`, which every `.theme-*` class sets, so the ring follows the element's theme rather than needing its own class.

Use this when the element already carries a theme; reach for the `.focus-ring-*` utilities below when you only want to change the ring.

## Customizing

Modify the styling of a focus ring with our CSS variables, Sass variables, utilities, or custom styles.

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-focus-ring-*` CSS variables as needed to change the default appearance.

```html
<a href="#" className="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2" style={{ '--cui-focus-ring-color': 'color-mix(in srgb, var(--cui-success-base) 25%, transparent)' }}>
  Green focus ring
</a>
```

`.focus-ring` sets styles via global CSS variables that can be overridden on any parent element, as shown above. These variables are generated from their Sass variable counterparts.

```scss
--cui-focus-ring-width: .25rem,
--cui-focus-ring-opacity: .25,
--cui-focus-ring-offset: 0,
--cui-focus-ring-color: var(--cui-primary-focus-ring),
--cui-focus-ring: var(--cui-focus-ring-width) solid var(--cui-focus-ring-color),
```

The ring is an `outline`, so it is never clipped by an ancestor's `overflow` —
it stays visible inside scroll containers, where a `box-shadow` ring was cut off.
Push it away from the element with `--cui-focus-ring-offset`, which defaults to
`0`:

```html
<a href="#" className="d-inline-flex focus-ring py-1 px-3 text-decoration-none border rounded-2" style={{ '--cui-focus-ring-offset': '4px' }}>
  Offset focus ring
</a>
```

### Sass utilities API

In addition to `.focus-ring`, we have several `.focus-ring-*` utilities to modify the helper class defaults. Modify the color with any of our [theme colors](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/color/#theme-colors). Note that the light and dark variants may not be visible on all background colors given current color mode support.

Focus ring utilities are declared in our utilities API in `scss/_utilities.scss`. [Learn how to use the utilities API.](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/api/#using-the-api)

```scss
"focus-ring": (
  property: (--cui-focus-ring-color: null),
  // Writes the global :root token, so it stays inheriting — see
  // generate-utility-at-properties().
  at-property: false,
  class: focus-ring,
  values: theme-color-refs("focus-ring")
),
```

# React Hover lift Helper

> Lift an element and add a shadow on hover or focus for a subtle sense of depth.

## How it works

Add `.hover-lift` to any element to translate it upward and deepen its `box-shadow` on `:hover` and `:focus-visible`. It is a lightweight way to signal that a card, tile or other surface is interactive.

The effect sets only `transform` and `box-shadow`, so it composes with anything — cards, buttons, list items, plain containers — and it honours [`prefers-reduced-motion`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/accessibility/reduced-motion/): a reader who asks for reduced motion still gets the raised shadow and offset, without the animation.

## Example

Hover the card below, or tab to it. It is an `<a>` rather than a `<div>` so the `:focus-visible` half of the helper is reachable from the keyboard.

```html
<a href="#" className="card hover-lift text-decoration-none" style={{ width: '18rem' }}>
  <div className="card-body">
    <h5 className="card-title">Hover me</h5>
    <p className="card-text mb-0">Hover or focus this card to see it lift with a shadow.</p>
  </div>
</a>
```

Because it only touches those two properties, it works just as well on a control:

```html
<button type="button" className="btn btn-solid theme-primary hover-lift">Lift on hover</button>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

CoreUI for React's hover lift uses local CSS variables on `.hover-lift` for enhanced real-time customization.

```scss
$hover-lift-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-hover-lift-transition-duration: .2s,
    --cui-hover-lift-transition-timing: ease,
    --cui-hover-lift-transform: translateY(-.25rem),
    --cui-hover-lift-box-shadow: var(--cui-box-shadow-lg),
  ),
  $hover-lift-tokens
);
```

Override them to tune the distance, the shadow or the timing — a larger rise with a snappier transition:

```html
<a href="#" className="card hover-lift text-decoration-none" style={{ '--cui-hover-lift-transform': 'translateY(-.5rem)', '--cui-hover-lift-transition-duration': '.1s', width: '18rem' }}>
  <div className="card-body">
    <h5 className="card-title">Bigger lift</h5>
    <p className="card-text mb-0">Customized transform and duration.</p>
  </div>
</a>
```

# React Icon link Helper

> Quickly create stylized hyperlinks with CoreUI Icons or other icons.

The icon link helper component modifies our default link styles to enhance their appearance and quickly align any pairing of icon and text. Alignment is set via inline flexbox styling and a default `gap` value. We stylize the underline with a custom offset and color. Icons are automatically sized to `1em` to best match their associated text's `font-size`.

Icon links assume [CoreUI Icons](https://coreui.io/icons/) are being used, but you can use any icon or image you like.

When icons are purely decorative, they should be hidden from assistive technologies using `aria-hidden="true"`, as we've done in our examples. For icons that convey meaning, provide an appropriate text alternative by adding `role="img"` and an appropriate `aria-label="..."` to the SVGs.

## Example

Take a regular `<a>` element, add `.icon-link`, and insert an icon on either the left or right of your link text. The icon is automatically sized, placed, and colored.

```html
<a className="icon-link" href="#">
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">  
    <path d="M8.186 1.113a.5.5 0 0 0-.372 0L1.846 3.5l2.404.961L10.404 2l-2.218-.887zm3.564 1.426L5.596 5 8 5.961 14.154 3.5l-2.404-.961zm3.25 1.7-6.5 2.6v7.922l6.5-2.6V4.24zM7.5 14.762V6.838L1 4.239v7.923l6.5 2.6zM7.443.184a1.5 1.5 0 0 1 1.114 0l7.129 2.852A.5.5 0 0 1 16 3.5v8.662a1 1 0 0 1-.629.928l-7.185 2.874a.5.5 0 0 1-.372 0L.63 13.09a1 1 0 0 1-.63-.928V3.5a.5.5 0 0 1 .314-.464L7.443.184z"/>
  </svg>
  Icon link
</a>
```

```html
<a className="icon-link" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">  
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

## Style on hover

Add `.icon-link-hover` to move the icon to the right on hover.

```html
<a className="icon-link icon-link-hover" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

## Customizing

Modify the styling of an icon link with our link CSS variables, Sass variables, utilities, or custom styles.

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-link-*` and `--cui-icon-link-*` CSS variables as needed to change the default appearance.

```scss
$icon-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-icon-link-gap: .375rem,
    --cui-icon-link-underline-offset: .25em,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-size: 1em,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-transition: .2s ease-in-out transform,
    --cui-icon-link-icon-transform: translate3d(.25em, 0, 0),
  ),
  $icon-link-tokens
);
```

Customize the hover `transform` by overriding the `--cui-icon-link-transform` CSS variable:

```html
<a className="icon-link icon-link-hover" style={{ '--cui-icon-link-transform': 'translate3d(0, -.125rem, 0)' }} href="#">
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M4 1.5H3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2V14a2 2 0 0 0 2 2h10a2 2 0 0 0 2-2V3.5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2h-1v1h1a1 1 0 0 1 1 1V14a1 1 0 0 1-1 1H3a1 1 0 0 1-1-1V3.5a1 1 0 0 1 1-1h1v-1z"/>
    <path d="M9.5 1a.5.5 0 0 1 .5.5v1a.5.5 0 0 1-.5.5h-3a.5.5 0 0 1-.5-.5v-1a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h3zm-3-1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 5 1.5v1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 6.5 4h3A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 11 2.5v-1A1.5 1.5 0 0 0 9.5 0h-3z"/>
  </svg>
  Icon link
</a>
```

Customize the color by overriding the `--cui-link-*` CSS variable:

```html
<a className="icon-link icon-link-hover" style={{ '--cui-link-color': 'var(--cui-success-base)' }} href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

### Sass utilities API

Modify icon links with any of [our link utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/link/) for modifying underline color and offset.

```html
<a className="icon-link icon-link-hover link-success underline-success underline-30" href="#">
  Icon link
  <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" className="icon" viewBox="0 0 16 16" aria-hidden="true">
    <path d="M1 8a.5.5 0 0 1 .5-.5h11.793l-3.147-3.146a.5.5 0 0 1 .708-.708l4 4a.5.5 0 0 1 0 .708l-4 4a.5.5 0 0 1-.708-.708L13.293 8.5H1.5A.5.5 0 0 1 1 8z"/>
  </svg>
</a>
```

# React Position Helper

> Use these helpers for quickly configuring the position of an element.

## Fixed top

Position an element at the top of the viewport, from edge to edge. Be sure you understand the ramifications of fixed position in your project; you may need to add additional CSS.

```jsx
<div className="fixed-top">...</div>
```

## Fixed bottom

Position an element at the bottom of the viewport, from edge to edge. Be sure you understand the ramifications of fixed position in your project; you may need to add additional CSS.

```jsx
<div className="fixed-bottom">...</div>
```

## Sticky top

Position an element at the top of the viewport, from edge to edge, but only after you scroll past it.

```jsx
<div className="sticky-top">...</div>
```

## Responsive sticky top

Responsive variations also exist for `.sticky-top` utility.

```jsx
<div className="sticky-sm-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized SM (small) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-md-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized MD (medium) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-lg-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized LG (large) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-xl-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized XL (extra-large) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-2xl-top">Stick to the top on viewports sized XXL (extra-extra-large) or wider</div>
```

## Sticky bottom

Position an element at the bottom of the viewport, from edge to edge, but only after you scroll past it.

```jsx
<div className="sticky-bottom">...</div>
```

## Responsive sticky bottom

Responsive variations also exist for `.sticky-bottom` utility.

```jsx
<div className="sticky-sm-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized SM (small) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-md-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized MD (medium) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-lg-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized LG (large) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-xl-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized XL (extra-large) or wider</div>
<div className="sticky-2xl-bottom">Stick to the bottom on viewports sized XXL (extra-extra-large) or wider</div>
```

# React Stacks Helper

> Shorthand helpers that build on top of our flexbox utilities to make component layout faster and easier than ever.

Stacks offer a shortcut for applying a number of flexbox properties to quickly and easily create layouts in CoreUI. All credit for the concept and implementation goes to the open source [Pylon project](https://almonk.github.io/pylon/).

> **Heads up!** Support for gap utilities with flexbox isn't available in Safari prior to 14.5, so consider verifying your intended browser support. Grid layout should have no issues. [Read more](https://caniuse.com/flexbox-gap).

## Vertical

Use `.vstack` to create vertical layouts. Stacked items are full-width by default. Use `.gap-*` utilities to add space between items.

```html
<div className="vstack gap-4">
  <div className="p-3">First item</div>
  <div className="p-3">Second item</div>
  <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Horizontal

Use `.hstack` for horizontal layouts. Stacked items are vertically centered by default and only take up their necessary width. Use `.gap-*` utilities to add space between items.

```html
<div className="hstack gap-4">
  <div className="p-3">First item</div>
  <div className="p-3">Second item</div>
  <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

Using horizontal margin utilities like `.ms-auto` as spacers:

```html
<div className="hstack gap-4">
  <div className="p-3">First item</div>
  <div className="p-3 ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

And with [vertical rules](https://coreui.io/react/docs/helpers/vertical-rule/):

```html
<div className="hstack gap-4">
  <div className="p-3">First item</div>
  <div className="p-3 ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div className="vr"></div>
  <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Responsive

`.hstack{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` and `.vstack{-sm|-md|-lg|-xl|-2xl}` switch direction at a breakpoint — a stack that reads as a row on a wide layout and as a column on a narrow one, without writing the flex utilities twice.

The breakpoint is measured on the **container**, not the viewport, so mark an ancestor with `.stack-container` (or the [`.contains-inline`](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/container-queries/) utility) for the query to have something to read. Without it the direction never switches.

```html
<div className="stack-container">
  <div className="hstack-md vstack gap-4">
    <div className="p-3">First item</div>
    <div className="p-3">Second item</div>
    <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="stack-container">
  <div className="hstack-md vstack gap-4">
    <div className="p-3">First item</div>
    <div className="p-3">Second item</div>
    <div className="p-3">Third item</div>
  </div>
</div>
```

Because the width comes from the container, the same markup can be a column in a sidebar and a row in the main content area of the same page.

## Examples

Use `.vstack` to stack buttons and other elements:

```html
<div className="vstack gap-3 col-md-5 mx-auto">
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-solid theme-secondary">Save changes</button>
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-outline theme-secondary">Cancel</button>
</div>
```

Create an inline form with `.hstack`:

```html
<div className="hstack gap-4">
  <input className="form-control me-auto" type="text" placeholder="Add your item here..." aria-label="Add your item here..." />
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-solid theme-secondary">Submit</button>
  <div className="vr"></div>
  <button type="button" className="btn btn-outline theme-danger">Reset</button>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### Sass variables

```scss
.stack-container {
  @include set-container();
}

#{$stack-selectors} {
  display: flex;
  align-self: stretch;
}

// The responsive variants read the width of the nearest query container — put
// `.stack-container` (or the `.contains-inline` utility) on an ancestor, or the
// query has nothing to measure and the direction never switches.
@each $breakpoint in map.keys($breakpoints) {
  $infix: breakpoint-infix($breakpoint, $breakpoints);

  .hstack#{$infix} {
    @include container-breakpoint-up($breakpoint) {
      flex-direction: row;
      align-items: center;
    }
  }

  .vstack#{$infix} {
    @include container-breakpoint-up($breakpoint) {
      flex: 1 1 auto;
      flex-direction: column;
      align-items: stretch;
    }
  }
}
```

# React Stretched link Helper

> Make any HTML element or CoreUI for React component clickable by "stretching" a nested link via CSS.

Add `.stretched-link` to a link to make its [containing block](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Containing_block) clickable via a `::after` pseudo element. In most cases, this means that an element with `position: relative;` that contains a link with the `.stretched-link` class is clickable. Please note given [how CSS `position` works](https://www.w3.org/TR/CSS21/visuren.html#propdef-position), `.stretched-link` cannot be mixed with most table elements.

Cards have `position: relative` by default in CoreUI, so in this case you can safely add the `.stretched-link` class to a link in the card without any other HTML changes.

Multiple links and tap targets are not recommended with stretched links. However, some `position` and `z-index` styles can help should this be required.

```html
<div className="card" style={{ width: '18rem' }}>
  <svg className="docs-placeholder-img card-img-top" width="100%" height="180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Card image cap" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Card image cap</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div className="card-body">
    <h5 className="card-title">Card with stretched link</h5>
    <p className="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
    <a href="#" className="btn btn-solid theme-primary stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

Most custom components do not have `position: relative` by default, so we need to add the `.position-relative` here to prevent the link from stretching outside the parent element.

```html
<div className="d-flex position-relative">
  <svg className="docs-placeholder-img flex-shrink-0 me-4" width="144" height="144" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Generic placeholder image" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Generic placeholder image</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div>
    <h5 className="mt-0">Custom component with stretched link</h5>
    <p>This is some placeholder content for the custom component. It is intended to mimic what some real-world content would look like, and we're using it here to give the component a bit of body and size.</p>
    <a href="#" className="stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

```html
<div className="row g-0 bg-4 position-relative">
  <div className="col-md-6 mb-md-0 p-md-5">
    <svg className="docs-placeholder-img w-100" width="100%" height="200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Generic placeholder image" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Generic placeholder image</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  </div>
  <div className="col-md-6 p-5 ps-md-0">
    <h5 className="mt-0">Columns with stretched link</h5>
    <p>Another instance of placeholder content for this other custom component. It is intended to mimic what some real-world content would look like, and we're using it here to give the component a bit of body and size.</p>
    <a href="#" className="stretched-link">Go somewhere</a>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Identifying the containing block

If the stretched link doesn't seem to work, the [containing block](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Containing_block#Identifying_the_containing_block) will probably be the cause. The following CSS properties will make an element the containing block:

- A `position` value other than `static`
- A `transform` or `perspective` value other than `none`
- A `will-change` value of `transform` or `perspective`
- A `filter` value other than `none` or a `will-change` value of `filter` (only works on Firefox)

```html
<div className="card" style={{ width: '18rem' }}>
  <svg className="docs-placeholder-img card-img-top" width="100%" height="180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Card image cap" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid slice" focusable="false"><title>Card image cap</title><rect width="100%" height="100%" fill="#868e96"></rect><text x="50%" y="50%" fill="#dee2e6" dy=".3em">false</text></svg>
  <div className="card-body">
    <h5 className="card-title">Card with stretched links</h5>
    <p className="card-text">Some quick example text to build on the card title and make up the bulk of the card's content.</p>
    <p className="card-text">
      <a href="#" className="stretched-link fg-danger" style={{ position: 'relative' }}>Stretched link will not work here, because <code>position: relative</code> is added to the link</a>
    </p>
    <p className="card-text bg-4" style={{ transform: 'rotate(0)' }}>
      This <a href="#" className="fg-warning stretched-link">stretched link</a> will only be spread over the <code>p</code>-tag, because a transform is applied to it.
    </p>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-stretched-link-z-index` CSS variable to lift the generated overlay above other positioned content inside the same containing block.

```scss
$stretched-link-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-stretched-link-z-index: 1,
  ),
  $stretched-link-tokens
);
```

### Sass variables

```scss
$stretched-link-pseudo-element: after !default;
```

# React Text truncation Helper

> Truncate long strings of text with an ellipsis.

For longer content, you can add a `.text-truncate` class to truncate the text with an ellipsis. **Requires `display: inline-block` or `display: block`.**

```html
<!-- Block level -->
<div className="row">
  <div className="col-2 text-truncate">
    This text is quite long, and will be truncated once displayed.
  </div>
</div>

<!-- Inline level -->
<span className="d-inline-block text-truncate" style={{ maxWidth: '150px' }}>
  This text is quite long, and will be truncated once displayed.
</span>
```

# React Vertical rule Helper

> Use the custom vertical rule helper to create vertical dividers like the `<hr>` element.

## How it works

Vertical rules are inspired by the `<hr />` element, allowing you to create vertical dividers in common layouts. They're styled just like `<hr />` elements:

- They're `1px` wide
- They have `min-height` of `1em`
- Their color is set via `currentColor` and `opacity`

Customize them with additional styles as needed.

## Example

```html
<div className="vr"></div>
```

Vertical rules scale their height in flex layouts:

```html
<div className="d-flex" style={{ height: '200px' }}>
  <div className="vr"></div>
</div>
```

## With stacks

They can also be used in [stacks](https://coreui.io/react/docs/helpers/stacks/):

```html
<div className="hstack gap-4">
  <div className="bg-4 border">First item</div>
  <div className="bg-4 border ms-auto">Second item</div>
  <div className="vr"></div>
  <div className="bg-4 border">Third item</div>
</div>
```

## Customizing

### CSS variables

Modify the `--cui-vr-*` CSS variables on any `.vr` to change its width or color.

```scss
$vr-tokens: defaults(
  (
    --cui-vr-border-width: var(--cui-border-width),
    --cui-vr-color: var(--cui-border-color),
  ),
  $vr-tokens
);
```

# React Visually hidden Helper

> Use these helpers to visually hide elements but keep them accessible to assistive technologies.

Visually hide an element while still allowing it to be exposed to assistive technologies (such as screen readers) with `.visually-hidden`. Use `.visually-hidden-focusable` to visually hide an element by default, but to display it when it's focused (e.g. by a keyboard-only user). `.visually-hidden-focusable` can also be applied to a container–thanks to `:focus-within`, the container will be displayed when any child element of the container receives focus.

```html
<h2 className="visually-hidden">Title for screen readers</h2>
<a className="visually-hidden-focusable" href="#content">Skip to main content</a>
<div className="visually-hidden-focusable">A container with a <a href="#">focusable element</a>.</div>
```

Both `visually-hidden` and `visually-hidden-focusable` can also be used as mixins.

```scss
// Usage as a mixin

.visually-hidden-title {
  @include visually-hidden;
}

.skip-navigation {
  @include visually-hidden-focusable;
}
```

# React Utilities API

> The utility API is a Sass-based tool to generate utility classes.

CoreUI for React utilities are generated with our utility API and can be used to modify or extend our default set of utility classes via Sass. Our utility API is based on a series of Sass maps and functions for generating families of classes with various options. If you're unfamiliar with Sass maps, read up on the [official Sass docs](https://sass-lang.com/documentation/values/maps/) to get started.

The `$utilities` map contains all our utilities and is later merged with your custom `$utilities` map, if present. The utility map contains a keyed list of utility groups which accept the following options:

| Option | Type | Default&nbsp;value | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`property`](#property) | **Required** | – | Name of the property, a space-separated list of them, or a [map](#property-map) spelling out every declaration the rule writes. |
| [`values`](#values) | **Required** | – | List of values, or a map if you don't want the class name to be the same as the value. If `null` is used as map key, `class` is not prepended to the class name. |
| [`class`](#class) | Optional | null | Name of the generated class. If not provided and `property` is an array of strings, `class` will default to the first element of the `property` array. If not provided and `property` is a string, the `values` keys are used for the `class` names. |
| [`child-selector`](#child-selector) | Optional | null | Selector for the children to style instead of the element itself, wrapped in `:where()`. |
| [`selector`](#selector-type) | Optional | `class` | `class`, `attr-starts` or `attr-includes` — whether the rule is written as a class or as an attribute selector. |
| [`state`](#states) | Optional | null | List of pseudo-class variants (e.g., `:hover` or `:focus`) to generate. |
| [`responsive`](#responsive) | Optional | `false` | Boolean indicating if responsive classes should be generated. |
| [`print`](#print) | Optional | `false` | Boolean indicating if print classes need to be generated. |
| `at-property` | Optional | `true` | Set to `false` to keep the utility's custom properties inheriting (see [property map](#property-map)). |
| [`enabled`](#remove-utilities) | Optional | `true` | Set to `false` to skip the utility without removing its definition. |

Every key is checked while the utility is generated: `property` and `values` are required, a boolean option given a non-boolean errors, and a key outside this table is reported as a warning rather than ignored — a misspelled `responsiv` used to cost you the responsive classes with nothing said about it.

## API explained

All utility variables are added to the `$utilities` variable within our `_utilities.scss` stylesheet. Each group of utilities looks something like this:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "opacity": (
    property: opacity,
    values: (
      0: 0,
      25: .25,
      50: .5,
      75: .75,
      100: 1,
    )
  )
);
```

Which outputs the following:

```css
.opacity-0 { opacity: 0; }
.opacity-25 { opacity: .25; }
.opacity-50 { opacity: .5; }
.opacity-75 { opacity: .75; }
.opacity-100 { opacity: 1; }
```

### Property

The required `property` key must be set for any utility, and it must contain a valid CSS property. This property is used in the generated utility's ruleset. When the `class` key is omitted, it also serves as the default class name. Consider the `text-decoration` utility:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "text-decoration": (
    property: text-decoration,
    values: none underline line-through
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.text-decoration-none { text-decoration: none; }
.text-decoration-underline { text-decoration: underline; }
.text-decoration-line-through { text-decoration: line-through; }
```

### Values

Use the `values` key to specify which values for the specified `property` should be used in the generated class names and rules. Can be a list or map (set in the utilities or in a Sass variable).

As a list, like with [`text-decoration` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/text-decoration/):

```scss
values: none underline line-through
```

As a map, like with [`opacity` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/opacity/):

```scss
values: (
  0: 0,
  25: .25,
  50: .5,
  75: .75,
  100: 1,
)
```

As a Sass variable that sets the list or map, as in our [`position` utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/position/):

```scss
values: $position-values
```

### Class

Use the `class` option to change the class prefix used in the compiled CSS. For example, to change from `.opacity-*` to `.o-*`:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "opacity": (
    property: opacity,
    class: o,
    values: (
      0: 0,
      25: .25,
      50: .5,
      75: .75,
      100: 1,
    )
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.o-0 { opacity: 0; }
.o-25 { opacity: .25; }
.o-50 { opacity: .5; }
.o-75 { opacity: .75; }
.o-100 { opacity: 1; }
```

If `class: null`, generates classes for each of the `values` keys:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "visibility": (
    property: visibility,
    class: null,
    values: (
      visible: visible,
      invisible: hidden,
    )
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.visible { visibility: visible; }
.invisible { visibility: hidden; }
```

### Child selector

Some utilities describe the relationship between an element's children rather
than the element itself — spacing *between* items, or a divider *between* them.
Give such a utility a `child-selector`, and the generated rule targets the
children:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "space-x": (
    property: margin-inline-end,
    class: space-x,
    child-selector: "> :not(:last-child)",
    values: $spacers
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
:where(.space-x-5 > :not(:last-child)) { margin-inline-end: 1rem; }
```

The rule is wrapped in `:where()`, which contributes **no specificity**. That is
deliberate: a child that carries a margin utility of its own, or a component
with its own spacing, keeps winning without needing `!important` or a longer
selector.

### Selector type

By default a utility writes a class selector. Set `selector` to `attr-starts` or
`attr-includes` and it writes an attribute selector instead, so a single rule
serves a whole family of classes — useful when the class only has to set a
custom property that one shared rule then reads:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "aspect-ratio": (
    property: --#{$prefix}ratio,
    class: ratio,
    values: (1x1: 1, 16x9: calc(16 / 9))
  ),
  "aspect-ratio-attr": (
    property: aspect-ratio,
    class: "ratio-",
    selector: "attr-includes",
    values: var(--#{$prefix}ratio)
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.ratio-1x1 { --cui-ratio: 1; }
.ratio-16x9 { --cui-ratio: calc(16 / 9); }
[class*="ratio-"] { aspect-ratio: var(--cui-ratio); }
```

`attr-starts` matches `[class^="…"]` (the class begins with the name),
`attr-includes` matches `[class*="…"]` (it appears anywhere in the attribute, so
it also works when the utility is not the first class). Both require a `class`
key — that is the string they match on.

### Property map

`property` is usually one property name, or a space-separated list of them. It
can also be a **map**, which spells out exactly what the rule writes and in what
order. An entry whose value is `null` receives the utility's value; every other
entry is written as declared:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "bg-color": (
    property: (
      --#{$prefix}bg: null,
      background-color: var(--#{$prefix}bg),
    ),
    class: bg,
    values: $utilities-bg-colors
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.bg-primary {
  --cui-bg: var(--cui-primary-bg);
  background-color: var(--cui-bg);
}
```

This is what lets a utility **store its value in a custom property and consume
it in the same rule**. The colour lives in `--cui-bg`, so anything that reads
the token sees the colour the class chose. A companion utility then reads it
back through an expression of its own:

```scss
$utilities: (
  "bg-opacity": (
    class: bg,
    property: background-color,
    values: theme-opacity-values(--#{$prefix}bg)
  )
);
```

```css
.bg-50 { background-color: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg) 50%, transparent); }
```

The two rules write the same property, so the order of the map decides: the
opacity family is declared after the colour family, and `.bg-primary.bg-50`
mixes the primary colour whichever order the classes appear in the attribute.
On its own, `.bg-50` reads a token nobody set, so the declaration is invalid at
computed-value time and the background stays as it was.

> Every custom property a utility assigns to is registered with
> `@property { inherits: false }`, so the value applies to the element that
> carries the class and does not leak into its descendants. A utility that
> deliberately writes an inheriting token — `.focus-ring-*` sets the global
> `--cui-focus-ring-color` — opts out with `at-property: false`.

### States

Use the `state` option to generate pseudo-class variations. Example pseudo-classes are `:hover` and `:focus`. When a list of states are provided, classnames are created for that pseudo-class. For example, to change opacity on hover, add `state: hover` and you'll get `.opacity-hover:hover` in your compiled CSS.

Need multiple pseudo-classes? Use a space-separated list of states: `state: hover focus`.

```scss
$utilities: (
  "opacity": (
    property: opacity,
    class: opacity,
    state: hover,
    values: (
      0: 0,
      25: .25,
      50: .5,
      75: .75,
      100: 1,
    )
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.opacity-0-hover:hover { opacity: 0; }
.opacity-25-hover:hover { opacity: .25; }
.opacity-50-hover:hover { opacity: .5; }
.opacity-75-hover:hover { opacity: .75; }
.opacity-100-hover:hover { opacity: 1; }
```

### Responsive

Add the `responsive` boolean to generate responsive utilities (e.g., `.opacity-md-25`) across [all breakpoints](https://coreui.io/react/docs/layout/breakpoints/).

```scss
$utilities: (
  "opacity": (
    property: opacity,
    responsive: true,
    values: (
      0: 0,
      25: .25,
      50: .5,
      75: .75,
      100: 1,
    )
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.opacity-0 { opacity: 0; }
.opacity-25 { opacity: .25; }
.opacity-50 { opacity: .5; }
.opacity-75 { opacity: .75; }
.opacity-100 { opacity: 1; }

@media (min-width: 576px) {
  .opacity-sm-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-sm-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-sm-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-sm-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-sm-100 { opacity: 1; }
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .opacity-md-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-md-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-md-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-md-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-md-100 { opacity: 1; }
}

@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .opacity-lg-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-lg-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-lg-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-lg-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-lg-100 { opacity: 1; }
}

@media (min-width: 1280px) {
  .opacity-xl-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-xl-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-xl-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-xl-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-xl-100 { opacity: 1; }
}

@media (min-width: 1536px) {
  .opacity-2xl-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-2xl-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-2xl-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-2xl-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-2xl-100 { opacity: 1; }
}
```

### Print

Enabling the `print` option will **also** generate utility classes for print, which are only applied within the `@media print { ... }` media query.

```scss
$utilities: (
  "opacity": (
    property: opacity,
    print: true,
    values: (
      0: 0,
      25: .25,
      50: .5,
      75: .75,
      100: 1,
    )
  )
);
```

Output:

```css
.opacity-0 { opacity: 0; }
.opacity-25 { opacity: .25; }
.opacity-50 { opacity: .5; }
.opacity-75 { opacity: .75; }
.opacity-100 { opacity: 1; }

@media print {
  .opacity-print-0 { opacity: 0; }
  .opacity-print-25 { opacity: .25; }
  .opacity-print-50 { opacity: .5; }
  .opacity-print-75 { opacity: .75; }
  .opacity-print-100 { opacity: 1; }
}
```

## Importance

Utilities carry no `!important`. They do not need it: the API emits them into the
`utilities` cascade layer, which is declared last, so every utility already wins
against every component and modifier class regardless of selector specificity.
See [cascade layers](https://coreui.io/bootstrap/docs/6.x/migration/v6/#cascade-layers) for the full order.

One case the suffix did cover is CSS of your own written **outside** any layer:
unlayered styles beat every layer, so a plain `.card-title { text-align: left }`
loaded after CoreUI wins over `.text-center`. Move that CSS into `@layer custom`
— the slot reserved for it, between components and helpers — and utilities win
again. There is no switch that brings the suffix back: the layer is the mechanism.
## Using the API

Now that you're familiar with how the utilities API works, learn how to add your own custom classes and modify our default utilities.

`$utilities` is a configurable variable of the `scss/utilities` module, so you change it with `@use ... with ()` rather than by reassigning it after an import. Two patterns cover every case:

- **One file** — configure `$utilities` where you load `@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui`. Use this to add a utility, replace one, or remove one.
- **Two files** — put the change in a partial that loads `@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities`, then load that partial before CoreUI. Use this when your change has to *read* the default definition: a new value on an existing group, a renamed class, or responsive variants on a group you keep.

Sass cannot read a module and configure the same module in one file, which is the whole reason the second pattern exists. In the partial, load the module with `as *` so `$utilities` needs no namespace prefix; assigning to it writes back into the module, and CoreUI picks the new map up when it loads.

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $utilities: (
    // Your utility groups go here
  )
);
```

Your map is merged over the defaults, and the merge is shallow: a group you supply replaces the whole default group under that key. Include `property` and `values` in every group that emits CSS.

For a utilities-only build, load the utilities module and then the API module, which emits the classes and nothing else:

```scss
// my-coreui-utilities.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" with (
  $utilities: (
    // Your utility groups go here
  )
);
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities/api";
```

### Override utilities

Override an existing utility by reusing its key. For example, to make the overflow utilities responsive and change their values:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $utilities: (
    "overflow": (
      property: overflow,
      responsive: true,
      values: visible hidden scroll auto,
    ),
  )
);
```

Your group replaces the default one, so keep the `property` key or the build stops with an error.

### Add utilities

Add a new utility the same way — supply only what is new:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $utilities: (
    "cursor": (
      property: cursor,
      class: cursor,
      responsive: true,
      values: auto pointer grab,
    ),
  )
);
```

### Modify utilities

Modifying a utility means reading its default definition first, so this needs the two-file pattern. Below we add another value to the `width` utilities:

```scss
// _my-utilities.scss
@use "sass:map";
// `as *` so `$utilities` needs no prefix, and assigning to it writes back
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    "width": map.merge(
      map.get($utilities, "width"),
      (
        values: map.merge(
          map.get(map.get($utilities, "width"), "values"),
          (10: 10%),
        ),
      ),
    ),
  )
);
```

Load your partial first, then CoreUI:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "my-utilities";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui";
```

#### Enable responsive

You can turn on responsive classes for a group that isn't responsive by default. This keeps the rest of the definition, so it takes the two-file pattern:

```scss
// _my-utilities.scss
@use "sass:map";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    "border": map.merge(
      map.get($utilities, "border"),
      (responsive: true),
    ),
  )
);
```

This will now generate responsive variations of `.border` and `.border-0` for each breakpoint. Your generated CSS will look like this:

```css
.border { ... }
.border-0 { ... }

@media (min-width: 576px) {
  .border-sm { ... }
  .border-sm-0 { ... }
}

@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .border-md { ... }
  .border-md-0 { ... }
}

@media (min-width: 1024px) {
  .border-lg { ... }
  .border-lg-0 { ... }
}

@media (min-width: 1280px) {
  .border-xl { ... }
  .border-xl-0 { ... }
}

@media (min-width: 1536px) {
  .border-2xl { ... }
  .border-2xl-0 { ... }
}
```

#### Rename utilities

Missing v4 utilities, or used to another naming convention? The utilities API can override the resulting `class` of a given utility — for example, to rename `.ms-*` back to `.ml-*`. It reads the default definition, so it takes the two-file pattern:

```scss
// _my-utilities.scss
@use "sass:map";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    "margin-start": map.merge(
      map.get($utilities, "margin-start"),
      (class: ml),
    ),
  )
);
```

### Remove utilities

Set a group to `null` to drop it:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $utilities: (
    "width": null,
  )
);
```

To switch one off while keeping its definition around — so you can read it, or turn it back on later — set `enabled: false` instead. That reads the default definition, so it takes the two-file pattern:

```scss
// _my-utilities.scss
@use "sass:map";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    "width": map.merge(map.get($utilities, "width"), (enabled: false)),
  )
);
```

### Add, remove, modify

Anything that only adds or removes goes in one file:

```scss
// my-coreui.scss
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/coreui" with (
  $utilities: (
    // Remove the `width` utility
    "width": null,

    // Add a new one
    "cursor": (
      property: cursor,
      class: cursor,
      responsive: true,
      values: auto pointer grab,
    ),
  )
);
```

As soon as one change has to read a default — making `border` responsive, say — the whole set moves into the partial:

```scss
// _my-utilities.scss
@use "sass:map";
@use "@coreui/coreui/scss/utilities" as *;

$utilities: map.merge(
  $utilities,
  (
    // Remove the `width` utility
    "width": null,

    // Make an existing utility responsive
    "border": map.merge(
      map.get($utilities, "border"),
      (responsive: true),
    ),

    // Add new utilities
    "cursor": (
      property: cursor,
      class: cursor,
      responsive: true,
      values: auto pointer grab,
    ),
  )
);
```

# React Aspect ratio Utilities

> Make an element hold an aspect ratio of your choosing. Perfect for responsively handling video or slideshow embeds based on the width of the parent.

## Example

Add an aspect ratio class to the element you want to size — an `<iframe>`, a `<video>`, an `<img>`, or a plain `<div>`. The class sets the CSS `aspect-ratio` property, so the element sizes itself; there is no wrapper to add and no child to position.

```html
<iframe className="w-100 ratio-16x9" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/zpOULjyy-n8?rel=0" title="YouTube video" allowFullScreen></iframe>
```

> **Pro-Tip!** You don't need `frameborder="0"` on your ``s as we override that for you in [Reboot](https://coreui.io/react/docs/content/reboot/).

## Aspect ratios

Swap the class for a different ratio. These come from the `$aspect-ratios` map:

```html
<div className="ratio-1x1">1x1</div>
<div className="ratio-4x3">4x3</div>
<div className="ratio-16x9">16x9</div>
<div className="ratio-21x9">21x9</div>
```

They pair with the [width utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/width/) — the ratio decides the height once the width is known.

## Custom ratios

The class sets `--cui-ratio` and a separate rule reads it, so a ratio the map does not name is an inline override away. Use `.ratio-auto` to opt in to the reading rule without picking a named ratio:

```html
<div className="w-25 ratio-auto" style={{ '--cui-ratio': '2 / 1' }}>
  2x1
</div>
```

Because it is a custom property, it can also change across breakpoints:

```scss
.ratio-4x3 {
  @include media-breakpoint-up(md) {
    --cui-ratio: 2 / 1;
  }
}
```

```html
<div className="ratio-4x3">4x3, then 2x1</div>
```

## Customizing

### Sass variables

Change the ratios you want to generate in the `$aspect-ratios` map.

```scss
$aspect-ratios: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$aspect-ratios: defaults(
  (
    "auto":  auto,
    "1x1":   #{"1 / 1"},
    "4x3":   #{"4 / 3"},
    "16x9":  #{"16 / 9"},
    "21x9":  #{"21 / 9"}
  ),
  $aspect-ratios
);
```

Aspect ratio utilities are declared in our utilities API in `scss/_utilities.scss`. [Learn how to use the utilities API.](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/api/#using-the-api)

```scss
// Two halves: `.ratio-*` sets the token, and any element carrying such a class reads
// it. Splitting them is what lets `--cui-ratio` be overridden inline for a
// ratio the map does not name.
"aspect-ratio-attr": (
  selector: "attr-includes",
  class: "ratio-",
  property: aspect-ratio,
  values: var(--cui-ratio)
),
"aspect-ratio": (
  property: --cui-ratio,
  class: ratio,
  values: $aspect-ratios
),
```

# React Align content Utilities

> Distribute the space between and around rows of a wrapped flex container.

## Align content

Use `align-content` utilities on flexbox containers to align flex items *together* on the cross axis. Choose from `start` (browser default), `end`, `center`, `between`, `around`, or `stretch`. To demonstrate these utilities, we've enforced `flex-wrap: wrap` and increased the number of flex items.

**Heads up!** This property has no effect on single rows of flex items.

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-start flex-wrap">
  ...
</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-end flex-wrap">...</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-center flex-wrap">...</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-between flex-wrap">...</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-around flex-wrap">...</div>
```

```jsx
<div className="d-flex align-content-stretch flex-wrap">...</div>
```

Responsive variations also exist for `align-content`.

- `.align-content-start`
- `.align-content-end`
- `.align-content-center`
- `.align-content-around`
- `.align-content-stretch`

- `.align-content-sm-end`
- `.align-content-sm-center`
- `.align-content-sm-around`
- `.align-content-sm-stretch`
- `.align-content-md-start`
- `.align-content-md-end`
- `.align-content-md-center`
- `.align-content-md-around`
- `.align-content-md-stretch`
- `.align-content-lg-start`
- `.align-content-lg-end`
- `.align-content-lg-center`
- `.align-content-lg-around`
- `.align-content-lg-stretch`
- `.align-content-xl-start`
- `.align-content-xl-end`

- `.align-content-2xl-stretch`

# React Background Utilities

> Convey meaning through `background-color` and add decoration with gradients.

## Background color

Similar to the contextual text color classes, set the background of an element to any contextual class. Background utilities **do not set `color`**, so in some cases you'll want to use `.fg-*` [color utilities](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/colors/).

Each theme color comes in three weights: the solid color, `.bg-muted-*` and `.bg-subtle-*`. The two lighter ones are surfaces to read text on, and `.fg-emphasis-*` is the color that reads on them — `.bg-muted-*` is the step you want when a subtle surface has to separate from a subtle surface behind it, which is what a hovered row or a selected item needs.

```html
<div className="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-${c.name}">.bg-${c.name}</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-muted-${c.name} fg-emphasis-${c.name}">.bg-muted-${c.name}</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-subtle-${c.name} fg-emphasis-${c.name}">.bg-subtle-${c.name}</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-body fg-body">.bg-body</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-black fg-white">.bg-black</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-white fg-black">.bg-white</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-transparent fg-body">.bg-transparent</div>
```

## Surface ladder

Five neutral surfaces run from the page background to the deepest panel. The numbers say how far a surface sits from the body — `.bg-1` is barely off the page, `.bg-4` is the deepest — and the ladder keeps its order in both color schemes.

```html
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-body">.bg-body</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-1">.bg-1</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-2">.bg-2</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-3">.bg-3</div>
<div className="p-4 mb-3 bg-4">.bg-4</div>
```

`.bg-body-secondary` and `.bg-body-tertiary` are deprecated names for `.bg-3` and `.bg-2` — they render identically and go away in v7. The ordinal names replace them because the old adjectives ran backwards for backgrounds: "tertiary" sat *closer* to the page than "secondary".

## Background gradient

By adding a `.bg-gradient` class, a linear gradient is added as background image to the backgrounds. This gradient starts with a semi-transparent white which fades out to the bottom.

Do you need a gradient in your custom CSS? Just add `background-image: var(gradient);`.

<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-primary bg-gradient">.bg-primary.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-secondary bg-gradient">.bg-secondary.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-success bg-gradient">.bg-success.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-danger bg-gradient">.bg-danger.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-warning bg-gradient">.bg-warning.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 text-bg-info bg-gradient">.bg-info.bg-gradient</div>
<div class="p-4 mb-3 bg-black bg-gradient fg-white">.bg-black.bg-gradient</div>

## Opacity

Every `.bg-*` utility writes its colour into `--cui-bg` and reads it back, so a companion `.bg-{percentage}` class can mix that colour with `transparent` through `color-mix()`, in the browser, without recompiling Sass.

```css
.bg-success {
  --cui-bg: var(--cui-success-bg);
  background-color: var(--cui-bg);
}

.bg-50 {
  background-color: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-bg) 50%, transparent);
}
```

Override `--cui-bg` to repaint the utility with another colour; the opacity class keeps working, because it reads whatever the token holds.

```html
<div className="text-bg-success p-3">This is default success background</div>
<div className="bg-success p-3 bg-90">This is 90% opacity success background</div>
<div className="bg-success p-3 bg-70">This is 70% opacity success background</div>
<div className="bg-success p-3 bg-50">This is 50% opacity success background</div>
<div className="bg-success p-3 bg-30">This is 30% opacity success background</div>
<div className="bg-success p-3 bg-10">This is 10% opacity success background</div>
```

`.bg-opacity-{10|15|25|50|75|100}` and `.bg-{color}-subtle` / `.bg-{color}-muted` are the deprecated v5 spellings of `.bg-{percentage}`, `.bg-subtle-{color}` and `.bg-muted-{color}`; they still render and are removed in v7.

## Customizing

In addition to the following Sass functionality, consider reading about our included [CSS custom properties](https://coreui.io/react/docs/customize/css-variables/) (aka CSS variables) for colors and more.

### Sass variables

Most `background-color` utilities are generated by our theme colors, reassigned from our generic color palette variables.

```scss
$primary: oklch(52.945% 0.19103 278.34) !default;
$success: oklch(55.1% 0.173 145) !default;
$info:    oklch(57.4% 0.196 256) !default;
$warning: oklch(84% 0.172 85) !default;
$danger:  oklch(58.7% 0.237 23.81) !default;
$gray:    oklch(60% 0.03948 265.02) !default;
```

### Sass maps

The surface ladder is one map: each key is one `.bg-{key}` utility and the `--cui-bg-{key}` token behind it, in light and dark mode. Add a key to add a rung, override one to retune it:

```scss
$theme-bgs: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$theme-bgs: defaults(
  (
    "body":        light-dark(var(--cui-white), var(--cui-gray-975)),
    "1":           light-dark(var(--cui-gray-025), var(--cui-gray-950)),
    "2":           light-dark(var(--cui-gray-050), var(--cui-gray-900)),
    "3":           light-dark(var(--cui-gray-100), var(--cui-gray-800)),
    "4":           light-dark(var(--cui-gray-200), var(--cui-gray-700)),
    "fg":          var(--cui-fg-body),
    "white":       var(--cui-white),
    "black":       var(--cui-black),
    "transparent": transparent,
    "inherit":     inherit,
  ),
  $theme-bgs
);
```

`.bg-{color}-subtle` and `.bg-{color}-muted` read the `bg-subtle` and `bg-muted` slot of every entry through `theme-color-refs()`, in light and dark mode.

Theme colors are then put into a Sass map so we can loop over them to generate our utilities, component modifiers, and more.

```scss
$theme-colors: () !default;
// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$theme-colors: defaults(
  (
    "primary": (
      "base":          var(--cui-primary-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-primary-600), var(--cui-primary-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-primary-800), var(--cui-primary-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-primary-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-primary-100), var(--cui-primary-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-primary-200), var(--cui-primary-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-primary-300), var(--cui-primary-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-primary-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "secondary": (
      "base":          var(--cui-gray-200),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-600), var(--cui-gray-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-gray-800), var(--cui-gray-200)),
      "bg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-100), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-gray-025), var(--cui-gray-800)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-050), var(--cui-gray-700)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-gray-300), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, light-dark(var(--cui-gray-500), var(--cui-gray-300)) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-white)),
    ),
    "success": (
      "base":          var(--cui-success-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-success-600), var(--cui-success-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-success-800), var(--cui-success-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-success-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-success-100), var(--cui-success-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-success-200), var(--cui-success-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-success-300), var(--cui-success-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-success-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "info": (
      "base":          var(--cui-info-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-info-700), var(--cui-info-300)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-info-800), var(--cui-info-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-info-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-info-100), var(--cui-info-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-info-200), var(--cui-info-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-info-300), var(--cui-info-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-info-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "warning": (
      "base":          var(--cui-warning-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-warning-700), var(--cui-warning-300)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-warning-800), var(--cui-warning-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-warning-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-warning-100), var(--cui-warning-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-warning-200), var(--cui-warning-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-warning-300), var(--cui-warning-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-warning-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-black),
    ),
    "danger": (
      "base":          var(--cui-danger-500),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-danger-600), var(--cui-danger-400)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-danger-800), var(--cui-danger-200)),
      "bg":            var(--cui-danger-500),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-danger-100), var(--cui-danger-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-danger-200), var(--cui-danger-800)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-danger-300), var(--cui-danger-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-danger-base) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      var(--cui-white),
    ),
    "inverse": (
      "base":          var(--cui-gray-900),
      "fg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-200)),
      "fg-emphasis":   light-dark(var(--cui-black), var(--cui-white)),
      "bg":            light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-100)),
      "bg-subtle":     light-dark(var(--cui-gray-100), var(--cui-gray-900)),
      "bg-muted":      light-dark(var(--cui-gray-200), var(--cui-gray-700)),
      "border":        light-dark(var(--cui-gray-400), var(--cui-gray-600)),
      "focus-ring":    color-mix(in oklch, light-dark(var(--cui-gray-900), var(--cui-gray-100)) calc(var(--cui-focus-ring-opacity) * 100%), transparent),
      "contrast":      light-dark(var(--cui-white), var(--cui-gray-900)),
    ),
  ),
  $theme-colors
);
```

Grayscale colors are also available as a Sass map. **This map is not used to generate any utilities.**

```scss
$grays: () !default;

// stylelint-disable-next-line scss/dollar-variable-default
$grays: defaults(
  (
    "025": gray("025"),
    "050": gray("050"),
    "100": gray("100"),
    "200": gray("200"),
    "300": gray("300"),
    "400": gray("400"),
    "500": gray("500"),
    "600": gray("600"),
    "700": gray("700"),
    "800": gray("800"),
    "900": gray("900"),
    "950": gray("950"),
    "975": gray("975")
  ),
  $grays
);
```

Background color opacities are applied through a map consumed by the utilities API, which mixes each color with `transparent` at the requested amount:

```scss
$utilities-bg-colors: map.merge(
  theme-color-refs("bg"),
  (
    "black": var(--cui-black),
    "white": var(--cui-white),
    "body": var(--cui-bg-body)
  )
) !default;

$utilities-bg-subtle: theme-color-refs("bg-subtle", "-subtle") !default;
$utilities-bg-muted: theme-color-refs("bg-muted", "-muted") !default;
```

### Sass mixins

**No mixins are used to generate our background utilities**, but we do have some additional mixins for other situations where you'd like to create your own gradients.

```scss
@mixin gradient-bg($color: null) {
  background-color: $color;

  @if $enable-gradients {
    background-image: var(--cui-gradient);
  }
}
```

```scss
// Horizontal gradient, from left to right
//
// Creates two color stops, start and end, by specifying a color and position for each color stop.
@mixin gradient-x($start-color: var(--cui-gray-700), $end-color: var(--cui-gray-800), $start-percent: 0%, $end-percent: 100%) {
  background-image: linear-gradient(to right, $start-color $start-percent, $end-color $end-percent);
}

// Vertical gradient, from top to bottom
//
// Creates two color stops, start and end, by specifying a color and position for each color stop.
@mixin gradient-y($start-color: var(--cui-gray-700), $end-color: var(--cui-gray-800), $start-percent: null, $end-percent: null) {
  background-image: linear-gradient(to bottom, $start-color $start-percent, $end-color $end-percent);
}

@mixin gradient-directional($start-color: var(--cui-gray-700), $end-color: var(--cui-gray-800), $deg: 45deg) {
  background-image: linear-gradient($deg, $start-color, $end-color);
}

@mixin gradient-x-three-colors($start-color: var(--cui-info-500), $mid-color: var(--cui-primary-500), $color-stop: 50%, $end-color: var(--cui-danger-500)) {
  background-image: linear-gradient(to right, $start-color, $mid-color $color-stop, $end-color);
}

@mixin gradient-y-three-colors($start-color: var(--cui-info-500), $mid-color: var(--cui-primary-500), $color-stop: 50%, $end-color: var(--cui-danger-500)) {
  background-image: linear-gradient($start-color, $mid-color $color-stop, $end-color);
}

@mixin gradient-radial($inner-color: var(--cui-gray-700), $outer-color: var(--cui-gray-800)) {
  background-image: radial-gradient(circle, $inner-color, $outer-color);
}

@mixin gradient-striped($color: color-mix(in oklch, var(--cui-white) 15%, transparent), $angle: 45deg) {
  background-image: linear-gradient($angle, $color 25%, transparent 25%, transparent 50%, $color 50%, $color 75%, transparent 75%, transparent);
}
```

### Utilities API

Background utilities are declared in our utilities API in `scss/_utilities.scss`. [Learn how to use the utilities API.](https://coreui.io/react/docs/utilities/api/#using-the-api)

```scss
"bg-color": (
  property: (
    --cui-bg: null,
    background-color: var(--cui-bg),
  ),
  class: bg,
  values: map.merge(
    map.merge($utilities-bg-colors, theme-token-refs($theme-bgs, "bg")),
    (
      "body-secondary": var(--cui-bg-3), // deprecated
      "body-tertiary": var(--cui-bg-2), // deprecated
    )
  )
),
"bg-color-subtle": (
  property: (
    --cui-bg: null,
    background-color: var(--cui-bg),
  ),
  class: bg-subtle,
  values: theme-color-refs("bg-subtle")
),
"bg-color-muted": (
  property: (
    --cui-bg: null,
    background-color: var(--cui-bg),
  ),
  class: bg-muted,
  values: theme-color-refs("bg-muted")
),
"bg-opacity": (
  class: bg,
  property: background-color,
  values: theme-opacity-values(--cui-bg)
),
// deprecated
"bg-color-subtle-legacy": (
  property: (
    --cui-bg: null,
    background-color: var(--cui-bg),
  ),
  class: bg,
  values: $utilities-bg-subtle
),
// deprecated
"bg-color-muted-legacy": (
  property: (
    --cui-bg: null,
    background-color: var(--cui-bg),
  ),
  class: bg,
  values: $utilities-bg-muted
),
// deprecated
"bg-opacity-legacy": (
  class: bg-opacity,
  property: background-color,
  values: theme-opacity-values(--cui-bg, null, (10: .1, 15: .15, 25: .25, 50: .5, 75: .75, 100: 1))
),
```
